title: 〜終わる
meaning: to finish doing (an action all the way through)
summary: 〜終わる attaches to the ます-stem of a verb to say you finish doing that action completely — 食べ終わる = finish eating, 読み終わる = finish reading. The whole compound conjugates like an ordinary る-verb (終わった, 終わって). Use it to mark the point where an action you are carrying out is done.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem, not the dictionary form: 書き終わる, not 書く終わる.
This compound is about finishing an action someone performs; when a situation ends on its own (会議が終わる = the meeting ends), 終わる is just an ordinary verb, not this stem-compound.

examples.ja: この本を読み終わったら、貸してあげます。
examples.en: Once I finish reading this book, I'll lend it to you.
examples.f: この｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]み｜終[お]わったら、｜貸[か]してあげます。

examples.ja: 手紙を書き終わって、ポストに入れました。
examples.en: I finished writing the letter and put it in the mailbox.
examples.f: ｜手紙[てがみ]を｜書[か]き｜終[お]わって、ポストに｜入[い]れました。

antonyms.note: 〜始める marks the start of an action; 〜終わる marks finishing it off.

related.note: 〜続ける keeps an action going; 〜終わる brings it to completion.
〜かけ・かける is an action left half-done; 〜終わる is one carried all the way to the end.

title: 〜がり
meaning: a person who readily feels ~; sensitive to ~ (personality trait)
summary: 〜がり turns a feeling-adjective into a noun for a person who is prone to feeling that way — 寒がり = someone who feels the cold easily, 寂しがり = someone who gets lonely easily. It describes a lasting personality trait, and often takes や on the end (寒がりや). The base is an adjective of emotion or sensation.
structure: い-adjective［stem, feeling word］＋ がり（や）
pitfalls: It pairs with adjectives of feeling or sensation (寒い, 怖い, 寂しい, 恥ずかしい), not with just any adjective.
Drop the final い before adding がり: 寒い → 寒がり, not 寒いがり.
It labels a habitual trait, not how someone feels at this moment; for 'I'm cold right now' just say 寒い.

examples.ja: 妹は寒がりで、冬はいつも厚いコートを着ています。
examples.en: My little sister feels the cold easily, so she always wears a thick coat in winter.
examples.f: ｜妹[いもうと]は｜寒[さむ]がりで、｜冬[ふゆ]はいつも｜厚[あつ]いコートを｜着[き]ています。

examples.ja: 彼は寂しがりだから、ひとりの時間が苦手です。
examples.en: He gets lonely easily, so he isn't good with time alone.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜寂[さび]しがりだから、ひとりの｜時間[じかん]が｜苦手[にがて]です。

synonyms.note: 怒りっぽい ('quick to anger') also builds a trait word, but from many kinds of base; 〜がり is limited to feeling-words and makes a noun.

related.note: 〜がち is about how often an event tends to happen; 〜がり is about a person's emotional make-up.

title: 〜出す
meaning: to suddenly start doing; to burst into (an action)
summary: 〜出す attaches to the ます-stem and marks the sudden, often unexpected start of an action — 泣き出す = burst into tears, 走り出す = break into a run. The nuance is that the action kicks off abruptly, not that you gently ease into it. The compound conjugates like a normal う-verb.
pitfalls: 〜出す stresses a sudden or spontaneous start; for a plain neutral 'begin to' with no abruptness, use 〜始める.
Attach it to the stem: 笑い出す, not 笑う出す.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが急に泣き出しました。
examples.en: The baby suddenly burst into tears.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんが｜急[きゅう]に｜泣[な]き｜出[だ]しました。

examples.ja: 私の話を聞いて、みんなが笑い出した。
examples.en: When they heard my story, everyone burst out laughing.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]の｜話[はなし]を｜聞[き]いて、みんなが｜笑[わら]い｜出[だ]した。

related.note: 〜始める is the neutral 'begin to'; 〜出す adds the sense of a sudden, abrupt onset.
〜出す marks an action starting; 〜終わる marks one finishing.

title: 〜続ける
meaning: to continue doing; to keep doing
summary: 〜続ける attaches to the ます-stem to say an action keeps going without stopping — 走り続ける = keep running, 待ち続ける = keep waiting. It focuses on carrying one action on and on. The compound conjugates like a る-verb (続けた, 続けて).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 読み続ける, not 読む続ける.
Keep 〜続ける (transitive, 'someone keeps doing') apart from 〜続く: use 続ける when a person keeps up the action, 続く when a situation goes on by itself.

examples.ja: 彼女は三時間も歌い続けました。
examples.en: She kept on singing for a full three hours.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜三[さん]｜時間[じかん]も｜歌[うた]い｜続[つづ]けました。

examples.ja: 医者になる夢を持ち続けています。
examples.en: I've kept holding onto my dream of becoming a doctor.
examples.f: ｜医者[いしゃ]になる｜夢[ゆめ]を｜持[も]ち｜続[つづ]けています。

antonyms.note: 〜続ける keeps an action going; 〜終わる ends it once it's done.

related.note: 〜始める marks the start of the action that 〜続ける then keeps going.

title: 〜づらい
meaning: hard to do (often uncomfortable or a strain for the doer)
summary: 〜づらい attaches to the ます-stem and means an action is hard or uncomfortable to do — often because doing it puts some strain or awkwardness on the speaker. 言いづらい = hard to bring myself to say; 歩きづらい = hard to walk. The compound behaves like an い-adjective (づらかった, づらくない).
pitfalls: 〜づらい often carries a sense that the difficulty is unpleasant or a burden on the doer; 〜にくい is more neutral and also fits purely objective difficulty.
Attach it to the stem: 読みづらい, not 読むづらい.

examples.ja: この字は小さくて読みづらいです。
examples.en: This writing is small and hard to read.
examples.f: この｜字[じ]は｜小[ちい]さくて｜読[よ]みづらいです。

examples.ja: 本当のことは、ちょっと言いづらいです。
examples.en: The truth is a little hard to bring myself to say.
examples.f: ｜本当[ほんとう]のことは、ちょっと｜言[い]いづらいです。

synonyms.note: 〜にくい is the neutral 'hard to'; 〜づらい adds that the difficulty is uncomfortable for the doer.
〜がたい is stronger — 'nearly impossible to' — and more formal or literary.

antonyms.note: 〜やすい means easy or comfortable to do — the opposite of 〜づらい.

title: 〜直す
meaning: to redo; to do (something) over again
summary: 〜直す attaches to the ます-stem to mean doing an action over again, usually to fix or improve the result — 書き直す = rewrite, 考え直す = reconsider, やり直す = start over. The idea is a fresh second attempt, not just repeating for its own sake. The compound conjugates like a う-verb.
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: やり直す, not やる直す.
On its own 直す means 'to fix or repair'; in this 'do over' meaning it must follow another verb's stem.

examples.ja: レポートを最初から書き直しました。
examples.en: I rewrote the report from the beginning.
examples.f: レポートを｜最初[さいしょ]から｜書き直[かきなお]しました。

examples.ja: もう一度考え直したほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You'd better think it over again.
examples.f: もう｜一度[いちど]｜考え直[かんがえなお]したほうがいいですよ。

related.note: Both follow a verb stem; 〜始める marks starting the action, 〜直す marks doing it over.

title: 〜にくい
meaning: difficult to do; hard to do
summary: 〜にくい attaches to the ます-stem and means an action is hard or troublesome to do — 食べにくい = hard to eat, 分かりにくい = hard to understand. It states the difficulty fairly neutrally and forms an い-adjective (にくかった, にくくない).
pitfalls: 〜にくい is the neutral 'hard to'; 〜づらい adds a nuance that the difficulty is unpleasant or a strain on the doer.
Attach it to the stem: 使いにくい, not 使うにくい.

examples.ja: このペンは書きにくいです。
examples.en: This pen is hard to write with.
examples.f: このペンは｜書[か]きにくいです。

examples.ja: 先生の説明は分かりにくかったです。
examples.en: The teacher's explanation was hard to understand.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]の｜説明[せつめい]は｜分[わ]かりにくかったです。

synonyms.note: 〜づらい also means 'hard to', but hints the difficulty is uncomfortable for the doer; 〜にくい stays neutral.
〜がたい is a stronger 'nearly impossible to', used in more formal or literary contexts.

antonyms.note: 〜やすい means easy to do — the direct opposite of 〜にくい.

title: 〜始める
meaning: to begin to do; to start doing
summary: 〜始める attaches to the ます-stem and marks the neutral beginning of an action — 食べ始める = start eating, 話し始める = start talking. It simply says the action gets underway, with no sense of suddenness. The compound conjugates like a る-verb (始めた, 始めて).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 読み始める, not 読む始める.
〜始める is a plain 'begin to'; for a sudden or unexpected start (burst into), use 〜出す instead.

examples.ja: 子どもが日本語を話し始めました。
examples.en: The child has started speaking Japanese.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもが｜日本語[にほんご]を｜話[はな]し｜始[はじ]めました。

examples.ja: 三月になって、桜が咲き始めた。
examples.en: March came, and the cherry blossoms began to bloom.
examples.f: ｜三月[さんがつ]になって、｜桜[さくら]が｜咲[さ]き｜始[はじ]めた。

synonyms.note: 〜出す also marks a start, but a sudden, abrupt one; 〜始める is the neutral choice.

antonyms.note: 〜始める marks starting an action; 〜終わる marks finishing it.

related.note: 〜続ける keeps going the action that 〜始める set in motion.

title: 〜やすい
meaning: easy to do; prone to (readily happens)
summary: 〜やすい attaches to the ます-stem and means an action is easy or comfortable to do — 食べやすい = easy to eat, 分かりやすい = easy to understand. It can also mean something readily happens (割れやすい = breaks easily). The compound conjugates like an い-adjective (やすかった, やすくない).
pitfalls: Attach it to the stem: 使いやすい, not 使うやすい.
The whole compound inflects as an い-adjective: past 〜やすかった, negative 〜やすくない.

examples.ja: このアプリはとても使いやすいです。
examples.en: This app is very easy to use.
examples.f: このアプリはとても｜使[つか]いやすいです。

examples.ja: 白いシャツは汚れやすいです。
examples.en: White shirts get dirty easily.
examples.f: ｜白[しろ]いシャツは｜汚[よご]れやすいです。

antonyms.note: 〜にくい is the neutral 'hard to' — the opposite of 〜やすい.
〜づらい is 'hard to (and uncomfortable)' — an opposite of 〜やすい with an added strain nuance.

title: ～化する
meaning: to turn into ~; to -ify; to become ~ized
summary: 〜化する attaches to a noun to mean turning into, or being turned into, that state — 国際化する = to internationalize, 悪化する = to worsen. The noun＋化 part is itself a noun (国際化 = internationalization), and adding する makes it a verb. It usually pairs with abstract, often two-kanji nouns and describes a shift into a new condition.
pitfalls: 〜化する attaches to nouns, not to verbs or adjectives.
Many 〜化 words describe large-scale or systemic change (society, systems, conditions); for a small everyday 'become', 〜になる is more natural than 〜化する.

examples.ja: 最近、この地域は少しずつ都市化しています。
examples.en: Lately this area has been gradually becoming more urbanized.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、この｜地域[ちいき]は｜少[すこ]しずつ｜都市[とし]｜化[か]しています。

examples.ja: パソコンで会社の仕事を自動化しました。
examples.en: We automated the company's work using computers.
examples.f: パソコンで｜会社[かいしゃ]の｜仕事[しごと]を｜自動[じどう]｜化[か]しました。

related.note: なる is the general 'become'; 〜化する is a heavier 'shift into (a state)', often abstract or systemic.
〜にする decides or makes something into a state deliberately; 〜化する describes the transformation itself.

title: ～代
summary: The suffix 〜代 after a round number of years marks a decade-wide age range — 20代 = someone in their twenties, 30代 = in their thirties. It groups people (or eras) into ten-year bands rather than naming a single exact age.
pitfalls: 〜代 gives a ten-year band (20代 covers 20 through 29), not an exact age; for an exact age use 〜歳 (20歳 = 20 years old).
Narrow the band with 前半 / 後半: 20代前半 = early twenties, 30代後半 = late thirties.

examples.ja: 母は50代ですが、とても若く見えます。
examples.en: My mother is in her fifties, but she looks very young.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]は50｜代[だい]ですが、とても｜若[わか]く｜見[み]えます。

examples.ja: この店の客は20代の女性が多いです。
examples.en: Most of this shop's customers are women in their twenties.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]の｜客[きゃく]は20｜代[だい]の｜女性[じょせい]が｜多[おお]いです。

title: ～て
summary: A bare て-form at the end of a sentence is a casual request — 'do this for me'. It is 〜てください with ください dropped, so 待って = wait (please), 見て = look. It sounds friendly but informal, so keep it for people you're close to.
pitfalls: This is casual: to a boss, teacher, or stranger, use 〜てください rather than a bare 〜て.
Don't confuse this sentence-final request 〜て with the connective て that links clauses (待って、電話します = wait and then call).

examples.ja: ちょっと待って。すぐ戻るから。
examples.en: Wait a sec. I'll be right back.
examples.f: ちょっと｜待[ま]って。すぐ｜戻[もど]るから。

examples.ja: ねえ、この写真を見て。
examples.en: Hey, look at this photo.
examples.f: ねえ、この｜写真[しゃしん]を｜見[み]て。

synonyms.note: 〜てください is the polite full form; a bare 〜て is its casual short version.

antonyms.note: 〜ないで is the casual negative request 'please don't'; 〜て is the positive 'please do'.

related.note: The same て-form links clauses mid-sentence; here it stands at the end as a request.

title: ～でも～でも
meaning: whether ~ or ~; both ~ and ~ alike (neither ~ nor ~ with a negative)
summary: Listing two nouns each with でも — 〜でも〜でも — presents them as an either-way pair: 'whether X or Y', 'both X and Y alike'. 肉でも魚でも食べます = I'll eat it whether it's meat or fish. It says the outcome holds no matter which of the two it is.
structure: Noun ＋ でも ＋ Noun ＋ でも
pitfalls: Each noun takes its own でも: 犬でも猫でも, not 犬でも猫.

With a negative ending it covers both alike as 'neither X nor Y': コーヒーでも紅茶でも飲みません = I drink neither coffee nor tea. For that plain 'neither' sense, 〜も〜も with a negative (コーヒーも紅茶も飲みません) is also common and often more natural.

examples.ja: 平日でも週末でも、いつでも来てください。
examples.en: Come anytime, whether it's a weekday or the weekend.
examples.f: ｜平日[へいじつ]でも｜週末[しゅうまつ]でも、いつでも｜来[き]てください。

examples.ja: 犬でも猫でも、動物なら何でも好きです。
examples.en: Dogs or cats — I like any animal at all.
examples.f: ｜犬[いぬ]でも｜猫[ねこ]でも、｜動物[どうぶつ]なら｜何[なに]でも｜好[す]きです。

synonyms.note: 〜なり〜なり also lists alternatives ('either X or Y'), but is more formal and often about choosing an action.

related.note: Single でも after one noun means 'even ~' or '~ or something'; doubled up it pairs two options as 'whether ~ or ~'.
〜や lists example items ('things like X and Y'); 〜でも〜でも frames two as an either-way pair.

title: ～ない～はない
meaning: there is no ~ that doesn't ~ (i.e. every ~ does)
summary: 〜ない〜はない stacks two negatives to make a strong positive: 'there is no X that does not ~' — meaning every X does. 読めない漢字はない = there's no kanji I can't read (= I can read them all). Use はない for things and はいない for people.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ Noun ＋ は ＋ ない／いない
pitfalls: The double negative flips to a strong affirmative: 'no X that doesn't ~' means 'all X do', so don't read it as a plain negative.
Pick the right existence verb: 〜人はいない for people, 〜ものはない for things.

examples.ja: あの店で買えないものはない。
examples.en: There's nothing you can't buy at that store — they have everything.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]で｜買[か]えないものはない。

examples.ja: 彼の名前を知らない人はいない。
examples.en: There's no one who doesn't know his name — everyone knows it.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]の｜名前[なまえ]を｜知[し]らない｜人[ひと]はいない。

title: ～ないで
summary: A ない-form plus で at the end of a sentence is a casual 'please don't' — 見ないで = don't look, 泣かないで = don't cry. It's 〜ないでください with ください dropped, so it stays friendly but informal. Keep it for friends and family.
pitfalls: Casual only: to someone you'd normally address politely, use 〜ないでください instead of a bare 〜ないで.
Build it on the ない-form: 来ないで (don't come), 食べないで (don't eat) — not on the dictionary form.

examples.ja: 心配しないで、大丈夫だから。
examples.en: Don't worry, it'll be fine.
examples.f: ｜心配[しんぱい]しないで、｜大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だから。

examples.ja: まだ入らないで。準備ができていないから。
examples.en: Don't come in yet. I'm not ready.
examples.f: まだ｜入[はい]らないで。｜準備[じゅんび]ができていないから。

synonyms.note: 〜ないでください is the polite full form; a bare 〜ないで is its casual short version.

antonyms.note: 〜て is the casual positive request 'please do'; 〜ないで is the negative 'please don't'.

related.note: 〜ないで also means 'without doing' inside a sentence (食べないで出かけた); the request use comes at the sentence end.

title: ～のだろうか
summary: 〜のだろうか expresses a thoughtful, often inward-directed 'I wonder...' — the speaker turning a question over in their own mind rather than asking someone. 本当にこれでいいのだろうか = I wonder if this is really okay. The の gives it a searching, reflective tone; だろうか is the musing question.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ のだろうか
pitfalls: It's reflective and a bit literary; in casual speech, かな or 〜のかな sound more natural for the same 'I wonder'.
After a noun or な-adjective, insert な: 学生なのだろうか, 静かなのだろうか — not 学生のだろうか.
The polite equivalent is 〜のでしょうか, common in careful or written questions.

examples.ja: 彼は本当のことを話しているのだろうか。
examples.en: I wonder if he's telling the truth.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜本当[ほんとう]のことを｜話[はな]しているのだろうか。

examples.ja: こんなに勉強して、試験に受かるのだろうか。
examples.en: I've studied this much — I wonder whether I'll pass the exam.
examples.f: こんなに｜勉強[べんきょう]して、｜試験[しけん]に｜受[う]かるのだろうか。

synonyms.note: かな is the casual, everyday 'I wonder'; 〜のだろうか is more reflective and literary.

related.note: だろう states a guess ('probably'); adding のか turns it into wondering about that guess.
〜のでしょうか is the polite version of this same musing question.

title: ～は～の一つだ
summary: 〜は〜の一つだ presents one thing as a member of a larger group — 'X is one of the Y'. 京都は人気のある町の一つだ = Kyoto is one of the popular cities. It's a simple, natural way to place something among many of its kind rather than singling it out as the only one.
structure: Noun［X］＋ は ＋ Noun［Y, group］＋ の一つだ
pitfalls: The group noun before 一つ is plural in sense, so a describing phrase usually comes first: 世界で一番大きい国の一つ = one of the biggest countries in the world.
一つ counts things; for people, use 〜の一人 (ひとり) instead — 優秀な学生の一人だ = one of the excellent students.

examples.ja: この公園は、町で最も美しい場所の一つです。
examples.en: This park is one of the most beautiful places in town.
examples.f: この｜公園[こうえん]は、｜町[まち]で｜最[もっと]も｜美[うつく]しい｜場所[ばしょ]の｜一[ひと]つです。

examples.ja: 彼は、クラスで最も背が高い学生のひとりです。
examples.en: He is one of the tallest students in the class.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は、クラスで｜最[もっと]も｜背[せ]が｜高[たか]い｜学生[がくせい]のひとりです。

related.note: 一番 singles out the one top item; 〜の一つだ instead places something among several of its kind.
の中で marks the group; 〜の一つだ picks out one member of that group.

title: ～風
summary: 〜風 after a noun means 'in the style of' or '-like' — 日本風 = Japanese-style, ヨーロッパ風 = European-style. It says something resembles or imitates that thing's manner or appearance, without necessarily being the real, authentic article.
pitfalls: In this 'style' meaning 〜風 is read ふう (和風 = わふう); don't read it かぜ ('wind') here.
It describes a resemblance or imitation, not the genuine thing: 日本風の料理 is food made in a Japanese style, which may not be authentically Japanese.

examples.ja: このカフェは昔風の作りで、とても落ち着きます。
examples.en: This cafe is built in an old-fashioned style and is very relaxing.
examples.f: このカフェは｜昔[むかし]｜風[ふう]の｜作[つく]りで、とても｜落ち着[おちつ]きます。

examples.ja: 母は今日、中華風のスープを作ってくれた。
examples.en: My mother made a Chinese-style soup for me today.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]は｜今日[きょう]、｜中華[ちゅうか]｜風[ふう]のスープを｜作[つく]ってくれた。

synonyms.note: 〜っぽい is a casual '-ish' about a quality something gives off; 〜風 is 'in the style/manner of'.

related.note: 〜らしい is 'typical of / befitting' the real thing; 〜風 is a made-to-resemble style, not the genuine article.
〜のようだ likens one thing to another ('like ~'); 〜風 fixes a style onto a noun.

title: ～ら
meaning: casual pluralizing suffix (僕ら = we, 彼ら = they)
summary: 〜ら is a casual pluralizing suffix attached to people-words and pronouns — 僕ら = we, 彼ら = they, 君ら = you (plural). It can also group demonstratives (これら = these). It sounds more informal and blunt than 〜たち.
pitfalls: 〜ら is casual and can sound rough attached to names or to others; the neutral, polite plural is 〜たち (子どもたち).
Pointing it at other people can feel dismissive (お前ら, あいつら), so use it with care.

examples.ja: 僕らは子どものころ、よくこの川で遊んだ。
examples.en: We often played in this river when we were kids.
examples.f: ｜僕[ぼく]らは｜子[こ]どものころ、よくこの｜川[かわ]で｜遊[あそ]んだ。

examples.ja: 彼らは来年、結婚するそうだ。
examples.en: They're apparently getting married next year.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]らは｜来年[らいねん]、｜結婚[けっこん]するそうだ。

title: 間
meaning: while; during; the whole time; between
summary: 間 marks a stretch of time and says the main action continues for that whole stretch. Whatever comes before 間 sets the period (母が寝ている間 = the whole time my mother is asleep), and the main clause holds true throughout it, running in parallel. It also has a spatial 'between' sense, but the everyday N4 use is this 'the whole time that ~' meaning.
pitfalls: 間 covers the entire period, so the main clause should also last the whole time (待っていた, 静かにしていた). If instead one thing happens at a single point inside the period, use 間に, not 間.
The verb before 間 is usually the ている form for an ongoing state: 食べている間, not 食べる間.

examples.ja: 夏休みのあいだ、毎日海で泳ぎました。
examples.en: During the summer holidays, I swam in the sea every day.
examples.f: ｜夏休[なつやす]みのあいだ、｜毎日[まいにち]｜海[うみ]で｜泳[およ]ぎました。

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが寝ているあいだ、私はずっと本を読んでいました。
examples.en: The whole time the baby was sleeping, I was reading a book.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんが｜寝[ね]ているあいだ、｜私[わたし]はずっと｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]んでいました。

related.note: 間に marks a point inside the period where one thing happens; 間 means the action lasts the entire period.
ながら links two actions by one person at once; 間 sets a period during which a separate action continues.
うちに (N3) stresses doing something before a period ends; 間 just spans the whole period.

title: 間に
summary: 間に sets a period of time and says the main action happens at some moment inside it, not across the whole thing. It is the 'catch the chance while ~' pattern: 出かけている間に電話が来た = a call came while I was out. The に pins the main event to a point within the period.
pitfalls: 間に = one event at a point inside the period; plain 間 (no に) = the main action lasts the whole period. 昼休みの間に食べた (ate at some point during the break) vs 昼休みの間ずっと食べていた (kept eating the whole break).
The main clause is usually a single, completed event (掃除した, 電話が来た), not a state that runs the whole time.

examples.ja: 昼休みのあいだに、少し買い物をしてきました。
examples.en: During the lunch break, I went and did a bit of shopping.
examples.f: ｜昼休[ひるやす]みのあいだに、｜少[すこ]し｜買い物[かいもの]をしてきました。

examples.ja: 母が出かけているあいだに、部屋をそうじしました。
examples.en: While my mother was out, I cleaned the room.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]が｜出[で]かけているあいだに、｜部屋[へや]をそうじしました。

related.note: 間 (no に) means the action fills the whole period; 間に pins it to a point inside.
うちに (N3) adds the nuance of acting before a chance is lost; 間に is neutral about that.
前に fixes the action just before the period starts; 間に places it somewhere within the period.

title: 後で
summary: 後で says one thing happens after another. Put the earlier action in the past (た) form before it (食べた後で = after eating), or a noun plus の (食事の後で = after the meal). On its own, 後で simply means 'later': 後で電話します = I'll call later.
pitfalls: Use the past (た) form before 後で even for future plans: 帰った後で, not 帰る後で.
後で just orders the two events in time. If you want to stress 'and only after that', 〜てから carries that 'once ~ is done' feeling more strongly.

examples.ja: 宿題をしたあとで、少しテレビを見ます。
examples.en: After I finish my homework, I'll watch a little TV.
examples.f: ｜宿題[しゅくだい]をしたあとで、｜少[すこ]しテレビを｜見[み]ます。

examples.ja: 昼ご飯のあとで、コーヒーを飲みませんか。
examples.en: Shall we have some coffee after lunch?
examples.f: ｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]のあとで、コーヒーを｜飲[の]みませんか。

synonyms.note: てから also means 'after doing', but emphasises that the second action waits until the first is finished.

antonyms.note: 前に is the opposite order — doing something before, where 後で is after.

related.note: とき marks 'when' something happens; 後で specifically means after it happens.

title: あまり～ない
summary: あまり teamed with a negative ending softens a 'no' into 'not very' or 'not much'. あまり sets up the expectation and the negative delivers it: あまり高くない = not very expensive, あまり食べない = doesn't eat much. In casual speech あまり often becomes あんまり.
structure: あまり ＋ い-adjective［くない］ ／ な-adjective［ではない］
pitfalls: あまり here must pair with a negative. Without a negative, 〜あまり means an excess ('so much that ~') — a completely different pattern.
It softens the statement to 'not very / not much'. For a flat 'not at all', use ぜんぜん〜ない instead.

examples.ja: この映画はあまり面白くなかったです。
examples.en: This movie wasn't very interesting.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]はあまり｜面白[おもしろ]くなかったです。

examples.ja: 最近、あまりテレビを見ません。
examples.en: Lately I don't watch much TV.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、あまりテレビを｜見[み]ません。

synonyms.note: ほとんど〜ない means 'hardly at all', a stronger denial than あまり〜ない's 'not very'.

antonyms.note: とても is the positive-degree opposite ('very'); あまり〜ない says 'not very'.

title: 以下
meaning: less than or equal to; and below
summary: 以下 attaches to a number or amount to mean 'that much or less'. It includes the number itself: 1000円以下 covers exactly 1000 yen and everything under it. Use it for prices, ages, quantities and any 'up to and including this line' cutoff.
pitfalls: 以下 includes the stated number: 12歳以下 counts a 12-year-old too. If you mean strictly under it (excluding the number), that is 未満.
以下 is the low side; do not mix it up with 以上 (that number and above).

examples.ja: この店の商品は、すべて1000円以下です。
examples.en: Everything in this shop is 1000 yen or less.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]の｜商品[しょうひん]は、すべて1000｜円[えん]｜以下[いか]です。

examples.ja: 12歳以下のお子さんは半額です。
examples.en: Children aged 12 and under are half price.
examples.f: 12｜歳[さい]｜以下[いか]のお｜子[こ]さんは｜半額[はんがく]です。

antonyms.note: 以上 is 'that number and above'; 以下 is 'that number and below'.

related.note: より marks a comparison point ('than'); 以下 gives a fixed upper cutoff that includes the number.

title: 以外
summary: 以外 attaches to a noun to carve out an exception: 'other than ~'. 日曜日以外 = every day except Sunday, 私以外 = everyone but me. It is often followed by は, に, or の (以外は, 以外に, 以外の).
pitfalls: 以外 (except, いがい) sounds exactly like 意外 (unexpected, いがい) but is a different word — watch the kanji.
以外 points at everything outside the named item, so the sentence usually then states what is true of that remainder (以外はみんな来た).

examples.ja: 水曜日以外は、家にいます。
examples.en: I'm home every day except Wednesday.
examples.f: ｜水曜日[すいようび]｜以外[いがい]は、｜家[いえ]にいます。

examples.ja: この問題は、私以外だれも分かりませんでした。
examples.en: Nobody but me could figure out this problem.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]は、｜私[わたし]｜以外[いがい]だれも｜分[わ]かりませんでした。

synonyms.note: ほかに asks/adds 'besides that'; 以外 excludes the named item and talks about the rest.

related.note: だけ limits things down to one item ('only'); 以外 does the reverse, pointing at everything but that item.

title: 意向形
summary: The volitional form is the plain 'let's ~' or 'I'll ~' ending — the casual counterpart of ましょう. For う-verbs, change the final -u sound to -ou (行く → 行こう); for る-verbs, drop る and add よう (食べる → 食べよう). It expresses a suggestion to a friend or your own resolve to do something.
structure: Verb［u-verb：〜う → 〜おう］（書く → 書こう）
Verb［ru-verb：〜る → 〜よう］（食べる → 食べよう）
する → しよう ／ 来る → こよう
pitfalls: This is the plain, casual form — fine among friends, but use ましょう to be polite.
It is a suggestion or personal resolve, not an order. To tell someone else to do something, you need a command or a request form, not the volitional.

examples.ja: 疲れたから、少し休もう。
examples.en: I'm tired, so let's take a short break.
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れたから、｜少[すこ]し｜休[やす]もう。

examples.ja: 今度の休みに、海へ行こう。
examples.en: Let's go to the sea on our next day off.
examples.f: ｜今度[こんど]の｜休[やす]みに、｜海[うみ]へ｜行[い]こう。

synonyms.note: ましょう is the polite version of this same 'let's ~'; the volitional is its plain form.

related.note: ようと思う adds と思う to the volitional to say 'I'm thinking of ~ing'.
つもり states a settled plan; the volitional voices a suggestion or on-the-spot resolve.

title: 以上
meaning: more than or equal to; and above
summary: 以上 attaches to a number or amount to mean 'that much or more'. It includes the number itself: 18歳以上 covers exactly 18 and everyone older. Use it for the 'this line and up' end of any range — ages, prices, counts.
pitfalls: 以上 includes the stated number: 20歳以上 counts a 20-year-old too.
以上 is the high side; 以下 is 'that number and below'. Don't swap them.

examples.ja: 18歳以上の人は、名前をここに書いてください。
examples.en: People aged 18 and over, please write your name here.
examples.f: 18｜歳[さい]｜以上[いじょう]の｜人[ひと]は、｜名前[なまえ]をここに｜書[か]いてください。

examples.ja: きのうのパーティーには20人以上来ました。
examples.en: 20 or more people came to yesterday's party.
examples.f: きのうのパーティーには20｜人[にん]｜以上[いじょう]｜来[き]ました。

antonyms.note: 以下 is 'that number and below'; 以上 is 'that number and above'.

related.note: より marks a comparison ('than'); 以上 gives a fixed lower cutoff that includes the number.

title: いたす
meaning: to do (humble form of する)
summary: いたす is the humble (kenjougo) verb for する. You use it to lower your own actions before someone you are being polite to, usually as いたします: 私がいたします = I'll do it. It also builds the humble お＋stem＋いたす pattern (お送りいたします), which is a notch more formal than お～する.
structure: ご ＋ Noun［する-verb］ ＋ いたす
pitfalls: いたす is humble, so it is only for your own or your group's actions. A respected person's 'doing' is なさる (honorific), never いたす.
It belongs to formal, polite speech (service, business). In casual conversation you just say する.

examples.ja: 受付では、私がご案内いたします。
examples.en: At the reception, I will show you the way.
examples.f: ｜受付[うけつけ]では、｜私[わたし]がご｜案内[あんない]いたします。

examples.ja: 書類は明日お送りいたします。
examples.en: I will send the documents tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜書類[しょるい]は｜明日[あした]お｜送[おく]りいたします。

synonyms.note: お～する is the general humble pattern; いたす is the humble する itself, and お～いたす is its more formal version.

related.note: いらっしゃる is honorific (raises the listener); いたす is humble (lowers yourself).
ございます is the polite form of ある/です; いたす is the humble form of する.

title: いらっしゃる
meaning: to be / to come / to go (honorific)
summary: いらっしゃる is the honorific (sonkeigo) verb covering いる (to be), 来る (to come) and 行く (to go). You use it to raise the actions of a customer, teacher or anyone you respect: 先生がいらっしゃる = the teacher is here / is coming. Its polite form is the irregular いらっしゃいます.
structure: いらっしゃる ＝ いる／来る／行く［honorific］
Verb［て form］ ＋ いらっしゃる
pitfalls: The polite form is いらっしゃいます, not the regular-looking いらっしゃります.
It is honorific, so it describes someone else's actions, not your own. For yourself use the humble おる (be) or まいる (come/go).

examples.ja: 先生は今、教室にいらっしゃいます。
examples.en: The teacher is in the classroom right now.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]は｜今[いま]、｜教室[きょうしつ]にいらっしゃいます。

examples.ja: 明日のパーティーにいらっしゃいますか。
examples.en: Will you be coming to tomorrow's party?
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]のパーティーにいらっしゃいますか。

antonyms.note: いたす humbly lowers your own actions; いらっしゃる honorifically raises someone else's.

related.note: お～になる makes ordinary verbs honorific; いらっしゃる is the ready-made honorific for いる/来る/行く.
ございます is a polite 'to be/exist'; いらっしゃる is the honorific 'to be' for people you respect.

title: お～ください
summary: お＋verb stem＋ください is a polished, honorific way to ask someone to do something — the kind of request you hear in shops and announcements. お待ちください = please wait; ご利用ください = please use. It is more respectful than the everyday 〜てください.
structure: ご ＋ Noun［する-verb］ ＋ ください
pitfalls: No する or して goes in the middle: it is お待ちください, not お待ちしてください.
する-verbs of Chinese origin usually take ご, not お: ご記入ください, ご注意ください.

examples.ja: 少々お待ちください。
examples.en: Please wait a moment.
examples.f: ｜少々[しょうしょう]お｜待[ま]ちください。

examples.ja: エレベーターをご利用ください。
examples.en: Please use the elevator.
examples.f: エレベーターをご｜利用[りよう]ください。

synonyms.note: 〜てください is the plain polite request; お～ください is the more honorific, formal version.

related.note: お～になる describes a respected person's action; お～ください asks them to perform one.
なさい is a firm command from a superior downward; お～ください is a respectful upward request.

title: お～する
summary: お＋verb stem＋する is the humble (kenjougo) pattern for your own action when it touches someone you respect. お持ちします = I'll carry it (for you); お送りします = I'll see you off. It lowers you to raise the other person. する-verbs of Chinese origin take ご instead: ご案内する.
pitfalls: It is humble, so the doer is you or your group — never use it for the listener's action (that would be お～になる).
Use the verb stem, not the dictionary form: お持ちします, not お持つします.

examples.ja: お荷物をお持ちします。
examples.en: I'll carry your luggage.
examples.f: お｜荷物[にもつ]をお｜持[も]ちします。

examples.ja: 駅まで車でお送りします。
examples.en: I'll drive you to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]まで｜車[くるま]でお｜送[おく]りします。

synonyms.note: お～いたす swaps する for the humble いたす — the same pattern, one step more formal.

antonyms.note: お～になる raises the other person's action; お～する humbly lowers your own.

related.note: お～ください asks the listener to act; お～する is you acting humbly for them.

title: お～になる
summary: お＋verb stem＋になる is the general honorific (sonkeigo) pattern for a respected person's action. お帰りになる = (they) go home; お書きになる = (they) write. It raises the subject, so you use it about a customer, boss or teacher — not about yourself.
structure: ご ＋ Noun［する-verb］ ＋ になる
pitfalls: It is honorific: it describes someone else's action. For your own action use the humble お～する.
Some verbs use a special honorific word instead of this pattern: 見る → ご覧になる, not お見になる.

examples.ja: 社長はもうお帰りになりました。
examples.en: The president has already left for home.
examples.f: ｜社長[しゃちょう]はもうお｜帰[かえ]りになりました。

examples.ja: 先生はこの本をお読みになりましたか。
examples.en: Did you read this book, sensei?
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]はこの｜本[ほん]をお｜読[よ]みになりましたか。

antonyms.note: お～する humbly lowers your own action; お～になる honorifically raises someone else's.

related.note: いらっしゃる is a ready-made honorific verb; お～になる turns ordinary verbs honorific.
お～ください requests an action; お～になる simply describes a respected person doing it.

title: おきに
summary: おきに follows a number-plus-counter to say something repeats with that gap left in between. 10分おきに = every ten minutes; 1日おきに = every other day. The idea is the space you leave between one occurrence and the next.
pitfalls: おきに names the gap left between times, so 1日おきに means every OTHER day (skipping a day), not every day. For 'every single day' use 1日ごとに.
It needs a counted interval in front of it; to say 'each (item)' generally, use ごとに or the prefix 各.

examples.ja: この電車は10分おきに来ます。
examples.en: This train comes every ten minutes.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は10｜分[ふん]おきに｜来[き]ます。

examples.ja: 花に1日おきに水をやっています。
examples.en: I water the flowers every other day.
examples.f: ｜花[はな]に1｜日[にち]おきに｜水[みず]をやっています。

related.note: ごとに counts every unit (毎回); おきに counts the gaps between, giving 'every other'.
各 is a prefix meaning 'each ~' on a noun; おきに measures a repeating interval.

title: かい
summary: かい is a casual sentence-ending particle that turns a plain statement into a friendly yes/no question. 元気かい = You doing okay? It sounds softer and warmer than a bare rising-intonation question, and carries a slightly older, masculine flavour, often used toward friends or children.
pitfalls: かい is for yes/no questions. Content (what/where/who) questions in this casual register take だい instead: 何をするんだい.
It is casual and has a familiar, masculine ring. In polite speech use the plain question particle か with です／ます.

examples.ja: 元気かい。
examples.en: You doing all right?
examples.f: ｜元気[げんき]かい。

examples.ja: もう昼ご飯は食べたのかい。
examples.en: Have you already had lunch?
examples.f: もう｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]は｜食[た]べたのかい。

related.note: か is the neutral, polite question particle; かい is its casual, friendly yes/no cousin.
かしら wonders to oneself; かい asks the listener directly.

title: かかる
summary: かかる says how much time or money something requires. The amount is the subject, marked with が (or は): 30分かかる = it takes 30 minutes, お金がかかる = it costs money. It is intransitive — the cost simply 'occurs' rather than being actively spent.
pitfalls: The amount of time or money takes が (or は), and かかる is intransitive: 時間がかかる, not 時間をかかる.
The transitive partner is 〜をかける ('to spend/apply'), for when you actively put time or money in.

examples.ja: 駅まで歩いて20分かかります。
examples.en: It takes 20 minutes to walk to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]まで｜歩[ある]いて20｜分[ふん]かかります。

examples.ja: 引っ越しには、お金がたくさんかかりました。
examples.en: The move cost a lot of money.
examples.f: ｜引っ越[ひっこ]しには、お｜金[かね]がたくさんかかりました。

related.note: くらい softens the amount to 'about'; it often pairs with かかる (30分くらいかかる).

title: 各～
summary: 各 is a prefix (read かく) that attaches straight to a noun to mean 'each' or 'every one of them': 各国 = each country, 各駅 = every station, 各自 = each person. It is a crisp, formal word common in announcements, signs and written notices.
pitfalls: 各 attaches directly to a noun (各国・各自・各駅) and belongs to formal or written style.
It does not attach to counted intervals. For 'every three days / every ten minutes', use ごとに or おきに, not 各.

examples.ja: この電車は各駅に止まります。
examples.en: This train stops at every station.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は｜各駅[かくえき]に｜止[と]まります。

examples.ja: 各自でお弁当を持ってきてください。
examples.en: Please each bring your own lunch.
examples.f: ｜各自[かくじ]でお｜弁当[べんとう]を｜持[も]ってきてください。

synonyms.note: ごとに follows a noun/count to mean 'each ~'; 各 is a prefix that sits in front of the noun.

related.note: おきに measures a repeating interval; 各 marks each member of a group.

title: かしら
summary: かしら is a sentence-ending particle for musing to yourself — 'I wonder ~'. 来るかしら = I wonder if they'll come. It attaches to the plain form and carries a soft, feminine tone in modern speech.
pitfalls: It sounds feminine. Men expressing the same 'I wonder' normally use かな.
な-adjectives and nouns drop the plain だ before it: 静かかしら, 学生かしら, not 静かだかしら.

examples.ja: 彼は本当に来るかしら。
examples.en: I wonder if he'll really come.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜本当[ほんとう]に｜来[く]るかしら。

examples.ja: この服、少し派手かしら。
examples.en: This outfit is a little flashy, isn't it — I wonder.
examples.f: この｜服[ふく]、｜少[すこ]し｜派手[はで]かしら。

synonyms.note: かな is the same 'I wonder', but neutral/masculine where かしら is feminine.

related.note: かい asks the listener a casual yes/no question; かしら wonders to oneself.
でしょう guesses with some confidence; かしら voices genuine, softer uncertainty.

title: がする
meaning: to give off / to sense (a smell, sound, taste)
summary: がする reports a sensation you pick up — a smell, sound, taste or feeling. The sensation noun takes が: においがする = there's a smell, 音がする = there's a sound, 味がする = it tastes (of something). Here する does not mean 'to do'; it means the sensation is present.
structure: Noun［におい／音／味／声 …］ ＋ が ＋ する
pitfalls: Mark the sensation with が, not を: においがする, not においをする.
This する is not the ordinary 'to do'. It is a fixed way of saying a sense-impression occurs, used with a limited set of nouns (smell, sound, taste, chill, feeling).

examples.ja: 台所から、いいにおいがします。
examples.en: A nice smell is drifting in from the kitchen.
examples.f: ｜台所[だいどころ]から、いいにおいがします。

examples.ja: さっき、外で大きな音がしました。
examples.en: A moment ago there was a loud noise outside.
examples.f: さっき、｜外[そと]で｜大[おお]きな｜音[おと]がしました。

related.note: する normally means 'to do'; in においがする it instead reports a sensation being present.

title: かどうか
summary: かどうか packs a yes/no question inside a bigger sentence, meaning 'whether (or not)'. You attach it to the plain form of a verb or い-adjective, and directly to a noun or な-adjective with no だ. The main clause then reacts to that embedded question — you don't know it, you'll check it, you'll decide it.
pitfalls: After a noun or な-adjective, drop だ: 本当かどうか, not 本当だかどうか.
かどうか is for yes/no questions. To embed a question with a question word (どこ・だれ・何), use 疑問詞＋か instead: どこにあるか分からない.

examples.ja: その話が本当かどうか、まだ分かりません。
examples.en: I don't know yet whether that story is true.
examples.f: その｜話[はなし]が｜本当[ほんとう]かどうか、まだ｜分[わ]かりません。

examples.ja: 彼がパーティーに来るかどうか、聞いてみます。
examples.en: I'll ask whether or not he's coming to the party.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]がパーティーに｜来[く]るかどうか、｜聞[き]いてみます。

related.note: 疑問詞＋か embeds a which/where/who question; かどうか embeds a plain yes/no one.
か alone marks a direct question; かどうか buries that question inside a larger sentence.

title: かな
summary: かな is a casual sentence-ender that shows you musing to yourself — 'I wonder...'. It sits after the plain form of a sentence and softens a statement into an open question you're turning over in your own head. Paired with a negative it can voice a quiet hope, as in 来ないかな (I wish they'd come).
pitfalls: かな is casual — keep it out of formal or polite speech, where でしょうか does the same job.
It expresses wondering to yourself, not asking the listener; for a real question to someone, use か or ですか.

examples.ja: 明日は晴れるかな。
examples.en: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜晴[は]れるかな。

examples.ja: この服、母は気に入ってくれるかな。
examples.en: I wonder if my mom will like these clothes.
examples.f: この｜服[ふく]、｜母[はは]は｜気に入[きにい]ってくれるかな。

synonyms.note: かしら carries the same 'I wonder', with a softer, traditionally feminine tone.

related.note: かもしれない states an actual possibility; かな just voices your wondering about it.
だろう leans toward a guess you half-expect; かな stays genuinely unsure.

title: が必要
summary: Noun＋が必要（だ／です）says that a thing is needed or necessary. 必要 is a な-adjective, and the thing required is marked with が, not を: パスポートが必要です = a passport is needed. It states what is called for in a situation without naming who must do anything.
structure: Noun ＋ が ＋ 必要 ＋ だ／です
pitfalls: Mark the needed thing with が, not を: お金が必要です, not お金を必要です.
が必要 says a thing is needed. To say you need to do an action, use the verb pattern 〜必要がある.

examples.ja: この仕事には英語が必要です。
examples.en: This job requires English.
examples.f: この｜仕事[しごと]には｜英語[えいご]が｜必要[ひつよう]です。

examples.ja: 旅行の前にビザが必要かどうか調べます。
examples.en: Before the trip I'll check whether a visa is needed.
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]の｜前[まえ]にビザが｜必要[ひつよう]かどうか｜調[しら]べます。

synonyms.note: 〜必要がある says you need to do an action; が必要 says a thing (noun) is needed.

related.note: 〜なければならない says you must do something; が必要 just states what is required.

title: が見られる
meaning: can be seen; can be viewed
summary: 見られる is the potential form of 見る: 'can see' or 'can watch', in the sense that the opportunity is there. With が marking what you're able to see, it fits places or events where a sight is available — 桜が見られる = you can see the cherry blossoms. It implies you get the chance to look, not that the view simply falls into your eyes.
pitfalls: 見られる = you have the chance/ability to see something; 見える = something is naturally within view without any effort.
The form 見られる is spelled the same as the passive 'be seen'; context tells the two apart.

examples.ja: 京都では古いお寺が見られます。
examples.en: In Kyoto you can see old temples.
examples.f: ｜京都[きょうと]では｜古[ふる]いお｜寺[てら]が｜見[み]られます。

examples.ja: 春になると、この公園できれいな桜が見られます。
examples.en: When spring comes, you can see beautiful cherry blossoms in this park.
examples.f: ｜春[はる]になると、この｜公園[こうえん]できれいな｜桜[さくら]が｜見[み]られます。

related.note: 見える is a sight coming into view on its own; 見られる is having the chance to view it.
聞こえる is the hearing counterpart — sound that reaches you spontaneously.
見られる is just the potential form of 見る built with 〜られる.

title: かもしれない
summary: かもしれない marks something as a real possibility — 'might' or 'perhaps'. It attaches to the plain form of verbs and い-adjectives, and to nouns and な-adjectives with no だ. The polite version is かもしれません. It signals genuine uncertainty, weaker than a confident guess.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ かもしれない
pitfalls: After a noun or な-adjective, drop だ: 病気かもしれない, not 病気だかもしれない.
かもしれない stays genuinely unsure. でしょう and だろう lean toward what you expect is likely, so they sound more confident.

examples.ja: 午後から雨が降るかもしれません。
examples.en: It might rain from the afternoon.
examples.f: ｜午後[ごご]から｜雨[あめ]が｜降[ふ]るかもしれません。

examples.ja: 彼はもう家に帰ったかもしれない。
examples.en: He may have already gone home.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はもう｜家[いえ]に｜帰[かえ]ったかもしれない。

related.note: だろう is a fairly confident guess; かもしれない admits it could easily be otherwise.
はずだ says you expect it on solid grounds; かもしれない is only a loose possibility.
かな just wonders out loud; かもしれない actually puts a possibility on the table.

title: から作る
meaning: to be made from (a raw material)
summary: Noun＋から作る／作られる describes making something out of a raw material that changes form in the process, so the original is no longer obvious in the product. 米から作る = made from rice. The passive 〜から作られる ('is made from') is common when stating what something is produced out of.
structure: Noun［material］＋ から ＋ 作る／作られる
pitfalls: Use から when the material is transformed and no longer recognizable (原料). Use で when the material stays visible in the product (材料): 木で作る = made of wood.
For 'is made from', the passive 作られる is natural: ワインはぶどうから作られます.

examples.ja: ワインはぶどうから作られます。
examples.en: Wine is made from grapes.
examples.f: ワインはぶどうから｜作[つく]られます。

examples.ja: チーズは牛乳から作られます。
examples.en: Cheese is made from milk.
examples.f: チーズは｜牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]から｜作[つく]られます。

synonyms.note: でできる・からできる also says 'is made from', using intransitive できる rather than 作る.

related.note: This is から's 'starting point' sense applied to the material a thing comes from.

title: がる・がっている
meaning: to show signs of; to seem to feel (someone else's emotion)
summary: がる attaches to the stem of feeling-adjectives (欲しい→欲しがる, 寂しい→寂しがる) and to 〜たい (食べたい→食べたがる) to describe someone else outwardly showing that feeling. がっている is the ongoing 'is showing it right now' form. It lets you talk about a third person's emotions, which you can only observe from the outside.
structure: い-adjective［stem］／〜たい［stem］＋ がる／がっている
pitfalls: Use がる for other people's feelings, not your own: 私は欲しい, but 彼は欲しがっている.
The wanted thing takes を with 欲しがる, not が: おもちゃを欲しがる, not おもちゃが欲しがる.

examples.ja: 子どもが新しいおもちゃを欲しがっています。
examples.en: The child wants a new toy.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもが｜新[あたら]しいおもちゃを｜欲[ほ]しがっています。

examples.ja: 弟は犬をとても怖がります。
examples.en: My little brother is really afraid of dogs.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜犬[いぬ]をとても｜怖[こわ]がります。

related.note: 〜たがる is this same がる on 〜たい, for someone else's wanting to do something.
欲しい states your own desire directly; 欲しがる reports someone else showing it.
〜がり labels a person prone to a feeling (寂しがり); がる describes them displaying it.

title: 聞こえる
summary: 聞こえる means a sound reaches your ears on its own, without you trying to listen — 'can hear' in the sense of 'is audible'. The sound is marked with が: 音が聞こえる. It's the hearing partner of 見える, and it's distinct from 聞ける, which is about having the chance or ability to listen to something on purpose.
pitfalls: 聞こえる = sound reaches you involuntarily; 聞ける = you get the chance/ability to listen on purpose (a concert, a recording).
Mark the sound with が, not を: 音が聞こえる, not 音を聞こえる.

examples.ja: 遠くから電車の音が聞こえます。
examples.en: I can hear the sound of a train in the distance.
examples.f: ｜遠[とお]くから｜電車[でんしゃ]の｜音[おと]が｜聞[き]こえます。

examples.ja: 隣の部屋から誰かの声が聞こえてきた。
examples.en: Someone's voice came through from the next room.
examples.f: ｜隣[となり]の｜部屋[へや]から｜誰[だれ]かの｜声[こえ]が｜聞[き]こえてきた。

related.note: 見える is the sight counterpart — something naturally coming into view.
聞ける is the plain potential 'can listen'; 聞こえる is sound reaching you on its own.

title: 疑問詞＋か
meaning: embedded question with a question word
summary: A question word (どこ・だれ・何・いつ・どう…) plus か wraps a wh-question into a noun-like clause that a larger sentence can act on: どこに行くか分からない = I don't know where to go. The main verb (know, ask, decide, tell…) then works on that embedded question. It's the wh-question partner of かどうか.
structure: 疑問詞（どこ・だれ・何…）＋ … ＋ か ＋ Verb
pitfalls: Before か, a noun or な-adjective drops だ: だれの本か分からない, not だれの本だか分からない.
Use this when there's a question word. For a yes/no question with no such word, switch to かどうか.

examples.ja: 彼がどこに住んでいるか知りません。
examples.en: I don't know where he lives.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]がどこに｜住[す]んでいるか｜知[し]りません。

examples.ja: 何を買うか、まだ決めていません。
examples.en: I haven't decided what to buy yet.
examples.f: ｜何[なに]を｜買[か]うか、まだ｜決[き]めていません。

related.note: かどうか embeds a yes/no question; 疑問詞＋か embeds a which/where/who one.
だれか・どこか use the same 疑問詞＋か shape to make indefinites (someone, somewhere).

title: く・に
summary: To describe how an action is done, adjectives take an adverb form. An い-adjective changes its final い to く (早い→早く), and a な-adjective adds に (静か→静かに). The result modifies a verb: 早く起きる = get up early, 静かに歩く = walk quietly.
pitfalls: い-adjectives use く, な-adjectives use に: 早く and 静かに, never 早に or 静かく.
いい is irregular: its adverb form is よく, not いく.

examples.ja: 今日は早く起きました。
examples.en: I got up early today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜早[はや]く｜起[お]きました。

examples.ja: 図書館では静かに話してください。
examples.en: Please speak quietly in the library.
examples.f: ｜図書館[としょかん]では｜静[しず]かに｜話[はな]してください。

related.note: 〜くする・〜にする uses the same く／に forms to make something become that way.
くは adds は to the 〜く adverb form for contrast, mostly in negatives.

title: くは
summary: Adding は to the adverbial 〜く form of an い-adjective sets that quality apart for contrast or partial denial, most often before a negative: 高くはない = it's not exactly expensive (as for being pricey, no). The は hints that while one thing may not hold, something else might — a softer, more qualified statement than the flat 〜くない.
structure: い-adjective［stem］＋ くは ＋ ない／ありません
pitfalls: 高くはない reads as a qualified 'not exactly expensive'; plain 高くない is a flat 'not expensive'.
This pattern almost always leads into a negative; a bare 安くは on its own sounds unfinished.

examples.ja: この店は安くはないが、料理はおいしい。
examples.en: This shop isn't exactly cheap, but the food is delicious.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜安[やす]くはないが、｜料理[りょうり]はおいしい。

examples.ja: 今日はそんなに寒くはありません。
examples.en: It's not all that cold today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]はそんなに｜寒[さむ]くはありません。

related.note: 〜く is the plain adverb form; くは adds は onto it to mark contrast.
〜くない is the flat negative; くはない adds a contrastive, hedging tone.

title: ございます
summary: ございます is a very polite equivalent of あります, used in formal and service settings to say something exists or is located somewhere. Paired with で it also forms でございます, the ultra-polite version of です. Staff use it toward customers; it sounds too formal for everyday chat.
structure: Noun ＋ が ＋ ございます
Noun ＋ で ＋ ございます
pitfalls: ございます is far more formal than あります — natural from shop staff, but stiff in casual conversation.
ございます states that things exist. For a person's existence in polite speech, use the honorific いらっしゃる instead.

examples.ja: お手洗いは二階にございます。
examples.en: The restroom is on the second floor.
examples.f: お｜手洗[てあら]いは｜二[に]｜階[かい]にございます。

examples.ja: 本日のおすすめは、こちらでございます。
examples.en: Today's recommendation is this one right here.
examples.f: ｜本日[ほんじつ]のおすすめは、こちらでございます。

synonyms.note: ある is the plain 'exist'; ございます is its very polite, formal-service form.

related.note: でございます is the copula side of this — an ultra-polite です.
いらっしゃる is the polite 'exist' for people; ございます is for things.

title: こと
meaning: nominalizer: turns a verb or clause into a noun
summary: こと turns a verb or a whole clause into a noun so it can act as a subject or object: 泳ぐこと = swimming, 早く寝ること = going to bed early. The verb stays in plain form right before こと. It's the tool for talking about actions and facts as things — hobbies, what's important, what you like.
pitfalls: Both こと and の nominalize; こと leans toward abstract facts and general statements, while の suits concrete, directly perceived actions.
Keep the verb in plain form before こと: 撮ること, not 撮りますこと.

examples.ja: 私の趣味は写真を撮ることです。
examples.en: My hobby is taking photographs.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]の｜趣味[しゅみ]は｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]ることです。

examples.ja: 毎日運動することは体にいいです。
examples.en: Exercising every day is good for your body.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜運動[うんどう]することは｜体[からだ]にいいです。

synonyms.note: の nominalizes too, but favors concrete, perceived actions; こと favors abstract facts.

related.note: ことができる is this こと plus ができる to express ability.
ことがある builds on this こと to say something happens on occasion.

title: ことがある
summary: With a verb in dictionary form, 〜ことがある says an action happens now and then — 'there are times when...'. 遅れることがある = the train is sometimes late. It describes occasional occurrence, and it's often paired with たまに or ときどき. Watch the tense: the past 〜たことがある means something completely different (past experience).
pitfalls: Dictionary form 〜ことがある = 'sometimes happens'; past 〜たことがある = 'have done before'. 食べることがある is 'I sometimes eat it', while 食べたことがある is 'I have eaten it'.
It states occasional events, so pairing it with たまに or ときどき reads naturally.

examples.ja: 朝、時間がなくて朝ご飯を食べないことがあります。
examples.en: In the morning there are times I skip breakfast because I'm out of time.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]、｜時間[じかん]がなくて｜朝[あさ]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べないことがあります。

examples.ja: この道はたまにとても混むことがある。
examples.en: This road sometimes gets very crowded.
examples.f: この｜道[みち]はたまにとても｜混[こ]むことがある。

related.note: 〜たことがある is the past-experience sibling ('have done'); this one is 'sometimes do'.
This pattern is the こと nominalizer plus がある ('there are occasions of').

title: ことができる
summary: Verb［dictionary form］＋ことができる expresses ability or possibility — 'can do'. 弾くことができる = can play. It means the same as the potential verb form (弾ける) but sounds a touch more formal and is common in writing and announcements. The verb before ことができる stays in plain dictionary form.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ ことができる
pitfalls: Keep the verb in dictionary form: 弾くことができる, not the potential 弾けることができる.
It's a little more formal than the plain potential form (弾ける), which is preferred in casual speech.

examples.ja: 田中さんはピアノを弾くことができます。
examples.en: Ms. Tanaka can play the piano.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんはピアノを｜弾[ひ]くことができます。

examples.ja: ここで写真を撮ることができますか。
examples.en: Can I take photos here?
examples.f: ここで｜写真[しゃしん]を｜撮[と]ることができますか。

synonyms.note: The potential verb form says the same 'can do' more casually; ことができる is a bit more formal.

related.note: This is the こと nominalizer plus ができる ('be possible').

title: ごとに
summary: ごとに means 'every' or 'each', attaching to a counter, a noun, or a dictionary-form verb. With a counter it marks a regular interval — 四年ごとに = every four years. With a verb it means 'each time...': 会うごとに = every time we meet. It picks out a repeating unit and says something holds for each one.
pitfalls: 三日ごとに means 'every three days' (a regular interval). Don't confuse it with 三日おきに, which leaves three-day gaps (every fourth day).
ごとに attaches freely to counters and verbs; まい (毎〜) instead prefixes set time-words like 毎日, 毎週.

examples.ja: オリンピックは四年ごとに開かれます。
examples.en: The Olympics are held every four years.
examples.f: オリンピックは｜四[よん]｜年[ねん]ごとに｜開[ひら]かれます。

examples.ja: 彼は会うごとに元気になっていく。
examples.en: Every time we meet, he seems more energetic.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜会[あ]うごとに｜元気[げんき]になっていく。

related.note: 〜に〜回 counts how often within a span (週に一回); ごとに marks the repeating unit itself.
〜おきに measures the gap between events; ごとに counts each event itself.

title: ことにする
summary: Verb［dictionary or ない form］＋ことにする marks a decision you make yourself. 走ることにする = I've decided to run; 飲まないことにする = I've decided not to drink. The past ことにした reports a decision already reached, and ことにしている describes a rule or habit you keep to on purpose.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことにする
pitfalls: ことにする is your own choice; ことになる is a decision made by circumstances or others.
ことにしている (ongoing) describes a habit you've resolved to keep, not a single fresh decision.

examples.ja: 来月から毎朝走ることにします。
examples.en: I've decided to run every morning from next month.
examples.f: ｜来月[らいげつ]から｜毎朝[まいあさ]｜走[はし]ることにします。

examples.ja: 今日はお酒を飲まないことにした。
examples.en: I decided not to drink today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]はお｜酒[さけ]を｜飲[の]まないことにした。

related.note: ことになる is when things get decided for you; ことにする is deciding yourself.
〜ようにする is making an ongoing effort toward a state; ことにする is a one-time decision.

title: ことになる
meaning: it has been decided that; it turns out that
summary: Verb［dictionary or ない form］＋ことになる says a decision or arrangement has come about, usually through circumstances or a group rather than your own will. 転勤することになった = it's been arranged that I'll transfer. Even when you were involved, it sounds more modest than ことにする. The form ことになっている describes a standing rule or fixed arrangement.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／［ない form］＋ ことになる
pitfalls: ことになる presents the decision as coming from circumstances or others; ことにする presents it as your own choice.
ことになっている (ongoing) states a standing rule or arrangement, not a new outcome.

examples.ja: 来月、大阪へ転勤することになりました。
examples.en: It's been decided that I'll transfer to Osaka next month.
examples.f: ｜来月[らいげつ]、｜大阪[おおさか]へ｜転勤[てんきん]することになりました。

examples.ja: 会議は来週に延期することになった。
examples.en: It's been decided to postpone the meeting to next week.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜来週[らいしゅう]に｜延期[えんき]することになった。

related.note: ことにする is a decision you make; ことになる is one that comes about around you.
ことになっている is the settled-rule form of this pattern.
〜ようになる is a gradual change reaching a state; ことになる is a decision being set.

title: 頃
summary: ころ／ごろ marks an approximate point in time — 'around'. Voiced ごろ attaches to a specific clock time or date (八時ごろ = around eight), while ころ follows periods or events (子どものころ = when I was a child). It pins down 'roughly when', not 'how long'.
pitfalls: ごろ is for a point in time (八時ごろ = around eight). For an approximate amount or duration, use くらい／ぐらい: 三時間ぐらい = about three hours.
Don't add に after ごろ when it already means 'around a time' — 八時ごろ会う is natural; 八時ごろに also occurs but the に is optional.

examples.ja: 明日は八時ごろ電話します。
examples.en: I'll call around eight tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜八[はち]｜時[じ]ごろ｜電話[でんわ]します。

examples.ja: 子どものころ、よくこの公園で遊びました。
examples.en: When I was a child, I often played in this park.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どものころ、よくこの｜公園[こうえん]で｜遊[あそ]びました。

related.note: くらい／ぐらい gives an approximate amount or degree; ごろ gives an approximate time point.
とき names the occasion 'when' something happens; ころ softens it to 'around the time'.

title: さ
meaning: -ness; turns an adjective into a noun of degree
summary: さ attaches to the stem of an adjective and turns the quality into a noun, usually one you can measure or compare: 高い → 高さ (height), 便利 → 便利さ (convenience). Reach for it when you want to talk about the degree of a quality — how deep, how important, how convenient something is.
pitfalls: Drop the い before adding さ: 高さ, never 高いさ.
さ tends to name a measurable degree; 〜み (as in 悲しみ) leans toward a felt, subjective quality and attaches to far fewer adjectives.

examples.ja: この川の深さを知っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know how deep this river is?
examples.f: この｜川[かわ]の｜深[ふか]さを｜知[し]っていますか。

examples.ja: 働いてみて、仕事の大変さがわかりました。
examples.en: After trying the job, I understood how tough work is.
examples.f: ｜働[はたら]いてみて、｜仕事[しごと]の｜大変[たいへん]さがわかりました。

synonyms.note: 〜み also nominalizes adjectives, but adds a subjective, felt flavor and works with a limited set of words.

related.note: の turns whole clauses into nouns; さ works only on adjective stems.

title: さすが
summary: さすが expresses admiration that someone or something lives up to its reputation: さすがプロだ = 'that's a pro for you'. As さすがに it can also mean that, given the circumstances, even a tough person or thing finally reaches a limit: さすがに疲れた = 'understandably, even I got tired'.
pitfalls: さすが before a person or thing is a compliment; さすがに before a clause usually signals 'given all that, even ~ finally...' rather than praise.
さすがの＋X＋も means 'even the (impressive) X' and pairs with something X could not manage: さすがの先生もわかりませんでした.

examples.ja: さすがプロですね。仕事がとても速いです。
examples.en: Just what you'd expect from a pro — the work is really fast.
examples.f: さすがプロですね。｜仕事[しごと]がとても｜速[はや]いです。

examples.ja: こんなにたくさん歩いて、さすがに疲れました。
examples.en: After walking this much, even I got tired, understandably.
examples.f: こんなにたくさん｜歩[ある]いて、さすがに｜疲[つか]れました。

related.note: 〜らしい says something is typical of its kind; さすが adds the speaker's open admiration.
だけあって (N1) also means 'true to its reputation', in a stiffer, more written register.

title: させてください
summary: させてください combines the causative with てください to ask permission politely: 使わせてください = 'please let me use it'. The speaker is the one who wants to act — you are asking the listener to allow it, not to do anything themselves.
structure: Verb［causative form: せる・させる → せて・させて］＋ ください
pitfalls: 〜てください asks the listener to act; 〜させてください asks the listener to let YOU act. 説明してください = 'please explain'; 説明させてください = 'please let me explain'.
In casual speech ください drops off: ちょっと休ませて.

examples.ja: すみません、この電話を使わせてください。
examples.en: Excuse me, please let me use this phone.
examples.f: すみません、この｜電話[でんわ]を｜使[つか]わせてください。

examples.ja: 今日は少し早く帰らせてください。
examples.en: Please let me go home a little early today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜少[すこ]し｜早[はや]く｜帰[かえ]らせてください。

synonyms.note: させてもらう also frames your action as permitted by someone; させてください is the direct request for that permission.

related.note: The causative せる・させる is the engine inside させてください.
〜てください requests the listener's action; 〜させてください requests permission for your own.

title: させられる
meaning: causative-passive: to be made to do
summary: させられる stacks the passive onto the causative to say the subject was made to do something by someone else, usually unwillingly: 食べさせられた = 'I was made to eat it'. The person who forces the action is marked with に.
structure: Godan verb［ない form: ない → せられる／される］
Ichidan verb［ない form: ない → させられる］
する → させられる ／ くる → こさせられる
pitfalls: The short form される is common with godan verbs (待たされる), but not when the verb ends in す: 話させられる, never 話さされる.
させられる carries a put-upon, 'against my will' nuance; if the arrangement was welcome, させてもらう fits better.

examples.ja: 子どものとき、母に野菜を食べさせられました。
examples.en: When I was a child, my mother made me eat vegetables.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どものとき、｜母[はは]に｜野菜[やさい]を｜食[た]べさせられました。

examples.ja: 友だちに駅で二時間も待たされました。
examples.en: My friend made me wait at the station for two whole hours.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちに｜駅[えき]で｜二[に]｜時間[じかん]も｜待[ま]たされました。

related.note: せる・させる is the plain causative; させられる shifts the viewpoint to the person who is forced.
られる alone is the plain passive; させられる adds that the action was compelled.

title: し
summary: し links clauses that each give a reason or supporting point, with the feeling that the list could go on: 安いし、おいしいし = 'it's cheap, it's tasty (and more besides)'. Attach it to the plain form; nouns and な-adjectives take だし.
pitfalls: し hints that the listed reasons are not the only ones; for a neutral, complete 'and' between clauses, the て form is enough.
Don't forget だ after nouns and な-adjectives: 雨だし, not 雨し.

examples.ja: この店は安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます。
examples.en: This place is cheap, and it's tasty, so I come here a lot.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜安[やす]いし、おいしいし、よく｜来[き]ます。

examples.ja: 今日は雨だし、家で映画を見ましょう。
examples.en: It's raining today, and all — let's watch a movie at home.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜雨[あめ]だし、｜家[いえ]で｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]ましょう。

related.note: から gives one explicit reason; し piles up several and implies there are more.
それに adds a further point as a separate sentence; し chains reasons inside one.
The て form lists actions neutrally, without the 'reasons, and more' flavor of し.

title: しか～ない
summary: しか follows a noun and pairs with a negative predicate to mean 'nothing but': 卵しかない = 'there's nothing but eggs'. Unlike だけ, it frames what remains as less than hoped or expected.
structure: Noun ＋ しか ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: The predicate must be negative: 百円しかありません, never 百円しかあります.
しか replaces が and を rather than stacking on them: 水しか飲みません, not 水をしか飲みません.

examples.ja: 冷蔵庫には卵しかありません。
examples.en: There's nothing but eggs in the fridge.
examples.f: ｜冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]には｜卵[たまご]しかありません。

examples.ja: 私はひらがなしか読めません。
examples.en: I can only read hiragana.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]はひらがなしか｜読[よ]めません。

synonyms.note: だけ states 'only' neutrally with an affirmative verb; しか〜ない adds a sense of insufficiency.

related.note: The same pattern applied to amounts: 三時間しか寝ていない.
だけしか combines both words for extra emphasis, still with a negative.
Verb＋しかない (N3) is a different point: 'there is no choice but to ~'.

title: じゃないか
meaning: isn't it?; hey, it's ~! (agreement or surprise)
summary: じゃないか tacks onto a statement to seek agreement or to voice surprise at something just noticed: 君の傘じゃないか = 'hey, isn't this your umbrella?'. Despite containing ない, it usually asserts the statement rather than negating it.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ じゃないか
pitfalls: It is casual and can sound blunt or reproachful; in polite speech soften it to じゃないですか or ではありませんか.
Context and intonation separate it from a real negative question: 学生じゃないか can be doubt ('isn't he a student?') or recognition ('hey, he's a student!').

examples.ja: これ、君の傘じゃないか。
examples.en: Hey, isn't this your umbrella?
examples.f: これ、｜君[きみ]の｜傘[かさ]じゃないか。

examples.ja: よくできたじゃないか。
examples.en: You did really well, didn't you!

synonyms.note: ではないか is the formal, written counterpart of the same assertion-question.

related.note: ね softly invites agreement; じゃないか pushes for it more forcefully.
じゃない (N5) is the plain negative that this pattern is built on.

title: 数字＋も
meaning: as many as ~; (with negative) not even one
summary: After a number plus counter, も signals that the speaker finds the amount remarkably large: 五杯も飲んだ = 'drank as many as five cups'. With 一＋counter and a negative verb it flips to total absence: 一つもない = 'not even one'.
structure: 一 ＋ Counter ＋ も ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: も after a number comments on size — it does not mean 'also'. コーヒーを五杯も飲んだ says the speaker feels five is a lot.
For 'not even one', the counter must be the 一 form and the verb negative: 一つも食べませんでした.

examples.ja: 昨日はコーヒーを五杯も飲みました。
examples.en: Yesterday I drank no fewer than five cups of coffee.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]はコーヒーを｜五[ご]｜杯[はい]も｜飲[の]みました。

examples.ja: 質問は一つもありませんでした。
examples.en: There wasn't a single question.
examples.f: ｜質問[しつもん]は｜一[ひと]つもありませんでした。

antonyms.note: 数量＋しか〜ない paints the amount as too small; 数字＋も paints it as strikingly large.

related.note: Plain も means 'also, too'; after numbers it becomes an amount-emphasizer.
少しも〜ない denies even a small degree, much as 一つも〜ない denies even one item.

title: 数量＋しか～ない
meaning: only ~ (an amount felt to be too little)
summary: しか〜ない after a quantity says you have no more than that amount, and that it feels insufficient: 五百円しかない = 'I've only got five hundred yen'. The verb must be negative even though the English comes out affirmative.
structure: Number ＋ Counter ＋ しか ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: The negative is grammatical, not semantic: 三時間しか寝ませんでした means you DID sleep — just only three hours.
だけ with the same number is a neutral report; しか〜ない adds the complaint that it isn't enough.

examples.ja: 財布に五百円しかありません。
examples.en: I only have five hundred yen in my wallet.
examples.f: ｜財布[さいふ]に｜五[ご]｜百[ひゃく]｜円[えん]しかありません。

examples.ja: 昨日は三時間しか寝ませんでした。
examples.en: I slept only three hours last night.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜三[さん]｜時間[じかん]しか｜寝[ね]ませんでした。

synonyms.note: 三時間だけ寝た reports the same amount without the 'not enough' feeling.

antonyms.note: 数字＋も stresses that the amount is impressively large — the opposite framing.

related.note: The parent pattern with plain nouns: 卵しかない.

title: 数量＋は
summary: は after a quantity marks it as a floor — 'at least that much': 二十分はかかる = 'it takes at least twenty minutes'. The speaker guesses the real figure is that big or bigger.
pitfalls: This is not the topic は: 五十人は来る doesn't topicalize 'fifty people', it estimates 'fifty at minimum'.
は doesn't work for 'at most' — for an upper limit use 数量＋しか〜ない or 多くても.

examples.ja: 駅まで歩いて二十分はかかります。
examples.en: It takes at least twenty minutes to walk to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]まで｜歩[ある]いて｜二[に]｜十[じゅう]｜分[ふん]はかかります。

examples.ja: パーティーには五十人は来ると思います。
examples.en: I think at least fifty people will come to the party.
examples.f: パーティーには｜五[ご]｜十[じゅう]｜人[にん]は｜来[く]ると｜思[おも]います。

related.note: The everyday topic marker は; after quantities は shifts to 'at least'.
数字＋も says the amount IS large; 数量＋は only sets a lower bound.
くらい gives a rough 'about'; 数量＋は commits to a minimum.

title: 少なくない
meaning: not a few; quite a lot
summary: 少なくない is the negative of 少ない used as understatement: by denying that something is few, it asserts there are actually quite a lot. It has a slightly written, objective tone, common in reports and opinion statements.
structure: Noun ＋ は／が ＋ 少なくない
pitfalls: It is deliberate understatement, not a neutral middle — 少なくない effectively claims 'many'.
Don't confuse it with 少しも〜ない ('not at all'), which negates degree, not quantity.

examples.ja: この町には古い家が少なくないです。
examples.en: There are quite a few old houses in this town.
examples.f: この｜町[まち]には｜古[ふる]い｜家[いえ]が｜少[すく]なくないです。

examples.ja: 朝ご飯を食べない学生は少なくないです。
examples.en: Quite a few students skip breakfast.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べない｜学生[がくせい]は｜少[すく]なくないです。

synonyms.note: たくさん says 'a lot' directly; 少なくない says it by understatement.

related.note: 〜くない is the plain い-adjective negative this expression is built from.

title: 少しも〜ない
meaning: not even a little; not at all
summary: 少しも teams up with a negative predicate to deny something down to the smallest degree: 少しも寒くない = 'it's not cold in the slightest'. It is emphatic — clearly stronger than あまり〜ない.
structure: 少しも ＋ Verb／い-adjective［ない form］
少しも ＋ な-adjective／Noun ＋ ではない
pitfalls: 少しも needs a negative to finish the thought: 少しも驚きませんでした is right; 少しも驚きました is wrong.

examples.ja: そのニュースを聞いても、少しも驚きませんでした。
examples.en: Even when I heard that news, I wasn't the least bit surprised.
examples.f: そのニュースを｜聞[き]いても、｜少[すこ]しも｜驚[おどろ]きませんでした。

examples.ja: 今日は少しも寒くないです。
examples.en: It's not even a little cold today.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜少[すこ]しも｜寒[さむ]くないです。

synonyms.note: 全然〜ない makes the same total denial and is more colloquial.
全く〜ない (N3) is a stiffer, more written 'not at all'.

related.note: あまり〜ない only says 'not much'; 少しも〜ない denies even a little.

title: せる・させる
meaning: causative: to make or let someone do
summary: せる・させる turns a verb causative: someone causes another person to act, whether by forcing ('make') or by allowing ('let'): 帰らせる = 'make/let someone go home'. The causer is the subject; the person who acts takes に with transitive verbs and usually を with intransitive ones.
structure: Godan verb［ない form: ない → せる］
Ichidan verb［ない form: ない → させる］
する → させる ／ くる → こさせる
pitfalls: Whether it means 'make' or 'let' comes from context, not the form — 休ませる can be forcing a rest or granting one.
Godan verbs take せる, not させる: 読ませる, never 読まさせる.
With intransitive verbs the actor is usually を (子どもを帰らせる); with transitive verbs the actor takes に, because を is already used by the object (妹に部屋をそうじさせる).

examples.ja: 母は妹に部屋のそうじをさせました。
examples.en: My mother made my little sister clean her room.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]は｜妹[いもうと]に｜部屋[へや]のそうじをさせました。

examples.ja: 先生は学生を少し早く帰らせました。
examples.en: The teacher let the students go home a little early.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]は｜学生[がくせい]を｜少[すこ]し｜早[はや]く｜帰[かえ]らせました。

related.note: させられる flips the viewpoint to the person who is made to act.
させてください uses the causative to ask permission for your own action.
られる is the plain passive; stacked on the causative it yields させられる.

title: 全然～ない
summary: 全然 in front of a negative predicate denies something completely: 全然読めない = 'can't read it at all'. It is the everyday, conversational way to make a negation total.
structure: 全然 ＋ な-adjective／Noun ＋ ではない
pitfalls: In casual speech 全然大丈夫 ('totally fine') is common, but in tests and careful writing 全然 pairs with a negative.
全然 denies completely; for a milder 'not very', use あまり〜ない.

examples.ja: 漢字が全然読めません。
examples.en: I can't read kanji at all.
examples.f: ｜漢字[かんじ]が｜全然[ぜんぜん]｜読[よ]めません。

examples.ja: このスープは全然熱くないです。
examples.en: This soup isn't hot at all.
examples.f: このスープは｜全然[ぜんぜん]｜熱[あつ]くないです。

synonyms.note: 少しも〜ない is an equally total denial, a touch more formal.
全く〜ない (N3) is the stiffer, more written 'not at all'.

related.note: あまり〜ない is partial ('not much'); 全然〜ない is total.

title: そういう
summary: そういう before a noun means 'that kind of ~', pointing at a type that has just come up in the conversation: そういう話 = 'a story like that'. It belongs to the こういう・そういう・ああいう・どういう family of kind-pointing words.
pitfalls: そういう points back at a kind already mentioned or understood; for something on your own side of the conversation use こういう.
そんな covers similar ground but often carries an emotional or dismissive shade (そんな話は信じない); そういう stays neutral.

examples.ja: そういう話は聞いたことがありません。
examples.en: I've never heard that kind of story.
examples.f: そういう｜話[はなし]は｜聞[き]いたことがありません。

examples.ja: 私もそういうかばんがほしいです。
examples.en: I'd like that kind of bag too.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]もそういうかばんがほしいです。

related.note: どんな asks 'what kind of'; そういう answers with 'that kind of'.
〜という spells out a noun's content; そういう points back at content already given.

title: そうだ
meaning: looks like; seems; about to (judged from appearance)
summary: This そうだ attaches to a verb stem or adjective stem and reports a guess from direct appearance: おいしそうだ = 'it looks tasty'. With verbs it often means something is on the verge of happening: 落ちそうだ = 'it's about to fall'. It conjugates like a な-adjective.
pitfalls: いい and ない are irregular: よさそう and なさそう, not いそう or なそう.
Appearance そう does not attach to plain nouns: for 'looks like a student' say 学生のようだ or 学生らしい, never 学生そうだ.
Keep it apart from hearsay そうだ, which follows the plain form: 落ちそうだ = 'about to fall'; 落ちるそうだ = 'I hear it will fall'.

examples.ja: テーブルからコップが落ちそうですよ。
examples.en: Careful — the cup looks like it's about to fall off the table.
examples.f: テーブルからコップが｜落[お]ちそうですよ。

examples.ja: このカレーはとてもおいしそうです。
examples.en: This curry looks really tasty.

synonyms.note: ようだ is a broader 'seems', drawing on any evidence; appearance そうだ is a snap judgment from what you see.
みたいだ is the casual cousin of ようだ and also takes nouns, which appearance そうだ cannot.

related.note: The homograph: hearsay そうだ follows the plain form and relays what you heard.
そうに・そうな are this same そう working as an adverb and a noun-modifier.

title: そうだ
meaning: I hear that ~; they say that ~ (hearsay)
summary: This そうだ follows the plain form of a whole statement and relays it as something you heard or read: 寒くなるそうだ = 'I hear it's going to get cold'. The source can be named with によると. It passes the information along as-is, without adding the speaker's own judgment.
pitfalls: Hearsay そうだ itself never changes form — put negation or past tense inside the reported clause instead: 来ないそうだ, 来たそうだ.
Attachment separates the twins: hearsay follows the plain form (寒くなるそうだ); appearance attaches to stems (寒そうだ).
Unlike らしい, hearsay そうだ adds no inference — it simply relays what was said.

examples.ja: ニュースによると、明日はとても寒くなるそうです。
examples.en: According to the news, it's going to get really cold tomorrow.
examples.f: ニュースによると、｜明日[あした]はとても｜寒[さむ]くなるそうです。

examples.ja: 田中さんは来月結婚するそうです。
examples.en: I hear Tanaka is getting married next month.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんは｜来月[らいげつ]｜結婚[けっこん]するそうです。

synonyms.note: 〜と聞いた states the same secondhand information as a plain 'I heard that ~'.
らしい can also relay reports, but mixes in the speaker's own inference.

related.note: The homograph: appearance そうだ attaches to stems and guesses from looks.
によると names the source that hearsay そうだ then quotes.

title: そうに・そうな
summary: The appearance そう conjugates like a な-adjective, so そうな can modify nouns and そうに can modify verbs: 高そうな時計 = 'an expensive-looking watch'; 楽しそうに遊ぶ = 'play in a way that looks fun'.
pitfalls: Only appearance そう has these forms — hearsay そうだ never becomes そうな or そうに.
そうな goes before a noun, そうに before a verb: 楽しそうな人 / 楽しそうに話す.

examples.ja: 子どもたちは楽しそうに遊んでいます。
examples.en: The kids are playing and look like they're having a great time.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもたちは｜楽[たの]しそうに｜遊[あそ]んでいます。

examples.ja: 彼は高そうな時計をしています。
examples.en: He's wearing an expensive-looking watch.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜高[たか]そうな｜時計[とけい]をしています。

related.note: そうだ is the predicate form; そうに・そうな are its adverbial and noun-modifying shapes.
ように・ような do the same job for ようだ, which covers likeness and examples rather than visual guesses.

title: それで
meaning: and so; because of that; so then?
summary: それで opens a sentence and links it to the previous one as its result: 熱があった。それで、休んだ = 'I had a fever. So I stayed home.' In conversation a bare それで？ nudges the other person to continue the story: 'and then?'.
pitfalls: それで states a natural result; commands and invitations tend to follow だから instead — だから早く来てください rather than それで早く来てください.

examples.ja: 昨日は熱がありました。それで、学校を休みました。
examples.en: I had a fever yesterday. That's why I stayed home from school.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜熱[ねつ]がありました。それで、｜学校[がっこう]を｜休[やす]みました。

examples.ja: へえ、それで、どうなりましたか。
examples.en: Wow — so then, what happened?

related.note: それから is plain time sequence ('after that'); それで is cause and result.
ので joins reason and result inside one sentence; それで links them across two.
そして simply continues the story; それで says the next part happened because of the last.

title: それでも
summary: それでも opens a sentence to say that, granting everything just stated, the result still went the other way. It concedes the previous fact and then pushes against it: 'even given that, ~ anyway.' Use it when an outcome defies what the earlier sentence would lead you to expect.
pitfalls: それでも concedes then contrasts ('even so'). Don't mix it up with それで, which draws a natural result ('and so') with no reversal.
It starts a fresh sentence. To link the two ideas inside one sentence, use 〜のに or 〜けど instead.

examples.ja: 彼は何度も失敗した。それでもあきらめなかった。
examples.en: He failed many times. Even so, he didn't give up.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜何[なん]｜度[ど]も｜失敗[しっぱい]した。それでもあきらめなかった。

examples.ja: この店は少し高い。それでも、いつも人でいっぱいだ。
examples.en: This shop is a little expensive. Even so, it's always full of people.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]は｜少[すこ]し｜高[たか]い。それでも、いつも｜人[ひと]でいっぱいだ。

synonyms.note: しかし is a plain 'however'; それでも adds 'even given that,' stressing the concession.

related.note: それで draws a natural result from the prior fact; それでも says the result went against it.
〜のに ties concession and result inside one sentence; それでも starts a new one.

title: それに
meaning: besides; moreover; on top of that
summary: それに opens a sentence to pile on an extra point that reinforces what you just said. Both ideas lean the same way — you add a further reason or advantage rather than turning against the first. It is the everyday way to say 'and besides, ~.'
pitfalls: それに adds a point in the same direction. For a contrast ('but even so'), switch to それでも or でも.
It often stacks a second reason onto a decision, so the two sentences should support each other.

examples.ja: この部屋は広い。それに、駅からとても近い。
examples.en: This room is spacious. Besides, it's very close to the station.
examples.f: この｜部屋[へや]は｜広[ひろ]い。それに、｜駅[えき]からとても｜近[ちか]い。

examples.ja: 今日は疲れた。それに、明日も朝が早い。
examples.en: I'm tired today. On top of that, I have to be up early tomorrow too.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜疲[つか]れた。それに、｜明日[あした]も｜朝[あさ]が｜早[はや]い。

synonyms.note: その上 is a slightly more formal 'on top of that'; それに is the everyday version.

related.note: そして simply joins two ideas; それに adds a reinforcing extra point.
それに piles on in the same direction; それでも turns against the previous point.

title: そんなに
summary: そんなに sets a degree at 'that much' — the amount just mentioned or shown by the person you're talking to. It very often teams with a negative to mean 'not that much / not so ~,' gently pushing back on an assumed level. Place it right before the verb or adjective.
pitfalls: With a negative, そんなに means 'not that much,' measured against a degree already in play — softer than a flat 'not at all.'
Keep そんなに (an adverb of degree) apart from そんな, which attaches to a noun to mean 'such a ~.'

examples.ja: そんなに急がなくてもいいですよ。
examples.en: You don't have to hurry that much.
examples.f: そんなに｜急[いそ]がなくてもいいですよ。

examples.ja: この問題はそんなに難しくない。
examples.en: This problem isn't that difficult.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]はそんなに｜難[むずか]しくない。

synonyms.note: あまり〜ない is 'not very'; そんなに〜ない is 'not that much,' pointing at an implied degree.

related.note: とても marks a high degree plainly; そんなに measures against an assumed 'that much.'

title: だが・ですが
summary: だが and ですが open a sentence with a contrast to what came before. だが is blunt and rather written or formal; ですが is its polite spoken counterpart, common for softening a disagreement. Both mean 'but / however' at the start of a new sentence.
pitfalls: だが sounds formal or curt; in polite conversation prefer ですが, or the casual でも／けど.
These begin a new sentence. To join a contrast within one sentence, use 〜が or 〜けど.

examples.ja: 彼に何度も電話した。だが、返事はなかった。
examples.en: I called him many times. But there was no reply.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]に｜何[なん]｜度[ど]も｜電話[でんわ]した。だが、｜返事[へんじ]はなかった。

examples.ja: 予約はしました。ですが、席が空いていませんでした。
examples.en: I did make a reservation. However, there were no seats free.
examples.f: ｜予約[よやく]はしました。ですが、｜席[せき]が｜空[あ]いていませんでした。

synonyms.note: しかし is the standard written 'however'; だが is blunter, ですが its polite spoken form.
でも is the casual sentence-initial 'but'; だが／ですが sound more formal.

related.note: けど joins a contrast inside a sentence; だが／ですが start a fresh one.

title: たがる
