meaning: to want to (of a third person, shown outwardly)
summary: たがる reports that someone else looks like they want to do something, judged from outside signs. It's built from the 〜たい stem plus がる, and conjugates like an u-verb. Use it for other people's desires; for your own, plain 〜たい is correct.
pitfalls: Use たがる for others' wants observed from outside; for your own desire say 〜たい (食べたい), not 食べたがる.
For a want happening right now, the ongoing 〜たがっている is usually more natural than plain 〜たがる.
たがる tends to take を for its object (お菓子を食べたがる), where 〜たい can also use が.

examples.ja: 弟はいつも外で遊びたがる。
examples.en: My little brother always wants to play outside.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]はいつも｜外[そと]で｜遊[あそ]びたがる。

examples.ja: 子どもはお菓子を食べたがっている。
examples.en: The child wants to eat some sweets.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもはお｜菓子[かし]を｜食[た]べたがっている。

synonyms.note: 〜がる makes an adjective of feeling into a third-person 'shows signs of'; たがる does the same for 〜たい.

related.note: 〜たい states your own desire; たがる reports someone else's, seen from outside.
〜が欲しい wants a thing; 〜たがる wants to do an action.

title: だけで
meaning: just by; just with; just from
summary: だけで means 'merely by ~' or 'with just ~.' The で marks the small means or cause, and the sentence usually notes that this little is enough to bring some notable result. Attach it to a dictionary-form verb or a noun.
pitfalls: だけで is 'just by/with,' not just 'only' — the で adds the sense of means or cause that plain だけ lacks.
After a verb, use the dictionary form directly: 見るだけで, not 見るのだけで.

examples.ja: あなたの声を聞くだけで、元気になる。
examples.en: Just by hearing your voice, I feel better.
examples.f: あなたの｜声[こえ]を｜聞[き]くだけで、｜元気[げんき]になる。

examples.ja: この一冊だけで、基本が分かります。
examples.en: With just this one book, you can understand the basics.
examples.f: この｜一[いち]｜冊[さつ]だけで、｜基本[きほん]が｜分[わ]かります。

synonyms.note: だけ alone means 'only'; だけで adds で to mean 'just by / with that much.'

related.note: だけで says 'merely by'; だけでなく says 'not only.'

title: だけでなく
summary: だけでなく says that the point isn't limited to the first item — a second one applies as well. The second item usually gets も ('also'). It joins both halves inside one sentence and sounds neutral, fitting both writing and everyday speech.
structure: Noun ＋ だけでなく ＋ Noun ＋ も
Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ だけでなく
pitfalls: The second item usually carries も: A だけでなく B も.
It's more neutral than the emphatic 〜ばかりでなく and more explicit than joining items with just 〜も.

examples.ja: 彼女は英語だけでなく、中国語も話せる。
examples.en: She can speak not only English but also Chinese.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜英語[えいご]だけでなく、｜中国[ちゅうごく]｜語[ご]も｜話[はな]せる。

examples.ja: この店はケーキだけでなく、パンも人気だ。
examples.en: At this shop, not only the cakes but also the bread is popular.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]はケーキだけでなく、パンも｜人気[にんき]だ。

synonyms.note: 〜ばかりでなく carries the same 'not only'; だけでなく is the more neutral, common choice.

related.note: だけで is 'just by'; だけでなく is 'not only.'
それに adds a point in a new sentence; だけでなく joins both inside one.

title: 他動詞・自動詞
summary: Japanese has many verb pairs: a 他動詞 (transitive), where someone acts on a thing marked with を, and a matching 自動詞 (intransitive), where the thing changes by itself and is marked with が. 開ける/開く, 閉める/閉まる, and 消す/消える are classic pairs you learn together.
pitfalls: The transitive verb takes を and needs a doer; the intransitive takes が and describes the thing changing on its own.
The pairs must be memorized: 始める/始まる, 出す/出る, 入れる/入る don't follow one fixed rule.
For a resulting state, use intransitive ＋ ている (ドアが開いている) or transitive ＋ てある (ドアが開けてある).

examples.ja: 私は電気を消した。
examples.en: I turned off the light.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜電気[でんき]を｜消[け]した。

examples.ja: 急に電気が消えた。
examples.en: The light suddenly went out.
examples.f: ｜急[きゅう]に｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えた。

related.note: 〜てある pairs with a transitive verb to show a state someone set up on purpose.
〜ている with an intransitive verb shows the state that resulted.
The passive also drops the doer, but reshapes を→が differently from an intransitive pair.

title: 例えば
summary: 例えば introduces a concrete example of a general statement, usually followed by a pause. After stating something broad, you use 例えば to name a specific case that illustrates it. It often teams up with listing words like 〜や, 〜とか, or 〜など.
pitfalls: 例えば announces that an example is coming; it usually takes a comma-length pause after it.
It pairs naturally with 〜など／〜とか, which follow the examples themselves.

examples.ja: 果物が好きです。例えば、りんごやみかんです。
examples.en: I like fruit. For example, apples and oranges.
examples.f: ｜果物[くだもの]が｜好[す]きです。｜例[たと]えば、りんごやみかんです。

examples.ja: 例えば、朝早く起きて散歩するのはどうですか。
examples.en: For example, how about getting up early and taking a walk?
examples.f: ｜例[たと]えば、｜朝[あさ]｜早[はや]く｜起[お]きて｜散歩[さんぽ]するのはどうですか。

related.note: など follows the examples that 例えば introduces.
〜とか lists casual examples; 例えば announces that one is coming.

title: たところ
meaning: have just finished doing (this very moment)
summary: Verb［た form］＋ ところ marks an action that finished a moment ago — you are right at the point just after it. It pins the event to the immediate present on a timeline, so it fits sentences like 'I just this second arrived.'
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ところ（だ／です）
pitfalls: 〜たところ is the moment just after finishing; 〜ているところ is the middle of doing, and 〜るところ is about to start.
Compared with 〜たばかり, 〜たところ points to the exact moment, while 〜たばかり just feels 'not long ago.'

examples.ja: 今、駅に着いたところです。
examples.en: I've just arrived at the station right now.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]、｜駅[えき]に｜着[つ]いたところです。

examples.ja: ご飯を食べたところだから、おなかがいっぱいだ。
examples.en: I just finished eating, so I'm full.
examples.f: ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べたところだから、おなかがいっぱいだ。

synonyms.note: 〜たばかり also means 'just did,' but stresses little time has passed rather than the exact moment.

related.note: 〜ているところ is in the middle of doing; 〜たところ is the moment just after finishing.
〜るところ is about to do; 〜たところ has just done.

title: たばかり
summary: Verb［た form］＋ ばかり says an action happened only a short while ago. The 'short while' is how the speaker feels — it can be minutes or, loosely, even longer, as long as it seems recent. Use it to explain that you're still new to or fresh from something.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ばかり（だ／です）
pitfalls: 〜たばかり is subjective 'not long ago,' while 〜たところ marks the exact moment right after finishing.
Don't confuse it with 〜てばかり, which means 'do nothing but ~.'

examples.ja: この会社に入ったばかりで、まだ分からないことが多い。
examples.en: I just joined this company, so there's still a lot I don't know.
examples.f: この｜会社[かいしゃ]に｜入[はい]ったばかりで、まだ｜分[わ]からないことが｜多[おお]い。

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんは生まれたばかりだ。
examples.en: The baby was only just born.
examples.f: ｜赤[あか]ちゃんは｜生[う]まれたばかりだ。

synonyms.note: 〜たところ marks the exact moment of finishing; 〜たばかり feels 'not long ago,' even loosely.

related.note: ばかり on its own means 'only / nothing but'; 〜たばかり means 'just did.'

title: たら
summary: 〜たら is the everyday conditional: take the plain past (た form) and add ら. Depending on context it means 'if ~,' 'when ~,' or 'after ~.' Its big strength is that the main clause can be a request, command, or wish, which many other conditionals block.
pitfalls: 〜たら covers both 'if' (hypothetical) and 'when/after' (sure to happen); context decides which.
Unlike 〜と, the main clause may be a request or command: 家に着いたら、電話してください.
Past ＋ 〜たら ＋ past can report a discovery: 窓を開けたら、雨が降っていた ('when I opened the window, it was raining').

examples.ja: 家に着いたら、電話します。
examples.en: When I get home, I'll call you.
examples.f: ｜家[いえ]に｜着[つ]いたら、｜電話[でんわ]します。

examples.ja: 安かったら、買います。
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.f: ｜安[やす]かったら、｜買[か]います。

synonyms.note: 〜ば is a more formal 'if'; 〜たら is the everyday conditional and also means 'when/after.'
〜と is for automatic, always-true results; 〜たら allows requests and one-off cases.
〜なら responds to a supposition someone raised; 〜たら sets up your own condition.

related.note: 〜たらどう suggests 'why don't you,' built on the 〜たら conditional.

title: たらいいですか
summary: 〜たらいいですか asks someone for instructions: 'what should I do?' It pairs a question word (何・どこ・どう…) with the 〜たら conditional plus いいですか, literally 'would it be good if I ~?' Use it to politely request guidance on the right course of action.
structure: 疑問詞（何／どこ／どう…）＋ Verb［た form］＋ ら ＋ いいですか
pitfalls: It needs a question word to work: 何をしたらいいですか, どこに行けば… — without one it just states a condition.
For a softer, more tentative feel, 〜たらいいでしょうか is common; the casual form is 〜たらいい？

examples.ja: この書類はどこに出したらいいですか。
examples.en: Where should I submit these documents?
examples.f: この｜書類[しょるい]はどこに｜出[だ]したらいいですか。

examples.ja: 旅行の前に何を準備したらいいですか。
examples.en: What should I prepare before the trip?
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]の｜前[まえ]に｜何[なに]を｜準備[じゅんび]したらいいですか。

synonyms.note: 〜ばいいですか asks the same 'what should I,' using 〜ば instead of 〜たら.

related.note: The conditional 〜たら underlies this fixed question pattern.
〜たらどう gives a suggestion; 〜たらいいですか asks for one.

title: たらどう
summary: 〜たらどう offers a suggestion to the listener: 'why don't you ~?' The どう is short for どうですか ('how would it be?'), attached to the 〜たら conditional. Use it to gently recommend that the other person try something.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ら ＋ どう（ですか）
pitfalls: It advises the other person, not yourself; you can't use it about your own actions.
Said bluntly it can sound pushy or critical, so soften it with どうですか or a caring tone.

examples.ja: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらどうですか。
examples.en: If you're tired, why don't you rest a little?
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れているなら、｜少[すこ]し｜休[やす]んだらどうですか。

examples.ja: 一度、医者に相談してみたらどう。
examples.en: How about consulting a doctor once?
examples.f: ｜一度[いちど]、｜医者[いしゃ]に｜相談[そうだん]してみたらどう。

synonyms.note: 〜ほうがいい recommends one choice over another; 〜たらどう floats a suggestion more gently.

related.note: 〜たらどう offers advice; 〜たらいいですか asks for it.
The conditional 〜たら is the base of this suggestion pattern.

title: だんだん
summary: だんだん describes a change that happens slowly and steadily over time. It sits before the verb and pairs naturally with verbs of change like 〜なる, 〜くなる, and 〜てくる／〜ていく. Reach for it when something shifts bit by bit, such as the weather warming up.
structure: だんだん ＋ Verb（〜なる／〜くなる…）
pitfalls: だんだん is a slow, steady 'gradually'; どんどん is faster and more vigorous, 'more and more.'
It teams up with change verbs; a one-time action ('I suddenly stood up') needs a different adverb.

examples.ja: 春になって、だんだん暖かくなってきた。
examples.en: Spring has come, and it's gradually getting warmer.
examples.f: ｜春[はる]になって、だんだん｜暖[あたた]かくなってきた。

examples.ja: 毎日練習して、だんだん上手になった。
examples.en: I practiced every day and gradually got better.
examples.f: ｜毎日[まいにち]｜練習[れんしゅう]して、だんだん｜上手[じょうず]になった。

synonyms.note: 次第に is a more formal 'gradually'; だんだん is the everyday word.

related.note: どんどん is fast, vigorous 'more and more'; だんだん is slow and steady.
だんだん often teams with なる to describe a gradual change of state.

title: って感じ
meaning: the vibe of ~; kind of like ~
summary: って感じ is casual speech for 'the feeling/vibe of ~.' The って is the colloquial quoting particle and 感じ means 'impression,' so together they wrap up a mood or a rough impression. It often trails off at the end of a thought or adds がする.
structure: Noun／Sentence［plain form］＋ って感じ（だ／がする）
pitfalls: It's very casual — avoid it in polite speech or formal writing.
って here is the spoken quotative; 感じ is 'impression,' so the whole thing gives a loose 'sort of like ~' feel.

examples.ja: もう疲れて、何もしたくないって感じ。
examples.en: I'm worn out now, kind of like I don't want to do anything.
examples.f: もう｜疲[つか]れて、｜何[なに]もしたくないって｜感[かん]じ。

examples.ja: 今日の映画は、まあまあかなって感じだった。
examples.en: Today's movie was like, so-so, I guess.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]の｜映画[えいが]は、まあまあかなって｜感[かん]じだった。

synonyms.note: 〜みたい also gives an impression ('seems like'); って感じ is looser, spoken slang.

related.note: って is the casual quoting particle used inside って感じ.
〜ようだ states an impression formally; って感じ is its casual cousin.

title: て・で
summary: The verb て-form links clauses together: it can list actions in order ('do A, and then B') or give a light reason ('B because A'). The voiced で appears with certain verbs (読んで, 遊んで). The final verb carries the tense — the て-form itself stays tense-neutral.
pitfalls: The て-form has no tense of its own; the last verb decides past or non-past for the whole sentence.
For a strong 'because,' use から／ので; the て-cause fits best when the result is an emotion or natural outcome (聞いて驚いた).
Some verbs voice the ending to で: 読んで, 飲んで, 遊んで — never 読んて.

examples.ja: 朝起きて、顔を洗った。
examples.en: I got up in the morning and washed my face.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]｜起[お]きて、｜顔[かお]を｜洗[あら]った。

examples.ja: 友だちからの手紙を読んで、うれしくなった。
examples.en: I read the letter from my friend and felt happy.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちからの｜手紙[てがみ]を｜読[よ]んで、うれしくなった。

synonyms.note: 〜てから marks a clear 'after doing'; the plain て-form just says 'and then.'
から states an explicit reason; the て-form gives a softer, often emotional cause.

related.note: い-adjectives and nouns link with 〜くて／〜で; verbs use the verb て-form.
〜と joins nouns ('A and B'); the て-form joins verbs and clauses.

title: てあげる
meaning: to do something (as a favor) for someone
summary: Verb［て form］＋ あげる does an action as a kindness for someone else, with the favor flowing away from the doer toward the receiver. It parallels あげる ('give'), but what's handed over is an action rather than an object. Use it when you help someone out.
pitfalls: The favor goes outward, from the doer to someone else; a favor done toward you takes 〜てくれる.
Said straight to a superior it can sound condescending ('I'll kindly do this for you'), so use it humbly or reword.

examples.ja: 友だちに本を貸してあげた。
examples.en: I lent my friend a book (as a favor).
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちに｜本[ほん]を｜貸[か]してあげた。

examples.ja: 母のかばんを持ってあげた。
examples.en: I carried my mother's bag for her.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]のかばんを｜持[も]ってあげた。

synonyms.note: 〜てやる does a favor for someone below you, a pet, or a plant; 〜てあげる is the neutral-polite version.

antonyms.note: 〜てあげる sends a favor away; 〜てくれる is a favor done toward you.

related.note: 〜てもらう receives a favor; 〜てあげる gives one.
あげる hands over an object; 〜てあげる does an action as the favor.

title: ていく
meaning: to go on doing; to do and then go; to continue from now
summary: Verb［て form］＋ いく carries an action or change away from the present into the future — 'keep on ~ing from here.' It can also mean 'do something, then head off.' Its mirror image is 〜てくる, which brings change up to now. Write the auxiliary いく in kana.
pitfalls: 〜ていく moves change away into the future (増えていく); 〜てくる traces it up to the present.
When いく is the 'continue' auxiliary, write it in kana (〜ていく) rather than as the full verb 行く.

examples.ja: これからも日本語を勉強していきます。
examples.en: I'll keep on studying Japanese from now on.
examples.f: これからも｜日本語[にほんご]を｜勉強[べんきょう]していきます。

examples.ja: 朝ご飯を食べていきます。
examples.en: I'll eat breakfast and then head out.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べていきます。

antonyms.note: 〜ていく moves change away into the future; 〜てくる brings it up to the present.

related.note: だんだん often pairs with 〜ていく to describe gradual change ahead.
〜ようになる marks reaching a new state; 〜ていく traces the ongoing change toward it.

title: ていた
meaning: was doing; had been doing (past progressive/state)
summary: ていた is simply the past of ている. It describes an action that was going on at some moment in the past (was ~ing), or a state that had come about and was still holding then. Casual ～ていた, polite ～ていました. Which reading applies depends on the verb, exactly as with ている.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ いた／いました
pitfalls: ていた is not the same as plain past: 食べていた = 'was eating' (in progress), while 食べた = 'ate' (simply happened).
With change-of-state verbs it reads as a lasting state, not an action: 住んでいた = 'lived / was living', 結婚していた = 'was married'.

examples.ja: 電話したとき、姉はテレビを見ていました。
examples.en: When I called, my older sister was watching TV.
examples.f: ｜電話[でんわ]したとき、｜姉[あね]はテレビを｜見[み]ていました。

examples.ja: 子どものころ、東京に住んでいました。
examples.en: When I was a child, I lived in Tokyo.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どものころ、｜東京[とうきょう]に｜住[す]んでいました。

related.note: ている places the ongoing action/state at the present; ていた places the same at a past reference point.
てきた traces a change continuing up to now; ていた just situates an action in the past.

title: ていただけませんか
summary: A very polite, softened way to ask someone to do something for you. It is built on the humble いただく (to receive) in its negative-potential-question shape, literally 'couldn't I receive the favor of your ~ing?' — which lands as a respectful 'could you please ~?'. Reach for it with superiors, customers, and strangers.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ いただけませんか
pitfalls: This is softer and more polite than てください or てくれませんか; the affirmative ～ていただけますか is fine too but a touch more direct.
The subject is you (the one receiving the favor). てくださいませんか instead frames the other person as the doer; both are polite, but the viewpoint differs.

examples.ja: すみません、少し待っていただけませんか。
examples.en: Excuse me, could you please wait a moment?
examples.f: すみません、｜少[すこ]し｜待[ま]っていただけませんか。

examples.ja: この漢字の読み方を教えていただけませんか。
examples.en: Could you please tell me how to read this kanji?
examples.f: この｜漢字[かんじ]の｜読み方[よみかた]を｜教[おし]えていただけませんか。

synonyms.note: ～てもらえない／～てくれない are the plain, casual versions of this same request.

related.note: ていただく is the humble equivalent of てもらう (receiving the favor of an action).
てください is a plainer, more direct 'please do'; ていただけませんか is far more deferential.

title: ているところ
meaning: in the middle of doing; right now doing
summary: ところ literally means 'place', but here it points to a stage in time. Verb＋ているところだ pins the action to exactly the stage of being in progress — 'I'm right in the middle of ~ing'. It is more pointed than plain ている, zooming in on this very moment.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ いるところ（だ／です）
pitfalls: There are three matching stages: 〜るところ (about to), 〜ているところ (in the middle), 〜たところ (just finished). Match the verb form to the stage you mean.
It describes a moment, so it pairs with 今 or ちょうど, not with a duration like 三時間.

examples.ja: 今、晩ご飯を作っているところです。
examples.en: I'm right in the middle of making dinner.
examples.f: ｜今[いま]、｜晩[ばん]ご｜飯[はん]を｜作[つく]っているところです。

examples.ja: ちょうどレポートを書いているところに、友だちが来た。
examples.en: Right as I was writing my report, a friend showed up.
examples.f: ちょうどレポートを｜書[か]いているところに、｜友[とも]だちが｜来[き]た。

related.note: plain ている says an action is ongoing; ているところ zooms in on the exact in-progress moment.
たところ marks an action just finished; ているところ marks one still in progress.
るところだ is about to start; ているところ is mid-action.

title: ておく
meaning: to do in advance; to do (and leave it that way) on purpose
summary: From 置く (to place), ておく means doing something ahead of time as preparation, or deliberately leaving something in a certain state. In casual speech it contracts: 〜ておく → 〜とく, 〜でおく → 〜どく.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ おく／おきます
pitfalls: Two senses share the form: preparing beforehand (予約しておく) and leaving something as-is on purpose (窓を開けておく).
The casual contraction drops いてお/んでお: 買っておく → 買っとく, 読んでおく → 読んどく.

examples.ja: 明日試験があるので、今夜勉強しておきます。
examples.en: I have an exam tomorrow, so I'll study tonight to be ready.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]｜試験[しけん]があるので、｜今夜[こんや]｜勉強[べんきょう]しておきます。

examples.ja: 客が来る前に、部屋をそうじしておいた。
examples.en: I cleaned the room before the guests came.
examples.f: ｜客[きゃく]が｜来[く]る｜前[まえ]に、｜部屋[へや]をそうじしておいた。

related.note: both attach a helper verb to the て form; てみる means 'try and see', ておく means 'do in advance'.
another て + helper; てしまう marks completion or regret, ておく marks doing ahead of time.

title: てくる
meaning: to do and come back; to come to ~; to have been ~ing (up to now)
summary: てくる attaches the motion verb 来る and carries several linked senses: (1) do something and come back (買ってくる = go buy and return); (2) a change moving toward the present or the speaker (寒くなってくる = it's getting cold); (3) an action or state continuing up until now (ずっと勉強してきた). It is the mirror of ていく.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ くる／きます
pitfalls: Direction is the key: てくる moves toward the speaker or up to the present, ていく moves away or into the future.
Don't read every てくる as literal 'come'. With change verbs it means 'come to / begin to': 慣れてくる = 'get used to it (gradually)'.

examples.ja: ちょっとパンを買ってきます。
examples.en: I'll go buy some bread and come right back.
examples.f: ちょっとパンを｜買[か]ってきます。

examples.ja: だんだん暖かくなってきましたね。
examples.en: It's gradually gotten warmer, hasn't it?
examples.f: だんだん｜暖[あたた]かくなってきましたね。

related.note: ていく moves away from the speaker or into the future; てくる moves toward the speaker or up to now.
plain 来る is literal coming; てくる uses it as a helper attached to another verb.

title: てくれてありがとう
summary: Thanks someone for doing something for you. It joins てくれる (someone does a favor for me) with ありがとう. Because it rests on てくれる, the action being thanked benefits the speaker. Polite: 〜てくれてありがとうございます, or with the honorific 〜てくださってありがとうございます.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ くれてありがとう
Verb［て form］＋ くださってありがとうございます［polite］
pitfalls: Because it uses てくれる, the thanked action must be a favor toward you: 手伝ってくれてありがとう.
For politeness, swap くれて for くださって and add ございます: 来てくださってありがとうございます.

examples.ja: 来てくれてありがとう。
examples.en: Thanks for coming.
examples.f: ｜来[き]てくれてありがとう。

examples.ja: 手伝ってくれてありがとうございました。
examples.en: Thank you for helping me.
examples.f: ｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれてありがとうございました。

related.note: てくれる (does a favor for me) is exactly what this phrase thanks the other person for.
てすみません apologizes for an action; てくれてありがとう thanks for one — parallel structures.

title: てくれない・てもらえない
kana: てくれない・てもらえない
summary: Two casual ways to ask a favor. 〜てくれない? = 'won't you do ~ for me?'; 〜てもらえない? = 'could I get you to ~?'. Both are the negative-question forms of てくれる and the potential もらえる, which softens the request. Say them with rising intonation.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ もらえない（？）
pitfalls: These are casual. For polite speech use 〜てくれませんか／〜てもらえませんか, or the humble 〜ていただけませんか.
てもらえない builds on the potential もらえる ('can receive'), while てくれない uses plain くれる — both function as requests.

examples.ja: ちょっと手伝ってくれない？
examples.en: Could you give me a hand?
examples.f: ちょっと｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれない？

examples.ja: その塩を取ってもらえない？
examples.en: Could you pass me that salt?
examples.f: その｜塩[しお]を｜取[と]ってもらえない？

synonyms.note: ていただけませんか is the polite, humble version of this same request.

related.note: てくれる states 'does me a favor'; its negative question turns that into a request.
てもらう underlies てもらえない — 'could I receive the favor of your ~ing?'.

title: てくれる
summary: てくれる marks that someone does an action as a favor for the speaker or the speaker's in-group. The doer is the subject (が/は); the beneficiary is you, often left unstated. The direction of the favor points toward the speaker's side.
structure: Noun［giver］＋ が ＋ Verb［て form］＋ くれる
pitfalls: The direction is fixed toward the speaker: 友だちが手伝ってくれる (my friend helps me). If you do the favor for someone else, switch to てあげる.
Contrast てもらう: with てくれる the giver is the subject (友だちが〜くれた); with てもらう the receiver is (私が友だちに〜もらった). Same event, different viewpoint.
The honorific version is てくださる: 先生が教えてくださった.

examples.ja: 友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれました。
examples.en: My friend helped me with my homework.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちが｜宿題[しゅくだい]を｜手伝[てつだ]ってくれました。

examples.ja: 母がお弁当を作ってくれた。
examples.en: My mom made me a boxed lunch.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]がお｜弁当[べんとう]を｜作[つく]ってくれた。

related.note: plain くれる gives an object toward the speaker; てくれる gives an action as a favor.
てあげる does a favor moving away from the speaker; てくれる, toward the speaker.
てもらう describes the same favor from the receiver's viewpoint (receiver = subject).

title: でございます
summary: でございます is the most formal form of です ('to be'). It belongs to polite/humble keigo and is used in service settings, announcements, and business — typically by staff toward customers. It is built on ございます, the very polite form of ある.
pitfalls: The register is very high: shop staff, receptionists, formal announcements. In everyday conversation でございます sounds stiff and over-formal — use です.
It replaces です as a unit; it attaches to nouns and な-adjective stems, not to plain だ.

examples.ja: こちらが会議室でございます。
examples.en: This is the meeting room.
examples.f: こちらが｜会議[かいぎ]｜室[しつ]でございます。

examples.ja: お手洗いは二階でございます。
examples.en: The restroom is on the second floor.
examples.f: お｜手洗[てあら]いは｜二[に]｜階[かい]でございます。

synonyms.note: ございます is the polite existence verb; でございます is the polite copula built on it.

related.note: お〜になる is respectful (sonkeigo) verb keigo; でございます is the matching polite copula, often used together.

title: てしまう・ちゃう
meaning: to do completely; to do (unfortunately, by accident)
summary: てしまう adds one of two nuances: (1) completion — doing something fully, all the way through — or (2) regret — an action that turned out badly or happened by mistake. Context decides which. Casual contractions: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう, 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ しまう／しまいます
Verb［て form］＋ ちゃう／じゃう［casual］
pitfalls: The two nuances overlap: 全部食べてしまった can mean 'ate it all up' (completion) or 'ate it, oops' (regret).
Watch the voiced contraction: 〜てしまう → 〜ちゃう (食べちゃう), but 〜でしまう → 〜じゃう (飲んじゃう, 死んじゃう).
The regret sense very often appears in the past: 〜てしまった／〜ちゃった.

examples.ja: 大事な書類をなくしてしまった。
examples.en: I went and lost an important document.
examples.f: ｜大事[だいじ]な｜書類[しょるい]をなくしてしまった。

examples.ja: 宿題はもう全部やってしまいました。
examples.en: I've already finished all my homework.
examples.f: ｜宿題[しゅくだい]はもう｜全部[ぜんぶ]やってしまいました。

related.note: both are て + helper verb; てしまう marks completion or regret, ておく marks doing in advance.

title: てすみません
summary: Apologizes for an action you did or are doing: 〜てすみません = 'sorry for ~ing'. For a finished action, use the past 〜てすみませんでした. More casual is 〜てごめん(なさい). It mirrors てくれてありがとう, but as an apology rather than thanks.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ すみません／すみませんでした
pitfalls: For a completed action, apologize in the past: 遅れてすみませんでした.
To apologize for NOT doing something, use the negative 〜なくてすみません (返事できなくてすみません = sorry for not replying).

examples.ja: 遅くなってすみません。
examples.en: Sorry for being late.
examples.f: ｜遅[おそ]くなってすみません。

examples.ja: 何度も電話してすみませんでした。
examples.en: I'm sorry for calling so many times.
examples.f: ｜何[なん]｜度[ど]も｜電話[でんわ]してすみませんでした。

related.note: てくれてありがとう thanks for an action; てすみません apologizes for one.

title: でできる・からできる
kana: でできる・からできる
meaning: to be made of; to be made from
summary: Two ways to state what something is made of. Noun＋で marks a material that is still recognizable in the product (木でできた机 = a desk made of wood). Noun＋から marks a raw material that has been transformed so it's no longer obvious (ワインはぶどうから). できている ('is made of') is used for the resulting state.
structure: Noun［material］＋ で ＋ できている
Noun［material］＋ から ＋ できる／作る
pitfalls: から tends to mark a material that has changed form (酒は米から); で tends to mark one still visible (かばんは革で).
For 'is made of', use the state できている, not plain できる: この机は木でできています, not 木でできます.

examples.ja: このテーブルは木でできています。
examples.en: This table is made of wood.
examples.f: このテーブルは｜木[き]でできています。

examples.ja: ワインはぶどうからできます。
examples.en: Wine is made from grapes.

synonyms.note: から作る actively says 'make from'; からできる says the result 'is made from' that material.

title: ではないか
summary: A formal, emphatic way to seek agreement or press a point — 'isn't it ~?', '~, right?'. It is more assertive and often rhetorical, pushing the listener to agree rather than genuinely asking. The everyday spoken counterpart is じゃないか.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ ではないか
pitfalls: The register is formal/written or emphatic speech; the casual spoken form is じゃないか (or じゃない with rising tone).
It is often rhetorical — used to nudge the listener into agreement, not to ask a real question.

examples.ja: これは大きな問題ではないか。
examples.en: Isn't this a big problem?
examples.f: これは｜大[おお]きな｜問題[もんだい]ではないか。

examples.ja: 君にもできるではないか。
examples.en: You can do it too, can't you?
examples.f: ｜君[きみ]にもできるではないか。

synonyms.note: じゃないか is the casual, everyday version of this same 'isn't it?'.

related.note: じゃない・ではない is the plain negation; ではないか turns it into a rhetorical confirmation.
だろう also seeks agreement ('right?'); ではないか is more emphatic and rhetorical.

title: てほしい
summary: てほしい expresses wanting another person to do something. The person you want to act is marked with に, and ほしい inflects like an い-adjective. The negative 'want you NOT to' is 〜ないでほしい.
structure: Noun［person］＋ に ＋ Verb［て form］＋ ほしい
Verb［ない form］＋ でほしい［negative］
pitfalls: The subject differs from 〜たい: 〜たい = I want to do it myself; てほしい = I want another person to do it.
Mark the person you want to act with に: 君に来てほしい.
'Want you not to' is 〜ないでほしい (来ないでほしい = I want you not to come).

examples.ja: 明日は早く来てほしいです。
examples.en: I want you to come early tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜早[はや]く｜来[き]てほしいです。

examples.ja: 私のことを忘れないでほしい。
examples.en: I don't want you to forget me.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]のことを｜忘[わす]れないでほしい。

related.note: がほしい wants an object; てほしい wants an action from someone.
〜たい is wanting to do something yourself; てほしい is wanting someone else to do it.
ように〜てほしい softens the request, often for outcomes not fully in the person's control.

title: てみる
meaning: to try doing (and see how it goes)
summary: From 見る, てみる means doing something to see how it turns out — 'try ~ing' / 'give it a go'. The focus is on the attempt and finding out the result, not on whether you succeed. It is usually written in kana, since 見る here is a helper, not literal 'look'.
structure: Verb［て form］＋ みる／みます
pitfalls: てみる is 'try and see the outcome'. For 'try hard to / attempt', use 〜ようとする instead.
Write it in kana (〜てみる); the auxiliary 見る has lost its literal 'look' meaning here.

examples.ja: この店のラーメンを食べてみます。
examples.en: I'll try this shop's ramen and see how it is.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のラーメンを｜食[た]べてみます。

examples.ja: 新しいくつをはいてみた。
examples.en: I tried on the new shoes.
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しいくつをはいてみた。

related.note: ようと思う intends or plans to do; てみる just gives it a try to see the result.
both attach a helper verb to the て form; てみる = try and see, ておく = do in advance.

title: ても
summary: ても sets up 'even if / even though' — the second clause holds regardless of the first. It attaches to the て form: 食べても, 高くても, 学生でも. It covers both the hypothetical ('even if it rains') and the actual ('even though I studied').
pitfalls: い-adjectives become 〜くても (高くても); nouns and な-adjectives take でも (雨でも, 便利でも).
With a question word it means 'no matter ~': だれが来ても (no matter who comes), いくら〜ても (no matter how much).
Don't confuse it with 〜てもいい ('may / it's okay'); ても on its own means 'even if'.

examples.ja: 雨が降っても、試合をします。
examples.en: Even if it rains, we'll hold the match.
examples.f: ｜雨[あめ]が｜降[ふ]っても、｜試合[しあい]をします。

examples.ja: たくさん食べても、太りません。
examples.en: Even though I eat a lot, I don't gain weight.
examples.f: たくさん｜食[た]べても、｜太[ふと]りません。

related.note: 〜てもいい grants permission ('may'); ても alone means 'even if'.
でも is the particle 'even'; in the ても pattern, nouns and な-adjectives likewise take でも.

title: でも
meaning: even; ~ or something; any~ (with a question word)
summary: The particle でも has several everyday uses: (1) 'even', giving an extreme example (子どもでもできる = even a child can do it); (2) '~ or something', a light, non-committal suggestion (お茶でも飲む?); (3) attached to a question word, 'any-' (だれでも, どこでも, なんでも).
pitfalls: Sentence-initial でも ('but…') is a different word; this でも is a particle attached to a noun or question word.
With a question word it means 'any~' and stays inclusive/positive: いつでも (anytime), だれでも (anyone).
お茶でも means 'tea or something' — a soft suggestion, not literally 'even tea'.

examples.ja: こんな問題は子どもでもできます。
examples.en: Even a child can do a problem like this.
examples.f: こんな｜問題[もんだい]は｜子[こ]どもでもできます。

examples.ja: 週末にえいがでも見ませんか。
examples.en: Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]にえいがでも｜見[み]ませんか。

related.note: sentence-initial でも means 'but / however'; this でも is a particle meaning 'even / any'.
〜ても ('even if') overlaps in feel; でも attaches to nouns and question words as a particle.
～でも～でも lists inclusive examples ('whether A or B').

title: てもらう
meaning: to have/get someone to do ~ (for one's benefit)
summary: てもらう describes receiving the favor of someone's action — you get someone to do something for you. The receiver (you or your in-group) is the subject; the doer is marked with に. The viewpoint is the receiver's.
structure: Noun［receiver］＋ が ＋ Noun［doer］＋ に ＋ Verb［て form］＋ もらう
pitfalls: Mark the doer with に: 友だちに手伝ってもらった (I had my friend help me).
Viewpoint flips vs てくれる: てもらう makes the receiver the subject (私が〜もらう); てくれる makes the giver the subject (友だちが〜くれる). Same event.
The humble/polite version is 〜ていただく (先生に教えていただいた).

examples.ja: 友だちに引っこしを手伝ってもらいました。
examples.en: I had my friend help me move.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちに｜引[ひ]っこしを｜手伝[てつだ]ってもらいました。

examples.ja: 駅で道を教えてもらった。
examples.en: I got someone to show me the way at the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]で｜道[みち]を｜教[おし]えてもらった。

related.note: plain もらう receives an object; てもらう receives an action as a favor.
てくれる frames the same favor with the doer as subject; てもらう, with the receiver as subject.
てあげる is doing a favor for someone else; てもらう is getting one done for you.

title: てやる
meaning: to do (a favor) for someone lower in status; to do (defiantly)
summary: てやる is like てあげる (do a favor) but directed at those lower in status — juniors, children, animals, plants — and in a blunter, more casual register. It can also carry a defiant 'just you watch' determination when the speaker is talking about themselves.
pitfalls: The register is blunt. Toward equals or superiors use てあげる, not てやる.
It's common with juniors and pets/plants: 弟に教えてやる, 犬にえさをやる.
A second nuance is defiance/determination: 絶対に勝ってやる = 'I'll definitely win — just watch me'.

examples.ja: 弟が困っていたので、手伝ってやった。
examples.en: My little brother was in trouble, so I helped him out.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]が｜困[こま]っていたので、｜手伝[てつだ]ってやった。

examples.ja: 子どもにえほんを読んでやった。
examples.en: I read a picture book to my child.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもにえほんを｜読[よ]んでやった。

synonyms.note: てあげる is the neutral, politer form; てやる is blunter and aimed at those below the speaker.

related.note: てくれる is a favor done toward the speaker; てやる is a favor the speaker does downward.

title: てよかった
meaning: I'm glad that ~; it was good that ~
summary: The て form plus よかった looks back on something and says you're glad or relieved it turned out that way: 来てよかった = I'm glad I came. Even though よかった is past, the feeling of relief is right now. For 'glad I didn't ~', switch the verb to the なくて form.
structure: Verb［ない form → なくて］＋ よかった
pitfalls: For 'I'm glad I didn't ~', use the なくて form: 行かなくてよかった (glad I didn't go), not the plain negative plus よかった.
Don't mix it up with 〜ばよかった／〜たらよかった, which express regret ('I should have ~'). てよかった is a positive, relieved feeling about what did happen.

examples.ja: 早めに家を出てよかったです。電車に間に合いました。
examples.en: I'm glad I left home early. I made the train.
examples.f: ｜早[はや]めに｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]てよかったです。｜電車[でんしゃ]に｜間に合[まにあ]いました。

examples.ja: あなたに相談してよかったです。気持ちが楽になりました。
examples.en: I'm glad I talked it over with you. I feel much better now.
examples.f: あなたに｜相談[そうだん]してよかったです。｜気持[きも]ちが｜楽[らく]になりました。

antonyms.note: 〜ばよかった regrets something you didn't do; 〜てよかった is glad about what you did.

related.note: The pattern attaches よかった to the plain て form of the verb.
The negative version 〜なくてよかった uses this なくて form.

title: と
summary: と marks the content of speech or thought and hands it to a reporting verb like 言う (say), 思う (think), or 書く (write). The quoted part stays in plain form, and と links it to what someone said, thought, or wrote.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ と ＋ 言う／思う／書く
pitfalls: The clause before と ends in plain form even in polite speech: 来ると言いました, not 来ますと言いました (a direct quote inside 「」 keeps its original politeness).
This quotative と is different from the conditional と ('when/if') and the と that joins nouns ('A and B').

examples.ja: 彼は明日来ると言いました。
examples.en: He said he would come tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜明日[あした]｜来[く]ると｜言[い]いました。

examples.ja: これでいいと思います。
examples.en: I think this is fine.
examples.f: これでいいと｜思[おも]います。

synonyms.note: って is the casual spoken version of quotative と.

related.note: 〜と思う is this quotative と with 思う, marking your opinion.
〜という uses the same と to attach a name or label to a noun.
Conditional と means 'when/if'; don't confuse it with this quotative と.

title: と
summary: と joins two clauses to say that whenever A happens, B follows automatically. It's for predictable, natural consequences — how machines work, directions, habits, and cause-and-effect that always plays out the same way.
pitfalls: The B clause usually can't be a request, invitation, or your own decision: avoid 〜と、〜てください. Use たら for those.
The part before と stays non-past plain, even about the past or the future: 春になると花が咲く.
This conditional と is separate from the quotative と ('that') and the noun-linking と ('and').

examples.ja: このボタンを押すと、切符が出ます。
examples.en: When you press this button, a ticket comes out.
examples.f: このボタンを｜押[お]すと、｜切符[きっぷ]が｜出[で]ます。

examples.ja: まっすぐ行くと、右に駅があります。
examples.en: If you go straight, the station is on your right.
examples.f: まっすぐ｜行[い]くと、｜右[みぎ]に｜駅[えき]があります。

synonyms.note: たら is the most flexible 'if/when' and allows requests in the result; と is limited to automatic results.
ば is a general conditional; と stresses that B always follows A.

related.note: なら reacts to a topic just raised; と states a repeatable, automatic consequence.

title: と～と、どちらが
meaning: between A and B, which one?
summary: This pattern asks someone to compare exactly two things and choose: AとBと、どちらが〜？ = 'Between A and B, which is more ~?' The reply typically comes back with 〜のほうが to name the winner.
structure: Noun［A］＋ と ＋ Noun［B］＋ と、どちらが ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective ＋ か
pitfalls: Use どちら (casual どっち) for a choice between two items; for three or more, ask with どれ or use 一番.
The second と is often dropped: AとB、どちらが〜 is equally natural.

examples.ja: 犬と猫と、どちらが好きですか。
examples.en: Which do you like better, dogs or cats?
examples.f: ｜犬[いぬ]と｜猫[ねこ]と、どちらが｜好[す]きですか。

examples.ja: 電車とバスと、どちらが速いですか。
examples.en: Which is faster, the train or the bus?
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]とバスと、どちらが｜速[はや]いですか。

related.note: より〜のほうが is the usual shape of the answer that names the chosen one.
For picking the top of three or more, use 〜の中で一番 instead of a two-way どちら.

title: といい・たらいい
meaning: I hope ~; it would be good if ~
summary: 〜といい and 〜たらいい express a hope, often about things you can't control: 晴れるといい = I hope it clears up. In advice contexts they also soften a suggestion into 'it would be good if you ~'.
pitfalls: For a hope about someone else, it reads as 'I hope they ~'; the wish stays gentle rather than a demand.
といい／たらいい／ばいい all overlap for wishes; といい and たらいい are the most common for a plain 'I hope ~'.

examples.ja: 明日、天気がいいといいですね。
examples.en: I hope the weather is nice tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]、｜天気[てんき]がいいといいですね。

examples.ja: 早く元気になるといいですね。
examples.en: I hope you get well soon.
examples.f: ｜早[はや]く｜元気[げんき]になるといいですね。

synonyms.note: 〜ばいい also voices a wish or suggestion, built on the ば conditional.

related.note: たらいい is the たら conditional plus いい; たら on its own just means 'if/when'.
〜てほしい directly wants someone to do something; 〜といい softly hopes it happens.

title: という
summary: XというY means 'a Y called/named X'. Use it to introduce a name or label the listener may not know: 「はな」という店 = a shop called Hana. Literally it's 'a Y that is said (to be) X'.
pitfalls: Reach for という when the name is new to the listener; a famous name usually doesn't need it.
The name before という takes the quotative と, so keep it: 「さくら」という, not 「さくら」の.

examples.ja: 田中さんという人から電話がありました。
examples.en: There was a call from a person named Tanaka.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんという｜人[ひと]から｜電話[でんわ]がありました。

examples.ja: 友だちは「ポチ」という犬を飼っています。
examples.en: My friend has a dog named Pochi.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちは「ポチ」という｜犬[いぬ]を｜飼[か]っています。

related.note: という is built from the quotative と plus 言う.
〜ということ nominalizes a whole statement; 〜という labels a noun.
〜というのは introduces a term and then explains what it means.

title: ということ
summary: ということ turns a whole sentence into a noun meaning 'the fact/matter that ~'. It lets a full statement work as the subject or object of another clause — handy for talking about information, meaning, or what was said.
pitfalls: Use ということ to package a whole statement or piece of information; plain こと or の nominalizes a single action instead.
Keep the と: it marks the preceding clause as a quoted idea, giving ということ, not just こと.

examples.ja: 彼が来ないということを聞きました。
examples.en: I heard that he isn't coming.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]が｜来[こ]ないということを｜聞[き]きました。

examples.ja: 約束を守るということは大切です。
examples.en: Keeping your promises is important.
examples.f: ｜約束[やくそく]を｜守[まも]るということは｜大切[たいせつ]です。

synonyms.note: plain こと nominalizes an action; ということ wraps a whole statement or fact.

related.note: の also turns a clause into a noun, but for concrete events rather than reported statements.
〜ということだ ends a sentence with 'it means that' or reported 'I hear that'.

title: と言ってもいい
meaning: you could say ~; one might say ~
summary: 〜と言ってもいい means 'you could say that ~' or 'it's fair to say ~'. It lets you put forward a strong or bold characterization while framing it as one acceptable way to describe something, softening the claim.
structure: Sentence／Noun［plain form］＋ と言ってもいい
pitfalls: Literally 'even if you say ~, it's fine', so it presents a claim as justifiable rather than as flat fact.
Drop the いい and 〜と言っても becomes concessive ('even though I say ~'), a different meaning.

examples.ja: 日本語はだいぶ上手になったと言ってもいいでしょう。
examples.en: You could say your Japanese has gotten quite good.
examples.f: ｜日本語[にほんご]はだいぶ｜上手[じょうず]になったと｜言[い]ってもいいでしょう。

examples.ja: 彼はこの町で一番の医者だと言ってもいい。
examples.en: You could call him the best doctor in this town.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はこの｜町[まち]で｜一番[いちばん]の｜医者[いしゃ]だと｜言[い]ってもいい。

related.note: 〜と言っても alone is concessive ('even though you say'); adding いい makes it 'you may say'.
Both use 言う; と言ってもいい offers a description as acceptable, という attaches a name.

title: と言われている
summary: 〜と言われている reports what people in general say or believe, with no named source: 'it is said that ~'. The passive 言われる ('is said') plus ている presents the statement as widely held.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ と言われている
pitfalls: It's deliberately source-less — for common knowledge or reputation, not something one person told you (there, use 〜と言っていた).
Its siblings とされている and と考えられている sound more formal or reasoned; 言われている is plain hearsay.

examples.ja: お茶は体にいいと言われている。
examples.en: Green tea is said to be good for your health.
examples.f: お｜茶[ちゃ]は｜体[からだ]にいいと｜言[い]われている。

examples.ja: この橋は百年以上前に作られたと言われています。
examples.en: This bridge is said to have been built over a hundred years ago.
examples.f: この｜橋[はし]は｜百[ひゃく]｜年[ねん]｜以上[いじょう]｜前[まえ]に｜作[つく]られたと｜言[い]われています。

synonyms.note: 〜とされている is more official-sounding; 〜と言われている is everyday hearsay.

related.note: 〜と考えられている implies a reasoned conclusion; 〜と言われている is just what people say.
〜そうだ also reports hearsay but usually from a specific recent source.

title: と思う
summary: 〜と思う states your opinion, guess, or judgment: 'I think that ~'. The idea before と stays in plain form, and 思う holds your personal view. Add the volitional to get 〜ようと思う ('I intend to').
pitfalls: Keep the clause before と in plain form even when polite: 高いと思います, not 高いですと思います.
と思う is your own current opinion. To report what someone else thinks, use 〜と思っている.

examples.ja: この映画は面白いと思います。
examples.en: I think this movie is interesting.
examples.f: この｜映画[えいが]は｜面白[おもしろ]いと｜思[おも]います。

examples.ja: 彼女はもう帰ったと思います。
examples.en: I think she has already gone home.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]はもう｜帰[かえ]ったと｜思[おも]います。

related.note: と思う is the quotative と plus 思う.
だろう states a guess directly; と思う frames it explicitly as your opinion.
〜ようと思う uses 思う with the volitional to say you intend to do something.

title: とか～とか
meaning: such as A and B; among other things
summary: とか〜とか lists a couple of examples out of many: 'things like A and B'. It's a casual, non-exhaustive list — you name a few and imply there's more you're not listing.
structure: Noun ＋ とか ＋ Noun ＋ とか
Verb／adjective［plain form］＋ とか ＋ Verb／adjective［plain form］＋ とか
pitfalls: Casual in tone; in formal writing prefer や or など.
Non-exhaustive — it means 'among others'. Plain と, by contrast, lists a complete, exact set.

examples.ja: 週末は掃除とか買い物とかをします。
examples.en: On weekends I do things like cleaning and shopping.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜掃除[そうじ]とか｜買い物[かいもの]とかをします。

examples.ja: 果物ならりんごとかみかんとかが好きです。
examples.en: As for fruit, I like things like apples and oranges.
examples.f: ｜果物[くだもの]ならりんごとかみかんとかが｜好[す]きです。

synonyms.note: や also lists examples but is more neutral; とか is more casual and can list actions.
など rounds off an example list ('and so on') more formally than とか.

related.note: 〜たり〜たり lists example actions with verbs; とか〜とか can list nouns or actions casually.

title: と考えられている
kana: とかんがえられている
meaning: is considered ~; is thought to be ~
summary: 〜と考えられている presents something as what people generally think or have reasoned to be true: 'it is considered / thought that ~'. Common in explanations, science, and news, it marks a conclusion rather than mere gossip.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ と考えられている
pitfalls: More analytical than 〜と言われている: 考えられている implies people reasoned their way to this view.
Formal, written register — you'll meet it in news and academic writing more than everyday chat.

examples.ja: この習慣は江戸時代に始まったと考えられている。
examples.en: This custom is thought to have begun in the Edo period.
examples.f: この｜習慣[しゅうかん]は｜江戸[えど]｜時代[じだい]に｜始[はじ]まったと｜考[かんが]えられている。

examples.ja: 運動は健康にいいと考えられています。
examples.en: Exercise is considered good for your health.
examples.f: ｜運動[うんどう]は｜健康[けんこう]にいいと｜考[かんが]えられています。

synonyms.note: 〜と言われている is general hearsay; 〜と考えられている implies a reasoned conclusion.

related.note: 〜とされている treats something as an official standard; 〜と考えられている reports a considered view.
〜と考えられる (N2) is the same idea without ている, often 'one can think that'.

title: と聞いた
summary: 〜と聞いた reports information you got from someone: 'I heard that ~'. The plain statement before と is what you were told, and 聞いた marks it as something you personally heard secondhand.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ と聞いた／と聞いています
pitfalls: This is firsthand hearsay — you heard it from a source, unlike source-less 〜と言われている ('people say').
〜と聞いています ('I understand / I've heard') presents the information as your current knowledge.

examples.ja: 田中さんは来月結婚すると聞きました。
examples.en: I heard that Tanaka is getting married next month.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんは｜来月[らいげつ]｜結婚[けっこん]すると｜聞[き]きました。

examples.ja: あの店は今日休みだと聞いたよ。
examples.en: I heard that shop is closed today.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]は｜今日[きょう]｜休[やす]みだと｜聞[き]いたよ。

synonyms.note: 〜そうだ also relays hearsay; 〜と聞いた stresses that you yourself heard it.

related.note: 〜と言われている is what people in general say; 〜と聞いた is what you were told.
Both take a plain-form clause plus と; 聞いた reports hearing, 思う reports thinking.

title: とされている
summary: 〜とされている says that something is officially or generally regarded and treated a certain way: 'is deemed / regarded as ~'. It's the most formal of the reporting siblings and fits rules, customs, and accepted facts.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ とされている
pitfalls: Strong official tone — used for rules, laws, and widely accepted standards, not casual rumor.
After a noun, insert だ: マナー違反だとされている, not マナー違反とされている in most cases.

examples.ja: この神社は町で最も古いとされている。
examples.en: This shrine is regarded as the oldest in town.
examples.f: この｜神社[じんじゃ]は｜町[まち]で｜最[もっと]も｜古[ふる]いとされている。

examples.ja: 会議中の電話はマナー違反だとされています。
examples.en: Taking calls during a meeting is considered bad manners.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]｜中[ちゅう]の｜電話[でんわ]はマナー｜違反[いはん]だとされています。

synonyms.note: 〜と言われている is casual hearsay; 〜とされている sounds official or authoritative.

related.note: 〜と考えられている reports a reasoned view; 〜とされている treats it as an established standard.
〜とされる (N1) is the same form without ている, common in formal definitions.

title: とみえる・とみえて
summary: 〜とみえる draws a conclusion from what you can observe: 'it seems that ~, judging by the evidence'. 〜とみえて connects that inference to a following clause that shows the evidence or result.
structure: Sentence［plain form］＋ とみえて ＋ Sentence
pitfalls: It's deductive — you infer a cause from a visible result — so it feels more reasoned than 〜そうだ ('looks like').
Somewhat literary; in everyday speech 〜らしい or 〜みたいだ are more natural.

examples.ja: 道が濡れている。夜に雨が降ったとみえる。
examples.en: The road is wet. It seems it rained during the night.
examples.f: ｜道[みち]が｜濡[ぬ]れている。｜夜[よる]に｜雨[あめ]が｜降[ふ]ったとみえる。

examples.ja: 疲れているとみえて、子どもはすぐに寝てしまった。
examples.en: The child must have been tired, since he fell asleep right away.
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れているとみえて、｜子[こ]どもはすぐに｜寝[ね]てしまった。

synonyms.note: 〜らしい also infers from evidence but is more colloquial; 〜とみえる is more deductive and literary.

related.note: 〜そうだ reads an appearance directly; 〜とみえる reasons back to a cause.
〜ようだ is a broad 'it seems'; 〜とみえる specifically infers from observed evidence.

title: どんどん
summary: どんどん is an adverb for something advancing steadily and fast — 'more and more', at a brisk, continuous pace. It often pairs with change verbs to show momentum building: どんどん増える = to increase rapidly.
pitfalls: どんどん is energetic and fast; for slow, step-by-step change use だんだん instead.
It's an adverb — place it before the verb, not directly before a noun.

examples.ja: 子どもたちはどんどん大きくなります。
examples.en: Children grow up so fast.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもたちはどんどん｜大[おお]きくなります。

examples.ja: 質問があれば、どんどん聞いてください。
examples.en: If you have any questions, go right ahead and ask.
examples.f: ｜質問[しつもん]があれば、どんどん｜聞[き]いてください。

related.note: だんだん is gradual, step-by-step change; どんどん is fast and energetic.

title: ないと
meaning: must ~; have to ~ (unless you do, it won't do)
summary: 〜ないと states an obligation by leaving a conditional hanging: literally 'if you don't ~, (it won't do)'. The consequence いけない／だめ is usually left unsaid, so 〜ないと by itself means 'I have to ~' or 'you must ~'.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ と ＋ （いけない／だめ）［often dropped］
pitfalls: Casual and spoken. The fuller form is 〜ないといけない; in formal writing use 〜なければならない.
Build it on the ない form plus と: 行かないと, not 行くないと.

examples.ja: もう遅いから、そろそろ帰らないと。
examples.en: It's late, so I'd better get going soon.
examples.f: もう｜遅[おそ]いから、そろそろ｜帰[かえ]らないと。

examples.ja: 明日は早いから、早く寝ないといけない。
examples.en: I have an early start tomorrow, so I have to go to bed early.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜早[はや]いから、｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]ないといけない。

synonyms.note: 〜なくちゃ is another casual 'have to'; 〜ないと leaves the consequence unspoken.
〜ないといけない spells out the いけない that 〜ないと usually leaves off.

related.note: 〜なければならない is the formal, written way to say the same obligation.
The と here is the conditional と — 'if you don't, then (trouble)'.

title: なかなか～ない
meaning: not easily ~; hardly ~; won't ~ despite trying
summary: With a negative verb, なかなか〜ない means something doesn't happen easily or as hoped — 'not readily', 'won't ~ no matter what'. It carries a hint of frustration that the expected result is slow to arrive.
structure: なかなか ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: This meaning needs a negative predicate: なかなか来ない = won't come. With a positive verb, なかなか instead means 'quite / considerably'.
The point is the gap between what you expect and what happens — it implies you're waiting or trying.

examples.ja: バスがなかなか来ません。
examples.en: The bus just won't come.
examples.f: バスがなかなか｜来[き]ません。

examples.ja: この問題はなかなか解けない。
examples.en: This problem is really hard to solve.
examples.f: この｜問題[もんだい]はなかなか｜解[と]けない。

synonyms.note: あまり〜ない means 'not much'; なかなか〜ない means 'not easily', with a sense of trying.

related.note: Positive なかなか means 'quite / fairly'; paired with 〜ない it flips to 'not easily'.
めったに〜ない means 'rarely'; なかなか〜ない is 'won't happen (though expected)'.

title: ながら
summary: 〜ながら joins two actions performed by one person at the same time: 'while doing ~'. Attach ながら to the verb stem; the ながら clause is the background action, and the main clause carries the primary one.
pitfalls: Both actions must share one subject: 歌いながら歩く = one person sings and walks. For two different people acting at once, use 〜間に.
The main point sits in the second clause: 音楽を聞きながら勉強する is about studying.

examples.ja: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
examples.en: I study while listening to music.
examples.f: ｜音楽[おんがく]を｜聞[き]きながら｜勉強[べんきょう]します。

examples.ja: お茶を飲みながら話しましょう。
examples.en: Let's talk over some tea.
examples.f: お｜茶[ちゃ]を｜飲[の]みながら｜話[はな]しましょう。

synonyms.note: 〜つつ is the formal, written equivalent of 〜ながら for simultaneous actions.

related.note: 〜間に is 'during the time that', often with two different subjects; 〜ながら is one person doing two things.
〜ながらも adds a concessive twist ('even while / although'), beyond simple 'while'.

title: なくて
summary: なくて is the negative て-form. It links two clauses where the first is a 'not' situation, either just joining ideas ('isn't ~ and ...') or giving the reason for the second clause ('because ~ isn't the case'). It attaches to い-adjectives (〜くない → 〜くなくて), to nouns and な-adjectives (〜ではなくて／じゃなくて), and to verbs (〜ない → 〜なくて), especially when the second clause is a feeling or state.
structure: Verb［ない form］ ＋ ［ない → なくて］
い-adjective ＋ ［くない → くなくて］
Noun／な-adjective ＋ ではなくて／じゃなくて
pitfalls: For verbs meaning 'without doing / instead of doing', use ないで, not なくて: 朝ご飯を食べないで出かけた, not 食べなくて出かけた. なくて leans toward stating a cause.
As a reason, なくて usually leads into an emotion or state (困る, 心配, 安心). For a plain 'because', から or ので is often more natural.

examples.ja: テストは思ったより難しくなくて、安心しました。
examples.en: The test wasn't as hard as I thought, and I felt relieved.
examples.f: テストは｜思[おも]ったより｜難[むずか]しくなくて、｜安心[あんしん]しました。

examples.ja: 友だちからの返事が来なくて、とても心配しています。
examples.en: The reply from my friend hasn't come, so I'm really worried.
examples.f: ｜友[とも]だちからの｜返事[へんじ]が｜来[こ]なくて、とても｜心配[しんぱい]しています。

related.note: ないで attaches to verbs for 'without doing ~'; なくて covers adjectives, nouns, and 'because not' reasons.
〜くて・〜で is the affirmative te-form link; なくて is its negative counterpart.
ので gives a plain 'because'; なくて states a negative cause that usually flows into a feeling.

title: なければいけない
summary: なければいけない expresses obligation — 'must do' or 'have to do'. Take the ない form, drop ない, and add なければいけない: 行かない → 行かなければいけない. Literally it says 'if you don't do it, it won't do', so it points to a specific duty the speaker feels bound to. In speech it is often shortened to なきゃ.
structure: Verb［ない form］ ＋ ［ない → なければいけない］
い-adjective ＋ ［くない → くなければいけない］
Noun／な-adjective ＋ でなければいけない
pitfalls: Don't leave the ない on: it's 行かなければいけない, never 行かないなければいけない.
The opposite is not the negative of this phrase but なくてもいい ('don't have to'); 〜なければいけない itself only says 'must'.

examples.ja: 明日は朝早く起きなければいけません。
examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow morning.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜朝[あさ]｜早[はや]く｜起[お]きなければいけません。

examples.ja: 旅行のとき、パスポートを持っていかなければいけない。
examples.en: When you travel, you have to bring your passport.
examples.f: ｜旅行[りょこう]のとき、パスポートを｜持[も]っていかなければいけない。

synonyms.note: なければならない is nearly identical; it feels a touch more formal and written.
なくてはいけない says the same 'must' with the なくては shape instead of なければ.
ないといけない is a more conversational way to say the same obligation.

antonyms.note: なくてもいい is the flip side: 'you don't have to do it'.

related.note: なくちゃ・なきゃ are the casual spoken contractions of this obligation pattern.

title: なければならない
summary: なければならない means 'must do / have to do', built the same way as なければいけない: ない form minus ない, plus なければならない. The ならない half suggests the obligation comes from a rule, social norm, or the nature of things rather than a personal whim, so it is common in written and formal contexts.
structure: Verb［ない form］ ＋ ［ない → なければならない］
い-adjective ＋ ［くない → くなければならない］
Noun／な-adjective ＋ でなければならない
pitfalls: Keep the なければ stem intact: 守らなければならない, not 守らないなければならない.
ならない here is fixed and does not mean 'must not' — that sense belongs to てはいけない. This whole phrase only means 'must do'.

examples.ja: だれでも約束は守らなければなりません。
examples.en: Everyone has to keep their promises.
examples.f: だれでも｜約束[やくそく]は｜守[まも]らなければなりません。

examples.ja: 図書館の本は来週までに返さなければならない。
examples.en: Library books must be returned by next week.
examples.f: ｜図書館[としょかん]の｜本[ほん]は｜来週[らいしゅう]までに｜返[かえ]さなければならない。

synonyms.note: なければいけない is the everyday twin; ならない feels slightly more formal or rule-based.
なくてはならない is the same obligation expressed with the なくては shape.
ないといけない carries the same 'must' in a more casual register.

antonyms.note: なくてもいい lifts the obligation: 'you don't have to'.

related.note: 必要がある also states a need ('it's necessary to'), a softer relative of this strong 'must'.

title: なさい
summary: なさい makes a firm command that is still gentler than the blunt imperative. Attach it to the verb stem (ます form minus ます): 食べます → 食べなさい. It is the tone a parent, teacher, or older person uses toward a child or student — instructive and caring, but clearly a command, not a request between equals.
pitfalls: Use the stem, not the dictionary form: 起きなさい, not 起きるなさい.
It talks down to the listener, so it is not for a boss, customer, or anyone above you — use てください there instead.
There is no negative なさい. To say 'don't do it' to a child, use the negative request 〜ないで.

examples.ja: もう遅いから、早く寝なさい。
examples.en: It's late already, so go to bed early.
examples.f: もう｜遅[おそ]いから、｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]なさい。

examples.ja: 静かにして、先生の話をよく聞きなさい。
examples.en: Be quiet and listen carefully to the teacher.
examples.f: ｜静[しず]かにして、｜先生[せんせい]の｜話[はなし]をよく｜聞[き]きなさい。

antonyms.note: な after a dictionary verb is the blunt 'don't do it'; なさい is the positive 'do it' command.

related.note: The plain imperative (行け) is harsher; なさい softens a command into something instructive.
てください is a polite request among equals; なさい is a command directed downward.
なさい comes from the imperative of the honorific verb なさる.

title: なさる
summary: なさる is the honorific (尊敬語) verb for する, used to raise the person whose action you are describing. Its polite form is irregular: なさる → なさいます (not なさります). Reach for it when a customer, teacher, or superior 'does' something and you want to show respect toward them.
pitfalls: The polite form drops the り: it's なさいます, not なさります.
なさる honors someone else's action; never use it about yourself — for your own actions the humble word is いたす.

examples.ja: 先生は毎朝、公園で散歩をなさいます。
examples.en: The teacher takes a walk in the park every morning.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]は｜毎朝[まいあさ]、｜公園[こうえん]で｜散歩[さんぽ]をなさいます。

examples.ja: 部長は明日の会議に出席なさいますか。
examples.en: Will the department head attend tomorrow's meeting?
examples.f: ｜部長[ぶちょう]は｜明日[あした]の｜会議[かいぎ]に｜出席[しゅっせき]なさいますか。

antonyms.note: お〜する humbly lowers your own action; なさる honorifically raises someone else's.

related.note: お〜になる is the general honorific frame; なさる is the special honorific specifically for する.
いらっしゃる is the matching special honorific for いる・行く・来る.
なさい, the child-directed command, is historically the imperative of なさる.

title: など
meaning: such as; and so on; etc.
summary: など comes after a noun (or a short list of nouns) to mean 'and so on' or 'things like ~'. It signals that the item named is only an example and the list is not exhaustive. It often follows nouns already linked with や: ペンやノートなど = pens, notebooks, and the like.
pitfalls: など marks the list as open-ended ('and others'). If you truly mean a complete list, drop it.
In casual speech なんか and なんて cover similar ground, but they can add a dismissive nuance that plain など does not.

examples.ja: 週末は買い物や掃除などをします。
examples.en: On weekends I do things like shopping and cleaning.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜買い物[かいもの]や｜掃除[そうじ]などをします。

examples.ja: かばんの中にペンやノートなどが入っています。
examples.en: There are pens, notebooks, and so on in the bag.
examples.f: かばんの｜中[なか]にペンやノートなどが｜入[はい]っています。

related.note: や links nouns as a partial list; など caps that list with 'and so on'.
とか〜とか lists casual examples; など tacks 'etc.' onto a noun or や-list.
なんか・なんて are the colloquial cousins that can add a belittling tone.

title: なら
meaning: if; if it's the case that ~
summary: なら sets up a condition by picking up something just mentioned or assumed: 'if (we're talking about) ~, then ...'. It attaches straight to a noun or to the plain form of a verb or adjective. Its special job is responding to a topic the other person raised — 'if that's what you mean, then here's my point'.
pitfalls: After a noun, use bare なら, not だなら: 日本語なら, not 日本語だなら.
Unlike たら or と, the なら clause need not happen before the main clause; it just frames 'given that ~'. 'If you're going to Kyoto (now/later), take the train' works either way.

examples.ja: 京都に行くなら、電車が便利ですよ。
examples.en: If you're going to Kyoto, the train is convenient.
examples.f: ｜京都[きょうと]に｜行[い]くなら、｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜便利[べんり]ですよ。

examples.ja: 「辞書はどこ？」「辞書なら、机の上にあるよ。」
examples.en: "Where's the dictionary?" "The dictionary? It's on the desk."
examples.f: 「｜辞書[じしょ]はどこ？」「｜辞書[じしょ]なら、｜机[つくえ]の｜上[うえ]にあるよ。」

related.note: たら is a general 'if/when' about what happens next; なら takes up a topic and reacts to it.
と states an automatic result; なら frames a supposition raised in the conversation.
ば gives a hypothetical condition; なら responds to a premise you accept for the sake of argument.

title: なるべく
summary: なるべく is an adverb meaning 'as much as possible' or 'if you can'. Place it before a verb, adjective, or whole clause to say you want that done to the greatest extent circumstances allow: なるべく早く = as early as possible. It softens a wish or instruction into 'do your best to ~' rather than a hard demand.
pitfalls: なるべく leaves room ('if you can'); it is not an absolute 'must'. For a firm requirement use 〜なければいけない.
It sits before the word it modifies, like other adverbs: なるべく安い店, not 安いなるべく店.

examples.ja: 明日は大事な日だから、なるべく早く寝ます。
examples.en: Tomorrow is an important day, so I'll go to bed as early as I can.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]は｜大事[だいじ]な｜日[ひ]だから、なるべく｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]ます。

examples.ja: お金があまりないので、なるべく安い店で買います。
examples.en: I don't have much money, so I buy at the cheapest shops I can.
examples.f: お｜金[かね]があまりないので、なるべく｜安[やす]い｜店[みせ]で｜買[か]います。

related.note: ようにする expresses making an effort; なるべく often pairs with it (なるべく〜ようにする) to mean 'try to ~ as much as possible'.

title: 何＋助数詞＋か
meaning: some; several; a few (of a counted thing)
summary: Putting 何 before a counter and か after it gives a vague 'some / several / a few' of that thing: 何回か = a few times, 何人か = several people, 何日か = a number of days. 何＋counter alone asks 'how many?'; the か turns that question into an unspecified small number.
pitfalls: The か is what makes it 'some'. Without it, 何回 is the question 'how many times?'.
This means a small, unspecified number, not 'many'. For 'many times' use 何回も with も instead of か.

examples.ja: 去年、京都へ何回か行きました。
examples.en: Last year I went to Kyoto several times.
examples.f: ｜去年[きょねん]、｜京都[きょうと]へ｜何[なん]｜回[かい]か｜行[い]きました。

examples.ja: パーティーには知らない人が何人かいました。
examples.en: There were several people I didn't know at the party.
examples.f: パーティーには｜知[し]らない｜人[ひと]が｜何[なん]｜人[にん]かいました。

related.note: 疑問詞＋か (だれか, どこか) is the same 'question word + か → some' idea applied to other question words.
だれか・どこか make 'someone / somewhere'; 何＋counter＋か makes 'some (number) of a counted thing'.

title: に
meaning: per; in (X times per a period)
summary: This に marks a period of time as the base for a frequency: 'X times per that period'. The pattern is [time span] に [number + counter]: 一週間に三回 = three times a week, 一日に二回 = twice a day. The time span comes first with に, then the count of how often within it.
pitfalls: Order matters: the period takes に and comes first — 一週間に三回, not 三回に一週間.
This is a frequency-per-period use of に, separate from に marking a point in time (三時に = at three o'clock).

examples.ja: 私は週に二回ジムに行きます。
examples.en: I go to the gym twice a week.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜週[しゅう]に｜二[に]｜回[かい]ジムに｜行[い]きます。

examples.ja: この電車は一時間に四本来ます。
examples.en: This train comes four times an hour.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は｜一[いち]｜時間[じかん]に｜四[よん]｜本[ほん]｜来[き]ます。

related.note: ごとに means 'every / at each ~'; the frequency に states how many times within one period.
おきに sets the interval between occurrences; this に sets how often per a fixed period.
The base particle に has many roles; this is its 'per (period)' frequency sense.

title: に気がつく
summary: に気がつく means to notice or realize something. The thing you become aware of is marked with に: 間違いに気がつく = to notice a mistake. To realize a whole fact, nominalize the clause with こと first: 〜ことに気がつく. It describes the moment awareness dawns, often something you hadn't been conscious of before.
structure: Sentence［plain form］ ＋ こと ＋ に気がつく
pitfalls: Mark what you notice with に, not を: 間違いに気がつく, not 間違いを気がつく.
To notice a fact stated as a clause, insert こと: 忘れたことに気がついた, not 忘れたに気がついた.

examples.ja: 家に帰ってから、傘を忘れたことに気がつきました。
examples.en: After getting home, I realized I'd forgotten my umbrella.
examples.f: ｜家[いえ]に｜帰[かえ]ってから、｜傘[かさ]を｜忘[わす]れたことに｜気[き]がつきました。

examples.ja: 自分の間違いに気がついて、恥ずかしくなりました。
examples.en: I noticed my own mistake and got embarrassed.
examples.f: ｜自分[じぶん]の｜間違[まちが]いに｜気[き]がついて、｜恥[は]ずかしくなりました。

related.note: The に here is the target-marking particle; it points at what you become aware of.

title: 〜にする・〜くする
summary: This pattern says someone deliberately changes a thing into a state. With nouns and な-adjectives, use にする (きれいにする = make it clean); with い-adjectives, swap い for く and add する (大きくする = make it bigger). The subject actively causes the change, unlike なる, where the thing changes on its own.
pitfalls: Match the connector to the word type: な-adjective/noun take に (静かにする), い-adjectives take く (安くする) — not 安いにする.
This is the 'make it become' pair to なる ('become'); don't confuse it with にする meaning 'decide on / choose' (コーヒーにする).

examples.ja: お客さんが来るので、部屋をきれいにしました。
examples.en: A guest is coming, so I made the room tidy.
examples.f: お｜客[きゃく]さんが｜来[く]るので、｜部屋[へや]をきれいにしました。

examples.ja: 音が大きいので、少し小さくしてください。
examples.en: The sound is loud, so please make it a little quieter.
examples.f: ｜音[おと]が｜大[おお]きいので、｜少[すこ]し｜小[ちい]さくしてください。

antonyms.note: 〜になる・〜くなる is a change that happens by itself; にする・くする is someone making the change happen.

related.note: にする also means 'decide on / choose'; here it means 'turn something into ~'.
ことにする decides on an action; にする・くする changes a thing's state.

title: に見える
summary: に見える describes the impression something gives to the eye: it 'looks like' or 'appears to be' ~. A noun or な-adjective takes に before 見える: お寺に見える = looks like a temple, 元気に見える = looks cheerful. It reports how a thing strikes you visually, which may differ from how it really is.
pitfalls: This 見える means 'appear/seem', not 'can be seen'. Plain 見える (山が見える = the mountain is visible) is the 'visible' sense.
い-adjectives don't take に here — say 若く見える (looks young) with 〜く, not 若いに見える.

examples.ja: あの建物は古いお寺に見えますが、実は新しいです。
examples.en: That building looks like an old temple, but it's actually new.
examples.f: あの｜建物[たてもの]は｜古[ふる]いお｜寺[てら]に｜見[み]えますが、｜実[じつ]は｜新[あたら]しいです。

examples.ja: 彼女はいつも元気に見えます。
examples.en: She always looks cheerful.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]はいつも｜元気[げんき]に｜見[み]えます。

related.note: Plain 見える means 'is visible / can be seen'; に見える adds 'appears to be'.
そうだ also reads an impression off appearance; に見える states what something resembles.
ようだ draws a broader 'it seems' inference; に見える stays with the visual look.

title: の次に
meaning: next after ~; second to ~ (in order or rank)
summary: の次に places one thing right after another in a sequence or ranking: 'next after ~' or 'second to ~'. Noun の次に names the reference point, and what follows is what comes immediately after it — the second-tallest after Mt. Fuji, or the thing you'll do next after English.
pitfalls: Use の, not を: 英語の次に, not 英語を次に.
For ranking, の次に marks second place behind the top item, so it usually appears alongside a superlative like 一番.

examples.ja: 富士山の次に高い山を知っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know the second-tallest mountain (after Mt. Fuji)?
examples.f: ｜富士山[ふじさん]の｜次[つぎ]に｜高[たか]い｜山[やま]を｜知[し]っていますか。

examples.ja: 英語の次に、フランス語を勉強したいです。
examples.en: After English, I want to study French next.
examples.f: ｜英語[えいご]の｜次[つぎ]に、フランス｜語[ご]を｜勉強[べんきょう]したいです。

related.note: 一番 names the outright top; の次に names what stands immediately below it.
の中で marks the group; の次に orders items within such a ranking.

title: の中で
summary: の中で marks a group or category as the field you are picking from or comparing within: 'among ~ / of all ~'. クラスの中で = among the class, 四季の中で = of the four seasons. It sets the scope, so it very often pairs with 一番 to single out the top member of that group.
pitfalls: For a group of concrete items, で after の中 is standard (クラスの中で). で (rather than に) fits because a comparison is being made within that scope.
This 中 is read なか, not じゅう/ちゅう; it means 'within the set', not 'throughout a time'.

examples.ja: クラスの中で、田中さんが一番背が高いです。
examples.en: In the class, Tanaka is the tallest.
examples.f: クラスの｜中[なか]で、｜田中[たなか]さんが｜一番[いちばん]｜背[せ]が｜高[たか]いです。

examples.ja: 四季の中で、秋が一番好きです。
examples.en: Of the four seasons, I like autumn the most.
examples.f: ｜四季[しき]の｜中[なか]で、｜秋[あき]が｜一番[いちばん]｜好[す]きです。

related.note: 〜の中で〜が一番〜 is the full superlative frame this phrase forms the first half of.
一番 picks the top item; の中で names the group it is picked from.

title: のに
summary: This のに links two clauses that clash, adding a feeling of surprise, dissatisfaction, or complaint: 'even though A, B (unexpectedly)'. It follows the plain form; after nouns and な-adjectives, insert な (な-adjective な のに, Noun な のに). Unlike neutral けど, のに carries an emotional 'and yet' that things didn't go as they should have.
pitfalls: Don't confuse it with the purpose のに ('in order to'); that one follows a dictionary verb and pairs with words like 使う/かかる/必要, with no sense of contrast.
Nouns and な-adjectives need な before のに: 学生なのに, 静かなのに — not 学生のに.

examples.ja: たくさん勉強したのに、テストの点が悪かった。
examples.en: Even though I studied a lot, my test score was bad.
examples.f: たくさん｜勉強[べんきょう]したのに、テストの｜点[てん]が｜悪[わる]かった。

examples.ja: 冬なのに、今日はとても暖かいです。
examples.en: Even though it's winter, today is very warm.
examples.f: ｜冬[ふゆ]なのに、｜今日[きょう]はとても｜暖[あたた]かいです。

related.note: Same shape のに but 'in order to'; it follows a dictionary verb and shows no contrast.
けど is a neutral 'but'; のに adds surprise or dissatisfaction that the result went against expectation.
ても is 'even if' about a supposed case; のに is 'even though' about something that actually happened.

title: のに
summary: This のに frames an action as the purpose you are evaluating something against: 'for doing ~ / in order to ~'. It follows a dictionary-form verb and leads into a comment on what that task takes — time, tools, cost, or convenience: 覚えるのに一週間かかった = it took a week to memorize. It commonly appears with 使う, かかる, いる, 必要, 便利.
pitfalls: Keep the verb in dictionary form: 行くのに, not 行ったのに (that would be the 'although' のに).
This purpose のに suits concrete tasks judged by cost or usefulness. For someone's goal or intention, ために is usually more natural.

examples.ja: このケーキを作るのに、二時間かかりました。
examples.en: It took two hours to make this cake.
examples.f: このケーキを｜作[つく]るのに、｜二[に]｜時間[じかん]かかりました。

examples.ja: 駅に行くのに、バスを使います。
examples.en: I use the bus to get to the station.
examples.f: ｜駅[えき]に｜行[い]くのに、バスを｜使[つか]います。

related.note: Same のに shape but 'although'; that one carries contrast and can follow past forms.
ために also means 'in order to'; のに focuses on what a concrete task requires (time, tools, cost).
ように sets an aim with non-volitional verbs; this のに measures effort against a purpose.

title: のは～だ
summary: のは〜だ builds a cleft sentence that spotlights one part of the idea. Nominalize a clause with の, mark it with は as the known information, and end with the highlighted element plus だ: 私が生まれたのは北海道です = it was in Hokkaido that I was born. It answers 'which / where / who / when' by putting that answer in the だ slot.
structure: Sentence［plain form］ ＋ の ＋ は ＋ Noun／Phrase ＋ だ
pitfalls: The の here nominalizes the clause; don't drop it — 生まれたのは, not 生まれたは.
The stressed answer lands right before だ. Compare 私が買ったのは本です (what I bought was a book) with a plain 私は本を買いました (I bought a book), which highlights nothing.

examples.ja: 私が生まれたのは北海道です。
examples.en: It was in Hokkaido that I was born.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]が｜生[う]まれたのは｜北海道[ほっかいどう]です。

examples.ja: 昨日のパーティーに来なかったのは山田さんです。
examples.en: The one who didn't come to yesterday's party was Yamada.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]のパーティーに｜来[こ]なかったのは｜山田[やまだ]さんです。

related.note: The の in のは〜だ is the nominalizer, turning a whole clause into a noun that は can mark.
Explanatory んです explains a situation; のは〜だ instead singles out one element as the focus.

title: のように・のような
romaji: no you ni no you na
summary: のように and のような compare something to a noun. Use のように before a verb or adjective (歌手のように歌う = sing like a singer) and のような before a noun (雪のような花 = flowers like snow). The noun before の is the thing being resembled, giving a vivid 'just like ~' comparison.
pitfalls: Pick the ending by what follows: のように modifies a verb or adjective, のような modifies a noun — 雪のような花, not 雪のように花.
Because のよう attaches to a noun, keep the の: 子どものように, not 子どもように.

examples.ja: 彼女は歌手のように歌が上手です。
examples.en: She sings well, like a professional singer.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜歌手[かしゅ]のように｜歌[うた]が｜上手[じょうず]です。

examples.ja: 雪のような白い花が咲きました。
examples.en: White flowers like snow bloomed.
examples.f: ｜雪[ゆき]のような｜白[しろ]い｜花[はな]が｜咲[さ]きました。

related.note: みたいに・みたいな is the casual equivalent of のように・のような after a noun.
ように・ような can follow verbs and clauses too; のように・のような attaches specifically to a noun.
ようだ is the predicate 'seems / is like' form of the same よう.

title: ば
summary: The ば conditional sets up a general 'if A, then B' link: when the condition holds, the result naturally follows. It suits natural consequences, general truths, and advice. Build it by changing a verb's final -u to -eba (押す → 押せば), an い-adjective's い to ければ (安い → 安ければ), and a noun or な-adjective with なら（ば）; the negative uses なければ.
structure: い-adjective［ー い → ければ］
pitfalls: ば leans toward general or hypothetical conditions. When the main clause is a request or command tied to a one-time action, 〜たら is more natural: 駅に着いたら電話して, not 着けば電話して.
The negative condition is 〜なければ: 行かなければ (if you don't go).

examples.ja: 春になれば、桜が咲きます。
examples.en: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.f: ｜春[はる]になれば、｜桜[さくら]が｜咲[さ]きます。

examples.ja: ボタンを押せば、電気がつきます。
examples.en: If you press the button, the light comes on.
examples.f: ボタンを｜押[お]せば、｜電気[でんき]がつきます。

related.note: たら fits one-time 'once A happens, B' sequences; ば states a more general condition-result rule.
と is for automatic, inevitable results; ば allows advice and commands more freely.
なら responds to a topic just raised ('if that's the case'); ば states a plain condition.

title: は～が～は
meaning: contrast: A is ~, but B is ~
summary: This pattern sets two things against each other in one sentence. Both A and B take the contrastive は, and the middle が works as the conjunction 'but', joining the two clauses. The result spotlights how A and B differ: 肉は食べますが、魚は食べません = I eat meat, but I don't eat fish.
structure: Noun A ＋ は ＋ ～ ＋ が、＋ Noun B ＋ は ＋ ～
pitfalls: Both は here are contrastive: they exist to highlight the A-versus-B difference, not merely to name topics.
The middle が is the conjunction 'but', not the subject-marking が.

examples.ja: 肉は食べますが、魚は食べません。
examples.en: I eat meat, but I don't eat fish.
examples.f: ｜肉[にく]は｜食[た]べますが、｜魚[さかな]は｜食[た]べません。

examples.ja: 夏は暑いですが、冬は寒いです。
examples.en: Summers are hot, but winters are cold.
examples.f: ｜夏[なつ]は｜暑[あつ]いですが、｜冬[ふゆ]は｜寒[さむ]いです。

related.note: けど is the casual 'but'; this pattern pairs it with double は to make the contrast explicit on both sides.
しかし is a formal 'however' that starts a new sentence; は～が～は draws the contrast inside one sentence.

title: 場合は
meaning: in the case that ~; in the event of ~
summary: 場合 means 'case' or 'situation', and 〜場合は presents a hypothetical situation and states what to do if it arises. It attaches to plain forms of verbs and adjectives, な-adjective＋な, and noun＋の. Common in rules, manuals, and official notices: 'in the case that A, (do) B'.
pitfalls: 場合 is on the formal side — think manuals, contracts, and notices; in casual speech 〜たら or 〜とき is more common.
A noun connects with の: 地震の場合は, not 地震場合は.

examples.ja: 雨の場合は、試合は中止です。
examples.en: In the event of rain, the match will be cancelled.
examples.f: ｜雨[あめ]の｜場合[ばあい]は、｜試合[しあい]は｜中止[ちゅうし]です。

examples.ja: 分からない場合は、係の人に聞いてください。
examples.en: If you don't understand, please ask a staff member.
examples.f: ｜分[わ]からない｜場合[ばあい]は、｜係[かかり]の｜人[ひと]に｜聞[き]いてください。

related.note: たら is the everyday 'if/when'; 場合は is the formal wording used in rules and notices.
とき marks the time an event actually happens; 場合は sets up a hypothetical situation to prepare for.
なら picks up a topic just raised; 場合は presents a condition on its own terms.

title: ばかり
summary: ばかり singles out one thing and says it's the only one — 'nothing but ~'. After a noun it means 'only that thing'; after a verb's て form (〜てばかり) it means someone does nothing but that action. It often carries a nuance of excess or complaint that neutral だけ lacks.
pitfalls: Unlike neutral だけ, ばかり often adds a critical 'always just / too much' feeling: 遊んでばかり implies too much playing.
This is the 'nothing but' ばかり — different from the 'just did' ばかり (〜たばかり) and the 'about/approximately' ばかり.

examples.ja: 弟はゲームばかりしています。
examples.en: My little brother does nothing but play games.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]はゲームばかりしています。

examples.ja: 甘いものばかり食べないでください。
examples.en: Please don't eat only sweet things.
examples.f: ｜甘[あま]いものばかり｜食[た]べないでください。

related.note: だけ is a neutral 'only' with no complaint; ばかり tends to imply excess.
しか〜ない means 'only' with a negative verb and a 'nothing more' feel; ばかり keeps a positive verb.
のみ is a formal, written 'only'; ばかり is conversational and often critical.

title: はずがない
meaning: there's no way ~; cannot possibly be
summary: はずがない voices the speaker's strong confidence that something is not so — 'there's no way that ~'. You reason from what you know and conclude the situation is impossible or highly unlikely. It attaches to plain forms, with な-adjective＋な and noun＋の; はずはない is a slightly softer variant.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ はずがない
な-adjective ＋ な ＋ はずがない
Noun ＋ の ＋ はずがない
pitfalls: This is confident logical deduction, not a sensory guess; for 'it doesn't look like it' use 〜そうにない or みたい.
It is the flat denial of an expectation — the negative counterpart of はずだ.

examples.ja: 彼がそんなうそをつくはずがない。
examples.en: There's no way he would tell such a lie.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]がそんなうそをつくはずがない。

examples.ja: あの店が今日休みのはずがない。
examples.en: There's no way that shop is closed today.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]が｜今日[きょう]｜休[やす]みのはずがない。

synonyms.note: わけがない is a very close 'there's no way'; はずがない frames it as a defied expectation.

antonyms.note: はずだ expects something to be true; はずがない insists it cannot be.

title: はずだ
meaning: should be; ought to be; supposed to be
summary: はずだ states a conclusion the speaker expects to be true based on reason or evidence — 'it should be the case that ~'. It reflects what logically follows from what you know, not a personal wish. It attaches to plain forms, with な-adjective＋な and noun＋の.
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ はずだ
pitfalls: はずだ means 'I expect this from what I know', not 'you should do it'. For advice or obligation use 〜べきだ or 〜たほうがいい.
It expresses expectation, not duty — don't read it as the 'must/have to' of obligation grammar.

examples.ja: この時間なら、店はもう閉まっているはずです。
examples.en: At this hour, the shop should already be closed.
examples.f: この｜時間[じかん]なら、｜店[みせ]はもう｜閉[し]まっているはずです。

examples.ja: 彼は毎日勉強しているから、試験に合格するはずだ。
examples.en: He studies every day, so he should pass the exam.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜毎日[まいにち]｜勉強[べんきょう]しているから、｜試験[しけん]に｜合格[ごうかく]するはずだ。

antonyms.note: はずがない denies the expectation ('no way'); はずだ affirms it ('should be').
