related.note: だろう is a looser 'probably'; はずだ rests on concrete grounds for the expectation.
ようだ reports how something seems from direct evidence; はずだ reasons out what ought to be true.

title: ばよかった
meaning: should have ~; I wish I had ~
summary: 〜ばよかった looks back on something and expresses regret — 'I should have ~ / I wish I had ~'. Built from the ば conditional plus よかった ('would have been good'), it says that meeting the condition would have led to a better outcome. To regret having done something, negate the condition with 〜なければよかった.
structure: Verb［え-stem］＋ ば ＋ よかった
Verb［ない → なければ］＋ よかった
pitfalls: Plain 〜ばよかった regrets NOT doing; to regret having done something, negate the condition: 言わなければよかった (I wish I hadn't said it).
It is hindsight about the past, so it pairs with outcomes already known, not future plans.

examples.ja: もっと早く家を出ればよかった。
examples.en: I should have left home earlier.
examples.f: もっと｜早[はや]く｜家[いえ]を｜出[で]ればよかった。

examples.ja: あんなことを言わなければよかった。
examples.en: I wish I hadn't said something like that.
examples.f: あんなことを｜言[い]わなければよかった。

related.note: ば is the underlying conditional; ばよかった adds よかった to turn it into hindsight regret.
〜たらよかった expresses the same regret with the たら conditional instead of ば.

title: 必要がある
meaning: it is necessary to ~; need to ~
summary: 必要 means 'necessity', so 〜必要がある states that doing something is necessary — 'there's a need to ~'. A verb in dictionary form plus 必要がある says an action is required; a noun takes が directly (Noun＋が必要). The negative 必要はない means 'there's no need to'.
pitfalls: Use the dictionary form before 必要がある: 予約する必要がある, not 予約した必要がある.
It states an objective need, softer and more factual than the forceful 'must' of 〜なければならない.
The negative 必要はない means 'no need to' — it removes the necessity rather than forbidding the action.

examples.ja: 明日までにこの書類を出す必要があります。
examples.en: You need to submit these documents by tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]までにこの｜書類[しょるい]を｜出[だ]す｜必要[ひつよう]があります。

examples.ja: パスポートを持っていく必要がありますか。
examples.en: Do I need to take my passport?
examples.f: パスポートを｜持[も]っていく｜必要[ひつよう]がありますか。

related.note: なければならない is a firmer 'must'; 必要がある states a plainer factual need.
なくてはいけない stresses an obligation you can't avoid; 必要がある simply notes what's required.
べきだ gives a 'should' based on what's right; 必要がある points to a practical necessity.

title: ほかに・ほかには
summary: ほかに means 'besides / in addition' and introduces something beyond what's already been mentioned. As a question it asks 'anything else?'; in a statement it adds a further item. With a negative, ほかに〜ない means 'nothing/no one else'. A noun connects with の: お茶のほかに (besides tea).
pitfalls: ほかに adds a further item ('and also'); to exclude something ('except X') use 〜以外.
With a negative, ほかに〜ない means 'nothing else': ほかに方法がない (there's no other way).

examples.ja: ほかに質問はありますか。
examples.en: Do you have any other questions?
examples.f: ほかに｜質問[しつもん]はありますか。

examples.ja: お茶のほかに、コーヒーもあります。
examples.en: Besides tea, we also have coffee.
examples.f: お｜茶[ちゃ]のほかに、コーヒーもあります。

related.note: 以外 excludes ('except for X'); ほかに adds something beyond what was mentioned.
だけでなく is a set 'not only X but also Y'; ほかに loosely tacks on 'and besides that'.

title: ほとんど
meaning: almost all; almost; hardly (with a negative)
summary: ほとんど means 'almost / nearly all' in positive sentences and 'hardly / almost never' when the verb is negative. As an adverb it comes before the verb: ほとんど終わった (almost finished), ほとんど分からない (hardly understand). Its meaning flips entirely with the polarity of the verb.
structure: ほとんど ＋ Verb［ない form］
pitfalls: Same word, opposite feel by polarity: ほとんど食べた (ate almost all of it) vs ほとんど食べない (hardly eats).
As a noun modifier it takes の: ほとんどの人 (almost everyone).

examples.ja: 宿題はほとんど終わりました。
examples.en: I've almost finished the homework.
examples.f: ｜宿題[しゅくだい]はほとんど｜終[お]わりました。

examples.ja: お酒はほとんど飲みません。
examples.en: I hardly drink alcohol.
examples.f: お｜酒[さけ]はほとんど｜飲[の]みません。

related.note: あまり〜ない means 'not very much'; ほとんど〜ない pushes further to 'hardly at all'.

title: 毎～のように
summary: 毎 means 'every', and 毎〜のように adds 'as if', giving 'almost every ~'. It attaches to time words such as 日 (day), 週 (week), or 年 (year): 毎日のように = practically every day. The のように softens 毎 from a strict 'every' into 'so often it might as well be every'.
structure: 毎 ＋ Noun［time period］＋ のように
pitfalls: The のように is what adds 'almost': 毎日 is literally 'every day', while 毎日のように is 'almost every day'.
Use it with recurring time nouns (日・週・月・年), not one-off events.

examples.ja: 彼は毎日のように外食している。
examples.en: He eats out almost every day.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]は｜毎日[まいにち]のように｜外食[がいしょく]している。

examples.ja: 最近、毎週のように出かけている。
examples.en: Lately I go out almost every week.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、｜毎週[まいしゅう]のように｜出[で]かけている。

related.note: ごとに marks a regular interval ('every X'); 毎〜のように means 'almost, but not strictly, every'.
たびに means 'every time (an event) happens'; 毎〜のように counts recurring time periods.

title: または
summary: または connects two options and means 'or / alternatively'. It's a formal, written-style connector used in instructions, forms, and rules to offer a choice between A and B. It can join nouns or whole clauses and is more formal than the casual ways of saying 'or'.
structure: Noun A ＋ または ＋ Noun B
pitfalls: または is formal and written; in casual speech people use 〜か or それとも.
It offers alternatives in a statement or instruction; to ask 'A or B?' as a question, それとも is more natural.

examples.ja: ペンまたは鉛筆で書いてください。
examples.en: Please write with a pen or a pencil.
examples.f: ペンまたは｜鉛筆[えんぴつ]で｜書[か]いてください。

examples.ja: 電話またはメールでご連絡ください。
examples.en: Please contact us by phone or email.
examples.f: ｜電話[でんわ]またはメールでご｜連絡[れんらく]ください。

related.note: それとも offers 'or' between choices in a question; または states alternatives in formal instructions.

title: 真っ～
meaning: intensifier prefix: completely; deep; right (in the middle)
summary: 真っ is a prefix that intensifies the word after it, meaning 'completely / deep / dead ~'. It attaches to a fixed set of color and position words: 真っ赤 (deep red), 真っ白 (pure white), 真っ暗 (pitch dark), 真ん中 (the very middle). The small っ (or ん) is part of the set form.
structure: 真っ ＋ Noun ／ Adjective root（真っ赤・真っ白・真っ黒・真っ暗）
真ん ＋ Noun（真ん中・真ん前）
pitfalls: 真っ combines only with a fixed set of words; you can't freely attach it to any adjective.
Before some sounds it becomes 真ん: 真ん中 (dead center), 真ん前 (right in front), not 真っ中.

examples.ja: 部屋が真っ暗で、何も見えなかった。
examples.en: The room was pitch dark and I couldn't see anything.
examples.f: ｜部屋[へや]が｜真っ暗[まっくら]で、｜何[なに]も｜見[み]えなかった。

examples.ja: 空が真っ赤になった。
examples.en: The sky turned deep red.
examples.f: ｜空[そら]が｜真っ赤[まっか]になった。

title: までに
summary: までに marks a deadline — the point by which an action must be finished. Unlike まで ('until', for continuous actions), までに is for one-time actions completed at or before a limit: 5時までに帰る (be home by 5). It attaches to a time noun or a verb in dictionary form.
pitfalls: までに (deadline, one-time action) vs まで (continuous action up to a point): 5時まで待つ (wait until 5), but 5時までに来る (come by 5).
Don't use までに with a continuing action like 'wait' or 'stay'; those take まで.

examples.ja: 金曜日までにレポートを出してください。
examples.en: Please hand in the report by Friday.
examples.f: ｜金曜日[きんようび]までにレポートを｜出[だ]してください。

examples.ja: 暗くなるまでに帰りましょう。
examples.en: Let's get home before it gets dark.
examples.f: ｜暗[くら]くなるまでに｜帰[かえ]りましょう。

related.note: まで marks a continuous action lasting up to a point; までに marks a deadline for a one-time action.

title: まま
summary: まま describes a state left unchanged while something else happens — 'as it is / still in that condition'. Something stays the way it was instead of being set right: 窓を開けたまま出かけた (went out with the window left open). It attaches to た form, ない form, な-adjective＋な, or noun＋の.
pitfalls: The state carries over into the next action: 靴をはいたまま入る (enter with shoes still on).
Different from ながら: ながら is two actions happening at once; まま is one unchanged state persisting during another action.

examples.ja: 窓を開けたまま出かけてしまった。
examples.en: I went out leaving the window open.
examples.f: ｜窓[まど]を｜開[あ]けたまま｜出[で]かけてしまった。

examples.ja: 立ったままで食べないでください。
examples.en: Please don't eat while standing.
examples.f: ｜立[た]ったままで｜食[た]べないでください。

related.note: ながら is doing two actions simultaneously; まま is keeping one state unchanged during another action.

title: 見える
summary: 見える means something comes into view on its own — it's visible, you can see it — without any deliberate effort to look. The thing seen is marked with が: 山が見える (a mountain is visible). It describes spontaneous visibility, distinct from the effortful 'be able to watch' of 見られる.
pitfalls: 見える is spontaneous visibility (something enters your sight); 見られる is the potential 'can watch/view' by choice, as in 映画が見られる (able to see a movie).
Mark what is seen with が, not を: 海が見える, not 海を見える.

examples.ja: ここから海が見えます。
examples.en: You can see the sea from here.
examples.f: ここから｜海[うみ]が｜見[み]えます。

examples.ja: 天気がいい日は、遠くの山がよく見える。
examples.en: On clear days, the distant mountains are clearly visible.
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]がいい｜日[ひ]は、｜遠[とお]くの｜山[やま]がよく｜見[み]える。

related.note: 聞こえる is the same spontaneous ability for sound ('can hear'); 見える is for sight.
〜ように見える means 'looks/appears as if'; plain 見える here means literally visible to the eye.

title: みたいだ
summary: みたいだ voices a guess or impression from what the speaker sees, hears, or senses — 'it seems / looks like ~'. It's the casual, conversational counterpart of ようだ. It attaches straight to plain forms and to nouns with no の: 雨みたいだ (looks like rain).
structure: Verb ／ い-adjective［plain form］＋ みたいだ
pitfalls: みたいだ attaches directly to a noun — 学生みたいだ, not 学生のみたいだ (that の belongs to ようだ: 学生のようだ).
It's casual; in formal writing or speech, ようだ is the safer choice.

examples.ja: 外は寒いみたいだ。みんなコートを着ている。
examples.en: It seems cold outside — everyone's wearing coats.
examples.f: ｜外[そと]は｜寒[さむ]いみたいだ。みんなコートを｜着[き]ている。

examples.ja: 彼はこの町のことをよく知っているみたいだ。
examples.en: He seems to know this town well.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はこの｜町[まち]のことをよく｜知[し]っているみたいだ。

synonyms.note: ようだ is the formal counterpart of the same 'seems like' guess; みたいだ is the casual version.

related.note: らしい leans on outside information ('apparently, I hear'); みたいだ leans on the speaker's own impression.
〜そうだ judges from immediate appearance ('looks like it will'); みたいだ draws a broader impression.
みたいな・みたいに is the same word used to say 'like/similar to'; みたいだ ends a sentence as a guess.

title: みたいに・みたいな
summary: みたいな and みたいに express resemblance — 'like / similar to' a given example. みたいな modifies a noun (夢みたいな話, a dream-like story), while みたいに modifies a verb or adjective (子どもみたいに笑う, laugh like a child). It's the casual counterpart of ような・ように.
structure: Noun ＋ みたいに ＋ Verb ／ Adjective
pitfalls: みたいな before a noun, みたいに before a verb or adjective — just like な vs に on な-adjectives.
This is the 'resemblance' use; the same word ending a sentence as みたいだ instead makes a guess ('seems like').

examples.ja: 彼女は歌手みたいに歌が上手だ。
examples.en: She sings as well as a professional singer.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜歌手[かしゅ]みたいに｜歌[うた]が｜上手[じょうず]だ。

examples.ja: 夢みたいな話ですね。
examples.en: That's a dream-like story, isn't it.
examples.f: ｜夢[ゆめ]みたいな｜話[はなし]ですね。

synonyms.note: ような・ように is the formal equivalent; みたいな・みたいに is the casual, conversational form.

related.note: みたいだ ends a sentence as a guess ('seems like'); みたいな・みたいに says 'like/similar to'.

title: 命令形
summary: The 命令形 (imperative) is the plainest, most forceful way to order someone to do something — 'Do it!'. Godan verbs change their final -u to -e (書く → 書け, 待つ → 待て), ichidan verbs replace る with ろ (食べる → 食べろ), and the irregulars are しろ (する) and 来い (来る). It is strong and rough, used for orders, warnings, signs, and cheering.
structure: Verb（godan）［ー u → e］（書く → 書け）
Verb（ichidan）［る → ろ］（見る → 見ろ）
する → しろ ／ 来る → 来い
pitfalls: The imperative is blunt and can sound harsh; for a polite request use 〜てください, built on the て form.
ください never attaches to the imperative: 食べろください is not Japanese — the polite form is 食べてください.
It shows up mostly in fixed contexts: sports cheers (頑張れ！), warning signs (止まれ), and quoting an order — not everyday polite conversation.

examples.ja: 頑張れ！あと少しだ。
examples.en: Go for it! Just a little more.
examples.f: ｜頑張[がんば]れ！あと｜少[すこ]しだ。

examples.ja: 危ないから、早く逃げろ！
examples.en: It's dangerous, so hurry and run!
examples.f: ｜危[あぶ]ないから、｜早[はや]く｜逃[に]げろ！

antonyms.note: 〜な is the negative command ('don't do it'); the 命令形 is the positive command ('do it').

related.note: なさい is a firm but gentler order (parent to child, exam instructions); the imperative is rougher.
〜てください is the polite request, built on the て form — the courteous alternative to a bare command.

title: もし
summary: もし is an adverb that signals a supposition is coming. It does not form the conditional by itself — it pairs with a conditional ending like たら, ば, なら, or と, and simply announces early in the sentence that what follows is hypothetical. It often adds a 'just supposing' feel.
structure: もし ＋ Verb［た form］＋ ら
もし ＋ Sentence［with たら／ば／なら］
pitfalls: もし needs a conditional ending to finish the thought; it does not replace たら／ば／なら. Say もし雨が降ったら, not もし雨が降る.
もし flags a hypothesis. For a fact that always follows, drop もし and use a plain conditional or と.

examples.ja: もし時間があったら、美術館に行きたいです。
examples.en: If I have time, I'd like to go to the art museum.
examples.f: もし｜時間[じかん]があったら、｜美術館[びじゅつかん]に｜行[い]きたいです。

examples.ja: もし何か困ったことがあったら、いつでも電話してください。
examples.en: If anything is troubling you, please call anytime.
examples.f: もし｜何[なに]か｜困[こま]ったことがあったら、いつでも｜電話[でんわ]してください。

related.note: もし most often leads into a たら clause, which carries the actual 'if'.
ば is another conditional ending もし can flag; the ば clause does the conditional work.
もし〜なら supposes 'if that's the case'; もし just marks it as hypothetical.

title: ようだ
meaning: it seems that; it appears (from evidence)
summary: ようだ expresses a conjecture the speaker draws from what they can see, hear, or otherwise sense. It is a fairly objective 'it seems / it appears', grounded in evidence rather than a wild guess. It attaches to plain forms; nouns take の and な-adjectives take な before よう.
pitfalls: Nouns need の, not だ: 学生のようだ, not 学生だようだ.
ようだ rests on the speaker's own observation. For something you only heard from someone else, use そうだ (hearsay) or らしい.
In casual speech みたい replaces ようだ with the same meaning: 雨が降ったみたい.

examples.ja: 電気が消えているので、誰もいないようです。
examples.en: The lights are off, so it seems no one is here.
examples.f: ｜電気[でんき]が｜消[き]えているので、｜誰[だれ]もいないようです。

examples.ja: 彼はこの町のことをよく知っているようだ。
examples.en: He seems to know this town well.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はこの｜町[まち]のことをよく｜知[し]っているようだ。

synonyms.note: みたい carries the same 'it seems' sense but is casual and spoken; ようだ is more neutral.

related.note: そうだ reads an impression straight off appearances; ようだ reasons from evidence.
らしい leans on outside or secondhand information; ようだ on the speaker's own observation.
The same よう builds ように・ような for 'like / similar to'.

title: ようと思う
meaning: I think I'll ~; I'm thinking of ~ing
summary: Volitional verb ＋ と思う states a personal intention the speaker has more or less just formed. It is softer than declaring a fixed plan — it presents the decision as your current thinking. Use ようと思っている for an intention you have been holding for a while.
structure: 食べようと思う ／ 行こうと思う
pitfalls: Attach it to the volitional (行こう), not the dictionary form: 行こうと思う, not 行くと思う (which just means 'I think he'll go').
ようと思う reports the speaker's own intention; you cannot use it to state someone else's will directly.
と思っている suggests a longer-held intention; plain と思う, a decision made at the moment of speaking.

examples.ja: 週末は家でゆっくりしようと思います。
examples.en: I think I'll relax at home over the weekend.
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]は｜家[いえ]でゆっくりしようと｜思[おも]います。

examples.ja: 来年、日本語の試験を受けようと思っています。
examples.en: I'm thinking of taking the Japanese exam next year.
examples.f: ｜来年[らいねん]、｜日本語[にほんご]の｜試験[しけん]を｜受[う]けようと｜思[おも]っています。

synonyms.note: つもりだ states a firmer, more settled intention; ようと思う is more 'I've just decided'.

related.note: 予定だ is an arranged, on-the-schedule plan; ようと思う is looser personal thinking.
つもりだ is a firmer intention already held; ようと思う leans toward a fresh decision.

title: ように
meaning: so that; in order to (a state comes about)
summary: ように states the purpose behind an action — you do the main action so that some situation will come about. The clause before ように is usually a state or a potential / negative verb (something you cannot directly will), like 聞こえる, わかる, or 忘れない. It contrasts with ために, whose front clause is a deliberate action.
pitfalls: ように takes a non-volitional verb (potential, negative, or change of state): 見えるように. For a goal reached by deliberate action, use ために: 車を買うために.
No の or な before this ように — it attaches straight to the plain verb.
The two clauses can have different subjects, which suits ように but is awkward for ために.

examples.ja: 後ろの席まで聞こえるように、大きな声で話しました。
examples.en: I spoke in a loud voice so that it would carry to the back seats.
examples.f: ｜後[うし]ろの｜席[せき]まで｜聞[き]こえるように、｜大[おお]きな｜声[こえ]で｜話[はな]しました。

examples.ja: 忘れないように、手にメモを書いた。
examples.en: I wrote a note on my hand so I wouldn't forget.
examples.f: ｜忘[わす]れないように、｜手[て]にメモを｜書[か]いた。

related.note: ために gives a purpose reached by deliberate action; ように, a state you aim to bring about.
ようにする turns such a goal into an ongoing effort to do something.
ようになる describes that aimed-for state actually coming about.

title: ように・ような
summary: This よう compares one thing to another: ような modifies a noun ('a ~ like X'), ように modifies a verb or adjective ('in a ~ way, like X'). It draws a resemblance or gives an example. Nouns connect with の: 夢のような ('dream-like').
structure: Noun ＋ の ＋ ような ＋ Noun
Noun ＋ の ＋ ように ＋ Verb／Adjective
Verb［plain form］＋ ように／ような
pitfalls: ような goes before a noun, ように before a verb or adjective: 子どものような笑顔 vs 子どものように笑う.
Nouns need の: 山のように, not 山ように.
This is the 'resemblance' よう; the same shape also builds ようだ ('it seems') — context tells them apart.

examples.ja: 彼女は歌手のようにきれいな声で歌います。
examples.en: She sings in a beautiful voice, like a singer.
examples.f: ｜彼女[かのじょ]は｜歌手[かしゅ]のようにきれいな｜声[こえ]で｜歌[うた]います。

examples.ja: 氷のように冷たい水でした。
examples.en: It was water as cold as ice.
examples.f: ｜氷[こおり]のように｜冷[つめ]たい｜水[みず]でした。

synonyms.note: みたい is the everyday spoken version of this 'like / similar to' comparison.

related.note: The predicate ようだ 'it seems' is built on the same よう.
らしい (typical of) says something is a fitting example; ように just draws a resemblance.

title: ように～てほしい
meaning: want someone to act so that ~ comes about
summary: This pattern layers a ように purpose clause onto a てほしい request: you name the outcome you are hoping for with ように, then say you want someone to act toward it with 〜てほしい. It makes the wish gentle and outcome-focused — you care about the result, not just the bare action.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／Verb［ない form］＋ ように ＋ Verb［て form］＋ ほしい
pitfalls: The ように clause usually takes a non-volitional verb (potential, negative, or change of state): 遅れないように, 間に合うように.
てほしい voices a want directed at another person; you cannot use it for your own actions.
The negative want is 〜ないでほしい: 心配しないでほしい ('I don't want you to worry').

examples.ja: 子どもが安心して遊べるように、公園をきれいにしてほしい。
examples.en: I want them to clean up the park so that the children can play with peace of mind.
examples.f: ｜子[こ]どもが｜安心[あんしん]して｜遊[あそ]べるように、｜公園[こうえん]をきれいにしてほしい。

examples.ja: 道に迷わないように、地図を用意してほしい。
examples.en: I'd like you to prepare a map so you won't get lost.
examples.f: ｜道[みち]に｜迷[まよ]わないように、｜地図[ちず]を｜用意[ようい]してほしい。

related.note: てほしい alone just states 'I want you to do X'; here ように adds the goal behind it.
ように言う reports telling someone to do it; ように〜てほしい voices your own wish.
Shares the purpose ように 'so that', here completed by a want.

title: ように言う
meaning: to tell / ask someone to do ~
summary: ように言う reports an instruction or request passed to someone: the ように clause holds what they were told to do, and 言う (or 頼む, 伝える) delivers it. It is the standard way to relay a command indirectly, without quoting the exact words.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／Verb［ない form］＋ ように ＋ 言う／頼む／伝える
pitfalls: For a negative instruction, use the ない form before ように: 遅れないように言う ('tell them not to be late').
This reports a command indirectly. To quote the exact words, use 「…」と言う instead.
言う can be swapped for 頼む (request), 伝える (pass on), or 注意する (warn), keeping the same ように frame.

examples.ja: 先生は学生に、毎日漢字を練習するように言いました。
examples.en: The teacher told the students to practice kanji every day.
examples.f: ｜先生[せんせい]は｜学生[がくせい]に、｜毎日[まいにち]｜漢字[かんじ]を｜練習[れんしゅう]するように｜言[い]いました。

examples.ja: 母に、遅くならないように言われた。
examples.en: I was told by my mother not to be late.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]に、｜遅[おそ]くならないように｜言[い]われた。

related.note: ように〜てほしい voices your own wish; ように言う reports an instruction given to someone.
ように祈る hopes for an outcome; ように言う relays a command.
Same ように frame, here filled by a request rather than a plain purpose.

title: ように祈る
meaning: to pray / hope that ~ comes true
summary: ように祈る expresses a hope or prayer that something will come about. The ように clause names the wished-for outcome — usually something outside your control — and 祈る ('pray') or 願う ('wish') voices the hope. It is common in well-wishes and set phrases.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］／Verb［ない form］＋ ように ＋ 祈る／願う
治るように／成功するように［often a potential or change-of-state verb］
pitfalls: The wished-for verb is non-volitional — a state or event you cannot force: 合格できるように祈る, not a plain action you would just do yourself.
In spoken well-wishes the 祈る is often dropped: 早くよくなりますように ('hope you get well soon').
ますように (polite stem ＋ ように) is the common set shape for a heartfelt wish.

examples.ja: 家族がずっと健康でいられるように祈っています。
examples.en: I'm praying that my family can stay healthy forever.
examples.f: ｜家族[かぞく]がずっと｜健康[けんこう]でいられるように｜祈[いの]っています。

examples.ja: 明日の試合で勝てるように願っている。
examples.en: I'm hoping we can win tomorrow's match.
examples.f: ｜明日[あした]の｜試合[しあい]で｜勝[か]てるように｜願[ねが]っている。

related.note: ように言う relays a command to someone; ように祈る voices a personal hope.
Same ように frame, here filled by a wished-for result rather than a plain purpose.

title: ようにする
meaning: to make sure to; to make an effort to
summary: ようにする says you deliberately arrange your behavior so a certain thing happens (or does not). It expresses making an effort or keeping a conscious habit: 毎日運動するようにする = 'make a point of exercising daily'. With ている (ようにしている) it stresses an ongoing habit you keep up.
structure: Verb［ない form］＋ ようにする
pitfalls: ようにする is a conscious effort you make; ようになる is a change that happens on its own. 早起きするようにする (I make myself get up early) vs 早起きするようになった (I've come to get up early).
For a firm one-time decision, ことにする fits better; ようにする leans toward ongoing effort or habit.
The ている form ようにしている marks a habit you are keeping up, not a single act.

examples.ja: 健康のために、甘い物を食べすぎないようにしています。
examples.en: For my health, I try not to eat too many sweets.
examples.f: ｜健康[けんこう]のために、｜甘[あま]い｜物[もの]を｜食[た]べすぎないようにしています。

examples.ja: 約束の時間には遅れないようにします。
examples.en: I'll make sure not to be late for our appointment.
examples.f: ｜約束[やくそく]の｜時間[じかん]には｜遅[おく]れないようにします。

related.note: ようになる is the change coming about on its own; ようにする is the effort you make.
ことにする is a firm decision to do something; ようにする is ongoing effort or habit.
The same purpose ように, here completed by する into a personal effort.

title: ようになる
meaning: to come to ~; to reach the point where
summary: ようになる describes a change over time — you reach a state or ability you did not have before. It pairs naturally with potential verbs (話せるようになる = 'become able to speak') and marks arriving at a new normal. The negative なくなる shows losing a habit or ability.
structure: Verb［ない form → なくなる, negative］
pitfalls: For 'stopped doing / can no longer', use なくなる, not ないようになる: 食べなくなった rather than 食べないようになった.
ようになる is a change that unfolds; ようにする is a conscious effort. 泳げるようになった (came to be able to swim) vs 泳ぐようにする (make a point of swimming).
ようになる highlights a gradual shift, so it pairs especially well with potential verbs.

examples.ja: 練習して、自転車に乗れるようになりました。
examples.en: After practicing, I became able to ride a bicycle.
examples.f: ｜練習[れんしゅう]して、｜自転車[じてんしゃ]に｜乗[の]れるようになりました。

examples.ja: 最近、からい料理も食べられるようになった。
examples.en: Lately I've become able to eat spicy food too.
examples.f: ｜最近[さいきん]、からい｜料理[りょうり]も｜食[た]べられるようになった。

related.note: ようにする is deliberate effort; ようになる is the change itself coming about.
ことになる is a decision or arrangement being settled; ようになる is a gradual change in ability or habit.
Potential verbs pair with ようになる to say you've become able to do something.

title: 予定だ
meaning: be scheduled to; plan to (an arranged plan)
summary: 予定だ marks something as a set, on-the-calendar plan — a schedule already arranged rather than a whim. Verbs attach in the dictionary form (行く予定だ) and nouns take の (旅行の予定だ). It is more concrete and official-sounding than つもり.
pitfalls: 予定だ is an arranged, scheduled plan; つもり is a personal intention. A booked trip is 予定, a private resolve is つもり.
Nouns take の before 予定: 旅行の予定です.
For a plan that fell through, 予定だった means 'was supposed to (but…)'.

examples.ja: 来月、京都へ旅行する予定です。
examples.en: I'm scheduled to travel to Kyoto next month.
examples.f: ｜来月[らいげつ]、｜京都[きょうと]へ｜旅行[りょこう]する｜予定[よてい]です。

examples.ja: 会議は三時から始まる予定です。
examples.en: The meeting is scheduled to start at three.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜三[さん]｜時[じ]から｜始[はじ]まる｜予定[よてい]です。

synonyms.note: つもりだ is a personal intention rather than a fixed, arranged schedule.

related.note: ようと思う is 'I think I'll', looser than a set 予定.

title: より
summary: より marks the standard you compare against — the 'than X' in a comparison. It attaches right after the noun used as the yardstick: 去年より暑い = 'hotter than last year'. The thing that comes out higher is usually marked with は or のほうが.
structure: A ＋ は ＋ B ＋ より ＋ adjective
pitfalls: より comes right after the standard being beaten: 電車は車より速い, so 車より sits next to 速い.
To pick the top out of three or more, use 一番, not より (which compares two things).
This より (comparison) is different from the formal より meaning 'from'.

examples.ja: 今日は昨日より涼しいです。
examples.en: Today is cooler than yesterday.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜昨日[きのう]より｜涼[すず]しいです。

examples.ja: 電車で行くほうが車より速いです。
examples.en: Going by train is faster than by car.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]で｜行[い]くほうが｜車[くるま]より｜速[はや]いです。

related.note: より〜のほうが is the fuller 'B is more ~ than A' frame built on this より.
一番 picks the single best of three or more; より compares just two things.
の中で names the group; pair it with 一番, not より, for the outright top.

title: らしい
meaning: apparently; it seems; I hear that
summary: らしい reports a conclusion the speaker draws from information that came from outside — something heard, read, or otherwise gathered. It is less about the speaker's own eyes and more 'from what I gather'. It attaches to plain forms; with nouns and な-adjectives it joins bare, with no の or な.
pitfalls: Nouns and な-adjectives attach bare — 学生らしい, 元気らしい — with no の or な, unlike ようだ (学生のようだ).
らしい leans on secondhand or gathered information; for a guess from what you directly see, ようだ fits better.
This hearsay らしい is a separate point from the らしい meaning 'typical of' (男らしい 'manly').

examples.ja: 天気予報によると、明日は雪が降るらしいです。
examples.en: According to the forecast, it's apparently going to snow tomorrow.
examples.f: ｜天気[てんき]｜予報[よほう]によると、｜明日[あした]は｜雪[ゆき]が｜降[ふ]るらしいです。

examples.ja: あの店のラーメンはとてもおいしいらしい。
examples.en: Apparently the ramen at that shop is really good.
examples.f: あの｜店[みせ]のラーメンはとてもおいしいらしい。

synonyms.note: そうだ (hearsay) passes on information more directly from its source; らしい filters it as 'from what I gather'.

related.note: ようだ reasons from the speaker's own observation; らしい from outside information.
Same shape, but 'typical of / befitting' rather than hearsay.
みたい is the casual 'it seems' from what you sense; らしい tilts toward secondhand info.

title: らしい
summary: This らしい is a suffix saying something has the ideal qualities of what it attaches to — 男らしい ('manly'), 子どもらしい ('fittingly childlike'), 春らしい ('spring-like'). It is praise for being a good, typical example of its kind, and it behaves like an い-adjective.
structure: らしくない／らしかった［conjugates like an い-adjective］
pitfalls: Positive nuance: 学生らしい means 'admirably student-like', not merely 'resembles a student' (which would be 学生のよう).
Don't confuse it with hearsay らしい: 彼は先生らしい can mean 'he seems to be a teacher' (hearsay) or 'he's every bit the teacher' (typical) — context decides.
Since it acts as an い-adjective, negate it as らしくない: 彼らしくない ('unlike him').

examples.ja: 今日は本当に春らしい天気ですね。
examples.en: Today's weather is really spring-like, isn't it?
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜本当[ほんとう]に｜春[はる]らしい｜天気[てんき]ですね。

examples.ja: そんなに簡単にあきらめるなんて、彼らしくないよ。
examples.en: Giving up that easily really isn't like him.
examples.f: そんなに｜簡単[かんたん]にあきらめるなんて、｜彼[かれ]らしくないよ。

synonyms.note: っぽい also adds '-ish', but tends to be plainer or slightly negative; らしい praises a fitting, ideal example.

related.note: The homophone らしい meaning 'apparently / I heard' — same shape, different job.
ように・ような draws a plain resemblance; らしい adds 'as it ideally should be'.

title: るところだ
meaning: be about to do; on the verge of doing
summary: A dictionary-form verb ＋ ところだ places you right before an action starts — you are just about to do it. ところ pins down the moment on a timeline: with the dictionary form it is 'about to', contrasting with ているところ ('in the middle of') and たところ ('just finished').
pitfalls: The form before ところ sets the timing: 食べるところ (about to eat) / 食べているところ (in the middle of eating) / 食べたところ (just ate).
This ところ is a point in time, not a physical place; a preceding これから or ちょうど often reinforces 'right about to'.
It marks the verge of an action, so use a dictionary-form verb, not a past one.

examples.ja: これから出かけるところなので、また後で電話します。
examples.en: I'm just about to head out, so I'll call again later.
examples.f: これから｜出[で]かけるところなので、また｜後[あと]で｜電話[でんわ]します。

examples.ja: ちょうど昼ご飯を作るところです。
examples.en: I'm just about to make lunch.
examples.f: ちょうど｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]を｜作[つく]るところです。

related.note: ているところ is being in the middle of the action; るところ is just before it.
たところ is having just finished; るところ is about to start.

title: れる・られる
meaning: passive: to be done (to someone or something)
summary: The passive れる・られる recasts a sentence so the receiver of an action becomes the subject. Group 1 verbs take the あ-row ＋ れる (読む → 読まれる), Group 2 take られる (食べる → 食べられる). The doer, when mentioned, is marked with に. Japanese often uses the passive to spotlight the affected person, including the 'suffering passive'.
structure: Verb Group 1: ［あ-row stem］＋ れる（読む → 読まれる）
Verb Group 2: ［stem］＋ られる（見る → 見られる）
する → される／来る → 来られる
pitfalls: The agent is marked with に: 先生にしかられた ('was scolded by the teacher').
Group 2 passive 食べられる looks identical to the potential 食べられる; only context separates 'be eaten' from 'can eat'.
Japanese has a 'suffering passive' for events that inconvenience you — 雨に降られた ('got rained on') — even from intransitive verbs.

examples.ja: 会議は来週の金曜日に開かれます。
examples.en: The meeting will be held next Friday.
examples.f: ｜会議[かいぎ]は｜来週[らいしゅう]の｜金曜日[きんようび]に｜開[ひら]かれます。

examples.ja: 電車の中で足を踏まれました。
examples.en: My foot got stepped on in the train.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]の｜中[なか]で｜足[あし]を｜踏[ふ]まれました。

related.note: Group 2 shares the られる shape but means 'can do'; context distinguishes them.
せる・させる is the causative 'make / let do'; the passive is 'be done to'.
てある also centers a result, but from a deliberate action and without naming a passive agent.

title: れる・られる
summary: The potential れる・られる says an action is possible. Group 1 verbs shift to the え-row ＋ る (書く → 書ける), Group 2 take られる (食べる → 食べられる, casually 食べれる). What is possible is usually marked with が rather than を. It is the single-word alternative to ことができる.
structure: Verb Group 1: ［え-row］＋ る（泳ぐ → 泳げる）
Verb Group 2: ［stem］＋ られる（見る → 見られる）
する → できる／来る → 来られる
pitfalls: The object of a potential verb is often marked with が, not を: 日本語が話せる.
In casual speech Group 2 drops the ら (ら抜き): 食べれる, 見れる — widespread but avoided in formal writing.
する has an irregular potential できる, not される (which is the passive).

examples.ja: この漢字が読めますか。
examples.en: Can you read this kanji?
examples.f: この｜漢字[かんじ]が｜読[よ]めますか。

examples.ja: 朝早く起きられなかったので、遅刻しました。
examples.en: I couldn't get up early in the morning, so I was late.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]｜早[はや]く｜起[お]きられなかったので、｜遅刻[ちこく]しました。

synonyms.note: ことができる expresses the same 'be able to' but is longer and a touch more formal.

ようになる pairs with the potential to say you've become able to do something.

title: んだけど・んですが
meaning: explanatory setup ＋ but; a soft lead-in
summary: This joins the explanatory んだ／んです with けど／が ('but'). It sets up background — 'the thing is…' — and then trails off into a request, question, or contrast. Often the 'but' is not really adversative; it just softens the approach: すみません、道に迷ったんですが… ('Excuse me, I've gotten lost, and…'). んですが is polite, んだけど casual.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ んだけど／んですが
な-adjective／Noun ＋ な ＋ んだけど／んですが
pitfalls: Nouns and な-adjectives need な before ん: 学生なんですが, not 学生だんですが.
The けど／が here often is not a real contrast — it is a soft hand-off into a request or question, so don't always render it as a hard 'but'.
んですが is the polite register; んだけど is casual. Match it to the situation.

examples.ja: あのう、ちょっと聞きたいことがあるんですが。
examples.en: Um, there's something I'd like to ask you...
examples.f: あのう、ちょっと｜聞[き]きたいことがあるんですが。

examples.ja: 頭が痛いんだけど、少し休んでもいい？
examples.en: I've got a headache — is it okay if I rest a little?
examples.f: ｜頭[あたま]が｜痛[いた]いんだけど、｜少[すこ]し｜休[やす]んでもいい？

related.note: んです・のです is the explanatory core this softening pattern builds on.
けど is the 'but' that here softens the lead-in rather than marking a real contrast.
